overview: The Thurgood Marshall Summer Law Internship Program (TMSLIP) is a paid summer internship for New York City public high school students interested in law. Run by the New York City Bar Association, TMSLIP places roughly 35 selected students each year with legal employers across the city, including law firms, corporations, nonprofits, and government organizations, to build a more diverse pipeline into the legal profession. The program runs annually from roughly March through August. It begins with a mandatory three-part pre-employment training in the spring, where students learn workplace skills and legal concepts before being matched with and interviewed by legal employers. The paid internship itself runs 6 to 8 weeks at full-time hours, with students paid directly by their host employer rather than by the NYC Bar Association. Students assist paralegals, manage documents and exhibits, and learn about different legal career paths. Applications open in late November and close in mid-to-late January. TMSLIP has run for more than twenty years and is one of the most established legal pipeline programs for high school students in New York City. Compensation: Stipend, hourly wage set by the host employer; the NYC Bar Association does not pay students directly.

Strong communication skills and demonstrated academic record.

overview:
The U.S. Senate Page Program is one of the most prestigious opportunities available to high school students, with pages serving since 1829. Pages are appointed by a U.S. Senator, must be 16 or 17 years old, and work as official Senate employees delivering correspondence and legislative materials within the Capitol complex while the Senate is in session. Pages also attend early morning classes at the United States Senate Page School, which is accredited by the Middle States Association of Colleges and Schools, with classes beginning around 6:15 AM and continuing until roughly an hour before the Senate convenes. After Page School, pages report to their cloakrooms and work until the Senate adjourns for the day, which can extend well past the 9 or 10 PM curfew. During fall and spring semesters, pages live in the Daniel Webster Senate Page Residence on Capitol Hill.

Semester eligibility is limited to high school juniors who are 16 or 17 years old on or before their appointment date. Summer sessions are open to rising juniors and rising seniors in the same age range. Students who are 18 may not be appointed. Pages must maintain a minimum cumulative 3.0 GPA. Only about 30 pages serve the Senate at any one time, split between the majority and minority parties.

Compensation: Stipend, based on an annual salary of $38,547. Room and board at the Daniel Webster Senate Page Residence is deducted from this stipend. Recent senator office listings differ on the monthly housing cost, some show approximately $1,380 per month, others still show an older $780 per month figure, so confirm the current cost with your sponsoring senator's office.

Students living on campus must take two in person courses or one in person plus one online course and are required to live on campus unless they live with family within commuting distance of New Haven; those under 18 living on campus follow a curfew and other residential rules while Yale undergraduates serve as residential counselors. Signature offerings include the Yale Writers' Workshop, Yale Young Writers' Workshop, the Yale Summer Session Seminar in Art History, and the English Language Institute for international students. Admission is holistic with no minimum GPA requirement, and standardized test scores (SAT, ACT, AP, IB, PSAT) are optional. 2026 tuition is $5,480 per one credit course and $10,705 for a two credit course, plus an $80 nonrefundable application fee, a $140 health insurance fee, and residential room and board of $4,380 per five week session ($8,760 for both sessions). International students face additional fees. Minors living on campus must submit five signed parental consent forms.
requirements: Current high school junior or senior (Class of 2026 or 2027), at least 16 years old by the program start date (students under 16 or current sophomores are not eligible). Required application materials: online application, high school transcript in English with at least 2.5 years of grades including fall 2025 grades, two letters of recommendation with at least one from a current teacher, valid US based health insurance card, photo ID (driver's license, passport, other government ID, or school ID), and optional standardized test scores. In person applicants must also submit immunization records after admission, and minors living on campus must submit five signed parental consent forms.
how_to_apply: Create an account and complete the online application through the MyYSS portal. Upload an unofficial high school transcript, arrange two letters of recommendation, upload a valid US health insurance card, and optionally submit standardized test scores. Select courses for credit or a signature program in the application. If admitted, pay the required deposit and administrative fee by the posted deadline, submit immunization records if attending in person or living on campus, and submit signed minor consent forms if under 18 and living on campus.

role: BrainSPORT Summer High School Research Internship
duration: ~12 weeks, part-time (16 hrs/week), June-Aug
overview:
The BrainSPORT Summer High School Research Internship is offered through the UCLA Steve Tisch BrainSPORT Concussion Program in the Department of Neurosurgery. Interns work alongside a multidisciplinary team of research scientists and clinicians led by Dr. Christopher Giza, Director of the program and Chief of Pediatric Neurology at UCLA. The team currently leads CARE4Kids, one of the largest studies of adolescents with persistent post concussion symptoms, involving neuroimaging, blood sampling, autonomic testing, and cognitive assessment.

Interns engage in a structured educational experience centered on clinical research practices, learning how patients are recruited, how research data are managed, and how study protocols are implemented in a real world clinical setting. Participants attend weekly Traumatic Brain Injury lab meetings and work alongside UCLA undergraduate and graduate medical students in the BrainSPORT program. The program runs from June through August, with a time commitment of three to four half days per week, and concludes with a final project in which interns present on a research topic of their choice.
requirements: Open to high school students, especially those interested in continuing into the academic year and potentially mentoring future interns. No prior research experience is required.
how_to_apply: Apply online via the Google Form linked on the BrainSPORT training page. Applications for the summer cycle are due April 1, with applicants typically notified about three weeks later.
ApplicationChecklist: Complete online Google Form application|Submit by April 1 deadline|Await notification (about 3 weeks)

role: Horizon Academic Research Program (HARP) - Virtual Research Seminars and Labs
deadline: Rolling admissions with periodic cohort deadlines. duration: Seminars: 10 to 12 weeks, summer only. Labs: 16 weeks, year round.
overview: Horizon Academic Research Program (HARP) is a selective, purely online research program founded in 2016 by Columbia University researchers. High school students work with professors and PhD or postdoctoral scholars from universities including Harvard, MIT, Dartmouth, Cambridge, and Oxford to produce an original research paper. Horizon offers two formats: Professor Seminar Courses, small group classes of 3 to 6 students with a professor, offered only in summer over 10 to 12 weeks; and 1-1 PhD Labs Courses, individualized mentorship with a PhD or postdoc scholar, offered year round over 12 to 16 weeks. Topics span computer science, economics, neuroscience, psychology, history, physics, chemistry, political science, and more, drawn from a list of over 300 pre-approved sub-topics. Program acceptance rate is 26 percent. Average admitted student GPA is 3.93 unweighted and median SAT is 1500. Tuition is 6450 dollars for both tracks, with need based financial aid available for households earning under 75000 dollars a year.
requirements: Enrolled in grades 9 to 12; most accepted students are in 10th or 11th grade. Minimum unweighted GPA of about 3.67, though average admitted student GPA is 3.93. Demonstrated interest or achievement in the chosen subject; prior research experience is not required. Reliable computer, internet, and webcam for weekly Zoom sessions. Able to commit 8 to 10 hours a week for 10 to 16 weeks depending on track. Open to US and international students. Some courses carry specific prerequisites: Protein Biophysics requires AP Chemistry, Theoretical Math and Knot Theory requires AP Calculus AB or BC, Fluid Dynamics and Physics requires one year of calculus and one year of physics, and Applications of Machine Learning requires at least 6 months of coding experience.
how_to_apply: Apply online through the application form linked at horizoninspires.com, selecting 3 to 5 pre-approved research sub-topics from more than 300 options. Shortlisted applicants complete a 30 minute virtual interview within 3 to 5 days of applying. Final admission decisions are issued within 7 days of the interview. Indicate need for financial aid in the application if household income is under 75000 dollars. Tuition of 6450 dollars is due upon acceptance for both Seminars and Labs tracks.
ApplicationChecklist: Apply online (pick 3-5 topics)|30-min interview if shortlisted|Decision within 7 days|Indicate financial aid need|Pay $6,450 tuition (aid available)

role: ámaxa Cohorts - Remote Leadership Program for High School Students
deadline: Fall cohort application deadline is August 31, 2026 (exact date shown on the live Airtable application form); Amaxa runs multiple cohorts per year with a new deadline each cycle
duration: 3 months (about 1 hr/week team meeting; 3-5 hrs/week total including project work)
overview: Amaxa Cohorts is a fully remote leadership and volunteer program for high school students ages 14-18 from anywhere in the world. Applicants submit a short application and complete a required interview, then are matched with a small team of global peers and a trained coach to deliver a real project for one of amaxa's 8 partner nonprofits or original initiatives. Current projects include providing solar lights for grandmothers in Uganda through Nyaka School, supporting Palestinian students through the Isnad Community Education Center, sponsoring Liberian students' education, planting and tracking trees through the Global Forest Initiative, a Mental Health First Aid peer education initiative, an LGBTQ+ in the Arts equality initiative, a women's literacy project called Karina's Library, and crisis support for families through Gaza Champions. Teams meet remotely about one hour per week with their coach, plus additional project work between meetings, for a total of roughly 3-5 hours per week over the 3 month cohort. Amaxa runs multiple cohorts per year. Participation carries an annual fee of $150, though full and partial scholarships are available for students in need, and the organization states cost is not intended to be a barrier. More than 120 students from over 52 countries have completed the program to date.
requirements: High school student, age 14-18, from anywhere in the world. Reliable internet access and a WhatsApp capable phone number, required for the application. Willingness to commit to a specific nonprofit partner project for the full 3 month cohort. Ability to meet remotely with a small global team and coach for about 1 hour per week, plus additional project work, totaling roughly 3-5 hours per week. Completion of a short application and a required interview before being matched to a team. $150 annual program fee, though full and partial scholarships are available on request.
how_to_apply: 1. Visit amaxaimpact.org/programs/cohorts and click Apply Now, which links to amaxa's Airtable application form. 2. Submit the application before the fall cohort deadline (August 31, 2026), including name, country, WhatsApp number, age, email, and ranked project interests. 3. Complete a required interview (held September 1-7 for the fall cohort) to discuss project fit, interests, and availability. 4. Get matched to a team of global peers and a coach based on interests and schedule. 5. Pay the $150 annual fee, or request a full or partial scholarship if cost is a barrier. 6. Begin the cohort (fall 2026 cohort starts September 15, 2026) and meet remotely about 1 hour per week for 3 months.

overview: The ThinkNeuro Science Research Internship Program (SRIP) is a 10 week, fully remote, project based research and certification program run by ThinkNeuro, LLC, based in Sacramento, California. SRIP welcomes high school, undergraduate, and post baccalaureate students from the United States and abroad with no prior research or coding experience required. The program offers three tracks: Neuroscience Bibliometrics (NSB), where students learn R programming, data visualization, and bibliometric analysis of research trends in neuroscience, medicine, and public health; Computer and Software Engineering (CSE), where students learn Git, build a GitHub portfolio, and ship a team based software project; and Business Data Analytics (BDA), which analyzes economic datasets using Python and is scheduled to launch in Spring 2027. Each track pairs a preparatory academy with a project based research or engineering experience and ends in a final symposium judged by faculty, physicians, and engineers from institutions including Harvard Engineering, Stanford Medicine, USC, OpenAI, Google, and Duolingo. Intensive Track students commit roughly 5 to 10 hours per week. requirements: Applicants must be a current high school, undergraduate, or post baccalaureate student; no prior research or coding experience is required, and international students are welcome. Interns are paid to attend biweekly job readiness workshops during school-year or summer sessions.

Interns work 20 hours a week alongside a City employee mentor and explore careers in architecture, business, engineering, and science. overview:
Cornell Urban Research to Action Youth (CURTA-Y) is a participatory research program of the Just Places Lab in Cornell's College of Architecture, Art, and Planning. It connects Cornell University students with high school students in the Binghamton and Vestal tri-city region of New York to identify opportunities for a more circular and sustainable built environment in their community.

Working as co-researchers, high school students use Photovoice, community mapping, and media making such as zines and videography to study circularity and reuse, learn to estimate greenhouse gas emissions from buildings and materials, and present proposals to local policymakers and community members. Along the way they build research, planning, and communication skills and explore careers in city and regional planning, historic preservation, architecture, public policy, and the building trades. The program runs each fall, is unpaid, and recruits participants through partner high schools in the Binghamton and Vestal area.

overview:
Urban Alliance is a nonprofit that connects under-resourced high school students with paid, year-long internships at partner employers in corporations, nonprofits, and government agencies in Baltimore, Chicago, Detroit, and the Greater Washington D.C. region. The flagship High School Internship Program is designed for rising high school seniors: students typically join as juniors through Urban Alliance's related 11th Grade Workforce Readiness Program, which builds career exposure and skills before they begin the paid internship as seniors. Interns are placed in fields such as technology, finance, healthcare, communications, marketing, and public policy while receiving mentorship, professional development training, and support with college and career planning from a dedicated Internship Program Lead and a one on one workplace mentor.

Interns work part time during the school year, Monday through Thursday for up to 12 hours per week, and full time during the summer, Monday through Thursday for up to 32 hours per week, for a total of up to 500 paid hours at minimum wage or higher. Since 1996, Urban Alliance has partnered with more than 500 businesses and 100 schools to provide over 6,000 young people with paid internships. According to the organization, 100 percent of Urban Alliance students graduate from high school and more than 90 percent are accepted to college. Compensation: paid, an hourly wage at or above the local minimum wage.
requirements: Must be a high school student on track to graduate, typically applying as a junior to begin the paid internship as a senior. School counselor and parent or guardian consent required.

overview: Algoverse is a fully remote 12 week AI research program pairing students and professionals with mentors from labs including OpenAI, Meta FAIR, Google DeepMind, Stanford, and CMU. Teams of 3 to 4 students work with a dedicated mentor on original research, aiming to publish at top AI conferences and workshops such as NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, ACL, and EMNLP. Each cohort involves two weekly meetings, optional office hours, and roughly 5 to 10 hours per week of work, with cohorts starting on a rolling basis throughout the year. Algoverse reports that 68 to 73 percent of its research teams have had work accepted at major AI conference workshops across recent cohorts, and that 311 students have been accepted to NeurIPS conferences and workshops to date. The program is open to high school students, undergraduate students, and industry professionals worldwide; Python programming experience is required. The program fee is 3,325 dollars, which covers computational resources, with need based and merit based financial aid available (families with annual income under 70,000 dollars are given priority, and the program has granted 1.2 million dollars in financial aid to date). Applications take about 5 minutes and are reviewed on a rolling basis.

Open to high school students, undergraduate students, and industry professionals worldwide
Python programming experience required
Strong technical signal such as projects, coursework, or competition results
Genuine interest in AI research
Program fee of 3,325 dollars; need based and merit based financial aid available
how_to_apply: Visit algoverseairesearch.org/apply and complete the 5 minute application sharing your background and technical experience, then choose a start date from an open cohort. Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis; if admitted you begin the mentored 12 week research program.

overview:
The Guide, Engage, Mobilize (GEM) High School Internship Program is run by the Idaho State Historical Society for Idaho high school students interested in history and museum work. GEM interns get a behind the scenes look at the Idaho State Museum while working alongside historians, curators, and designers on research, exhibit design, and event coordination. The program includes required biweekly Tuesday meetings from 4pm to 7pm at the museum, tours of the Old Idaho Penitentiary and the State Capitol Building, and at least three volunteer shifts at museum events and Community Days. Interns curate a poster exhibition and help plan a Teen Takeover event for other teens.

A select number of applicants will be invited to group interviews at the Idaho State Museum on October 6, 7, or 8, 2026. Interns receive a 500 dollar stipend split into two payments, typically in December and June. Based on the prior cycle, the program is expected to run from November through the following June with meetings every other Tuesday.

Able to attend required biweekly Tuesday meetings from 4pm to 7pm at the Idaho State Museum in Boise. Able to complete at least 4 volunteer shifts during Family Second Saturdays, camps, and community days.

overview: SYEP Foundations is the entry-level track of the Learn and Earn program within the City of Seattle's Youth Employment Program (SYEP), run by the Human Services Department. It is open to people ages 16 to 24 at the start of the program who are new to the workforce, so it is not limited to current high schoolers. Sessions run weekly for about two hours over six months and are hybrid: most workshops are held virtually over Microsoft Teams, with several required in-person sessions, a field trip, and a capstone celebration held in Downtown Seattle. Topics include orientation and goal setting, team bonding, career exploration, a young professionals panel, wellness strategies, and financial literacy. Participants who attend the required sessions and complete assignments in each module can earn up to $325 per module, paid to those with a valid Social Security Number or ITIN. Eligibility also requires living within Seattle city limits or attending a Seattle public school or Seattle college, and a household income at or below 80% of the Area Median Income. The 2025-2026 cycle took applications from September 15 to October 15, 2025, with workshops running from October 15, 2025 to March 5, 2026.
requirements: Be 16 to 24 years old at the start of the program. Live within Seattle city limits or attend a Seattle Public School, North Seattle College, South Seattle College, or Seattle Central College. Live in a household with income at or below 80% of the Area Median Income. Have not previously completed SYEP Foundations or SYEP Learn and Earn programming. Be willing to attend weekly sessions for six months, both virtual and in-person. A valid Social Security Number or ITIN is required to receive the stipend, though not required to participate.
how_to_apply: Create an account and submit an application through the SYEP Youth Portal at youthconnect.powerappsportals.us during the annual application window (mid-September to mid-October). Submit required eligibility documentation for age, residency, and income. SYEP staff review applications on a rolling basis and offer placements based on availability. If placed, attend a semi-formal intake or placement interview, then attend weekly two-hour sessions for six months, mostly virtual with some required in-person sessions in Downtown Seattle.

overview:
The Bronx Museum of the Arts, the only major art museum in the Bronx, offers two paid internship programs for New York City high school students ages 14 to 19: Teen Council and Teen Summer. Twelve students are accepted into each cycle. Teen Council runs in two four month sessions each year, one in the fall and one in the spring, with participants meeting twice a week after school at the museum to discuss issues affecting young people today, create art around those issues, meet and interview contemporary artists, curate exhibitions, and collaborate on a zine. The Fall 2025 session ran late October 2025 through mid February 2026 and the Spring 2026 session ran early March through mid June 2026, both meeting Mondays and Wednesdays from 4:30 to 6:30 pm; the Fall 2026 application window had not yet been posted as of this verification, though based on the Fall 2025 pattern the deadline is expected in late September.

Teen Summer is a four week paid program held during the New York City public school summer break, meeting three afternoons a week at the museum to explore art, community, and the role of museums, culminating in a curated exhibition drawn from the museum's permanent collection. The 2026 Teen Summer application ran from May 22 through July 5, 2026, with the program meeting Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays from 1 to 5 pm in late July through mid August 2026. That cycle has already concluded as of this verification, and the 2027 window has not yet been posted. Students are paid a stipend for their participation in both programs and may take part in both Teen Council and Teen Summer in the same year.
requirements: Currently enrolled in a New York City high school, grades 9 through 12, ages 14 to 19, or enrolled in a New York State High School Equivalency Diploma Program. Interest in contemporary art, visual media, community storytelling, or exhibition curation. Teen Council applicants must be able to commit to twice weekly after school meetings for a four month session. Teen Summer applicants must be available three afternoons a week for four weeks during the summer. No prior art or museum experience is required for either program.
how_to_apply: Visit bronxmuseum.org/learn/teens for current program information. Choose the program that fits your schedule, Teen Council or Teen Summer. Watch the museum's events page for the application window to open; Teen Council typically opens about a month before its deadline and Teen Summer opens in May. Complete the online application through the linked Wufoo form during the open window. Email education@bronxmuseum.org with any questions.
ApplicationChecklist: Choose Teen Council or Teen Summer|Watch for application window to open|Apply online via Wufoo form|Email education@bronxmuseum.org w/ Qs|Await selection notice

overview: Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL), a U.S. Department of Energy national laboratory in northern New Mexico, offers paid internships to New Mexico high school seniors through its High School Internship Program. Interns work directly with LANL scientists and engineers on projects spanning physics, chemistry, biology, computer science, engineering, business, and administrative fields. Internship start dates and hours are determined by the assigned mentor. Students who are second-semester juniors may apply for the Fall hiring cycle, but must have senior status when the internship begins. There are three hiring periods per year with deadlines of September 30 (Fall), February 13 (Spring), and April 15 (Summer). Applications are submitted through LANL's online iRecruitment system. overview: Mystic Aquarium in Mystic, CT offers a range of unpaid internships across multiple departments: Animal Rescue Program (sea turtle and marine mammal rehabilitation), Research (marine animal health, husbandry, and ecology), Environmental Quality Lab (water quality testing), Education & Conservation (teaching and curriculum support), and several animal husbandry tracks (California sea lions, fish & invertebrates, penguins, and pinnipeds/beluga whales). | Requirements vary significantly by track. Most husbandry tracks (Fish & Invertebrates, Penguins, Pinnipeds/Beluga) require 50-lb lift capacity and passing a swim test (100-yd swim under 5 min, tread water 10 min, deploy a flotation device). The California Sea Lion track has a harder swim test: 200m continuous swim under 6 minutes, tread water 10 minutes, 50-ft underwater swim, and 50-ft tired swimmer tow. Education & Conservation has a flexible schedule with no swim test or driver's license required and may qualify for college credit. | All internships are unpaid and housing is not provided. Application deadlines: Spring = September 30, Summer = January 31, Fall = May 31.

overview: The Chicago Zoological Society (CZS), operator of Brookfield Zoo Chicago, offers the King Conservation Science Scholars program, a year-round program for high school students in grades 9 to 12, ages approximately 14 to 18, who want to explore conservation, zoology, and environmental science. New cohorts are onboarded each May and November. Scholars take part in interactive workshops, immersive experiences, and public engagement opportunities at Brookfield Zoo and in the community, covering topics such as sociology and psychology, art and media, communication and marketing, college and career prep, natural science, and community engagement. The program uses a one time application in which students share their interest in the program, recent accomplishments, and college and career aspirations. Letters of recommendation are not required but welcome. Applications open twice a year, March 1 to April 1 for grades 9 to 11 only, and September 1 to October 1 for grades 9 to 12. Regular and consistent participants can access scholarships, travel experiences, seasonal job opportunities, and specialty certifications. The program itself is free to join. Compensation is unpaid, though long term participants may be considered for paid seasonal jobs at the Zoo.
requirements: High school student in grades 9 to 12, approximately ages 14 to 18. Spring applicants, March 1 to April 1, must be in grades 9 to 11, grade 12 students are not accepted in spring since they graduate before summer programming begins. Fall applicants, September 1 to October 1, can be in grades 9 to 12. Applicants and a parent or guardian must attend an onboarding session in May or November. Scholars must complete a minimum number of engagement hours each year and a capstone project. No prior conservation experience is required and no letters of recommendation are required, though they are welcome.
how_to_apply: Visit brookfieldzoo.org/education/king-scholars for the current application. Applications open March 1 to April 1 for the spring cycle and September 1 to October 1 for the fall cycle. Complete the one time online application describing your interest in the program, recent accomplishments, and college and career goals. Contact Brookfield Zoo Chicago Education at info@brookfieldzoo.org with questions.

overview:
The Science Matters Research Internship (SMRI) is a biomedical research internship run by Columbia University for New York City high school students enrolled in the Minds Matter NYC program. It is affiliated with the Graduate School of Arts and Sciences at Columbia University Medical Center and with Women in Science at Columbia, and it aims to foster interest and confidence in science among students who are curious about careers in STEM fields.

Selected juniors first attend a rigorous Bio-Boot Camp in the fall, with lectures from Columbia graduate students and postdoctoral researchers and an introductory laboratory tutorial. They then complete a roughly three month research internship in the spring, paired with a pre or postdoctoral mentor in a Columbia laboratory and spending at least six hours per week in the lab, culminating in a final presentation. The program is unpaid, applications are accepted each fall and are due in early October, and admission is moderately selective among Minds Matter NYC juniors.
requirements: Applicants must be Minds Matter NYC students beginning their junior year and interested in a STEM career. Enrollment in prior or current science courses is not required. Parental consent is mandatory and students must have health insurance to intern in a Columbia laboratory. Students must attend all fall Bio-Boot Camp lectures and spend at least six hours per week in the lab during the spring semester.
how_to_apply: Applications open in the fall through Minds Matter NYC and are due in early October. Attend the SMRI information session during the Minds Matter summer sessions, complete the SMRI application with personal and academic information, activities, and short essays, and submit two letters of recommendation. Interviews are held in October at a Minds Matter Saturday session.
ApplicationChecklist: Be a Minds Matter NYC junior|Complete app at bit.ly/CSMRI_app|Two rec letters by early October|Interview at Saturday session

overview: The NSA High School Work Study Program (HSWS) lets high school juniors apply in the fall for a paid, part time position that runs during senior year at an NSA facility. Students work in tracks such as business or office support, computer support, engineering, manufacturing, construction, Chinese language, or intelligence analysis aide roles while continuing to attend high school classes part time. The program operates at multiple NSA locations nationwide, including Fort Meade, Maryland, Denver, Colorado, Fort Gordon, Georgia, San Antonio, Texas, sites in Utah, and Hawaii, and students apply through the site nearest their home.
requirements: Applicants must be current high school juniors (11th grade), U.S. citizens, at least 16 years old by December 31 of the application year, and have an unweighted GPA of 2.5 or higher. Students must be enrolled in relevant coursework, such as business, computer, engineering, manufacturing, construction, or Chinese language courses, and must plan to participate in their school's Work Experience Program during senior year. Reliable transportation to the NSA worksite is required, and continued employment depends on passing a security background investigation and polygraph.
how_to_apply: Students should first contact their high school's Work Experience Coordinator to confirm participation and learn any school specific steps. The application requires a Student Evaluation form requested from the local HSWS program email, an official transcript showing junior year courses in progress, and a resume listing relevant coursework and the desired position track. These materials are emailed to the NSA site's HSWS office, with the exact address varying by location, for example HSWS@uwe.nsa.gov for the Fort Meade, Maryland site. The online application must be submitted by 11:59 PM on September 30 each year, and incomplete or late packets are not considered.

overview: Pioneer Academics is a fully online, accredited provider of two research programs for high school students in grades 9-12, open to students worldwide. The Pioneer Research Institute (PRI) is billed as the world's only fully accredited online research program for high schoolers. Students begin with group research seminars and a literature review, then work one on one with a college professor across one of 30 possible research areas, from Biology and Computer Science to History, Psychology, and Music Theory, to produce an original undergraduate level paper. Students who earn a C- or higher receive 4 transferable college credits through Oberlin College and Conservatory. PRI tuition is $7,465, plus up to a 2 percent lab fee for certain science concentrations. The Global Problem-Solving Institute (GPSI) is a 12 week virtual, interdisciplinary innovation lab where students work with a panel of professors from universities such as Stanford, Northwestern, Notre Dame, Davidson, and UNC Chapel Hill to tackle practical challenges in AI ethics, chronic disease, food and climate systems, clean water access, and entrepreneurship. GPSI graduates earn 2 college credits from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill for a grade of C- or higher; tuition is $3,100. Both programs offer need based scholarships (over $11 million granted since 2014) and enroll students from more than 90 countries.
requirements: PRI: highly selective, multi stage application. Requires short essays, an unofficial transcript, an official transcript, a counselor or teacher evaluation, a video interview, and a proctored timed writing test. Admitted PRI scholars average a 3.9 unweighted GPA and roughly 1480-1529 SAT, which is test optional. GPSI: unweighted GPA of 3.3 or higher, with no more than one C grade across the full high school transcript, plus English proficiency shown through instruction in English, qualifying coursework grades, or a test score (TOEFL 95+, IELTS 7.0+, SAT Evidence-Based Reading and Writing 600+, ACT English/Reading subscores 28+, or AP English Language and Composition 3+). GPSI also requires an official transcript and a teacher evaluation.
how_to_apply: 1. Attend a free online info session, strongly recommended. 2. Submit the online application with short essays and an unofficial transcript; standardized test scores are optional. 3. Have your school send an official transcript and counselor or teacher evaluation, ideally within 2 weeks of applying. 4. If advanced, complete a video interview and a proctored timed writing test for PRI; GPSI applicants are evaluated on application materials and a teacher evaluation without this interview step. 5. Await the holistic admissions decision, which typically takes 6-8 weeks, and apply for need based financial aid if eligible.
ApplicationChecklist: Attend a free Pioneer info session|Submit essays and unofficial transcript|Request counselor send official docs|Complete interview and timed writing|Apply for need-based scholarship

overview:
The ORNL Next Generation STEM Internship Program, NGSI, places rising high school juniors and seniors, and recent graduates who have not yet started college, into STEM and STEM related projects with research and professional staff at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, the U.S. Department of Energy's largest multiprogram science and energy laboratory. NGSI covers disciplines including business, chemistry and materials science, communications and graphics design, computer and data science, earth and geosciences, engineering, environmental and marine science, life health and medical sciences, mathematics and statistics, physics, and social and behavioral sciences, so placements vary widely by mentor and project.

NGSI runs multiple cycles each year. The Spring 2027 cycle is 16 to 17 weeks, conducted virtually and part time, running from January 26 to May 15 or 22, 2027, with a stipend of 125 dollars per week; applications for this cycle are open now through October 21, 2026. Separate Summer and Fall cycles are also offered, with Summer appointments typically running 7 to 10 weeks full time onsite in Oak Ridge, Tennessee at a higher stipend rate. Eligible counties are Anderson, Blount, Campbell, Knox, Loudon, McMinn, Monroe, Morgan, Roane, and Sevier in East Tennessee. Applicants must be U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents, at least 16 years old by the appointment start date, in good standing at an accredited high school or home school program, and have a minimum GPA of 3.0 out of 4.0. All applications are submitted through Zintellect and require one recommendation from a STEM teacher, principal, or home school curriculum coordinator.

overview:
Virginia Aerospace Science and Technology Scholars (VASTS) is a free, interactive STEM program for Virginia high school juniors and seniors, run by the Virginia Space Grant Consortium in partnership with NASA Langley Research Center, the Commonwealth of Virginia, and industry sponsors.

The program features an online STEM learning experience consisting of six web-based modules beginning in late November, with modules due every two weeks through spring (more time may be given for the first two modules depending on holiday dates). Students provide solutions to real-world questions, develop and present failure analysis reports on prior space exploration attempts, design a new crew exploration vehicle, and take part in discussion forums with other scholars to hone their technical writing skills.

Based on performance in the online coursework, the top 180 performing scholars statewide are selected to attend a six-day residential Summer Academy at NASA Langley, where students design a crewed mission to Mars, tour NASA Langley facilities, and receive mentoring from NASA engineers, scientists, and technologists. Scholars selected for the Summer Academy are provided transportation, housing at Christopher Newport University, and meals. VASTS is entirely free, and students may also earn dual enrollment college credit.

Compensation: Free, no cost and no stipend.
requirements: Currently a high school junior or senior in a Virginia school. Virginia resident. Minimum 2.7 GPA. Interest in or aptitude for math, science, engineering, or technology. A teacher recommendation and a school counselor letter confirming Virginia high school enrollment, grade level, and GPA, both submitted electronically through the online application system. Ability to complete the 6-module online curriculum from late November through spring. Available for the 6-day summer residential academy at NASA Langley in Hampton, VA if selected.

overview:
The Pre-Collegiate Enrichment Program (PEP) at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte allows highly qualified high school juniors and seniors to enroll in college credit courses at UNC Charlotte while still completing high school. The program is designed specifically for students who have exhausted all relevant course options available at their own high school, giving them access to university level coursework across the full range of subjects offered at UNC Charlotte, including science, engineering, business, computer science, the arts, and the social sciences.

To participate, students must have a minimum cumulative weighted GPA of 3.8 and test scores consistent with UNC Charlotte's first year admission ranges, though SAT/ACT submission is currently optional under the UNC system's test score waiver. Applicants submit an online application along with official transcripts, a letter of permission from their high school counselor or principal, and a non-refundable $75 application processing fee. Admitted students are responsible for their own transportation and campus parking, and tuition is charged per the university's standard cost of attendance; students seeking in-state tuition rates must separately complete the Residency Determination Service process.
requirements: Applicants must be a junior or senior in high school with a minimum cumulative weighted GPA of 3.8 and standardized test scores (SAT or ACT, currently optional under a UNC system waiver) consistent with UNC Charlotte's first year admission ranges. Students must have exhausted all related course options available at their current high school in the subject area they wish to study. A letter of permission from the student's high school counselor or principal is required, along with official high school transcripts and payment of a non-refundable $75 application processing fee. Students are responsible for their own transportation to campus and for paying for on campus parking.
how_to_apply: Students apply online through UNC Charlotte's admissions application portal at future49er.charlotte.edu/apply. The application requires official transcripts, SAT/ACT scores if submitted, a letter of permission from a high school counselor or principal, and the $75 non-refundable application fee. Application deadlines are term specific: November 15 for Spring term, May 1 for Summer Full/First Half term, June 1 for Summer Second Half term, and July 1 for Fall semester. Once all materials are received, UNC Charlotte reviews the file and mails a decision letter to the applicant's home address, and admitted students then receive instructions for academic advising and course registration.

overview:
Whiting Internships in Science and Engineering (WISE) is a paid research internship run by the Johns Hopkins Center for Educational Outreach that pairs Baltimore City public high school students one on one with Johns Hopkins Engineering graduate student, postdoc, and faculty mentors. 

Students carry out a mentored research project and meet with their mentor to take lectures and discuss research progress, gaining hands on lab experience while building a supportive network. Created about a decade ago to encourage women in STEM, the program is now co ed and aims to increase the diversity of students pursuing science and engineering in college. The summer term includes about 80 research hours, while the spring term includes about 90 hours.
requirements: Open to students who attend a Baltimore City public high school and have A and B grades in all high school math and science classes. Students must be available for 3 hours a day, two days a week for 15 weeks in the fall or spring term, or 4 to 5 hours every weekday for 4 weeks in the summer, and must provide their own transportation to and from campus.

overview: The Lumiere Research Scholar Program pairs high school students with PhD-level researchers from top universities for one-on-one independent research projects. Students work 1-on-1 with a PhD mentor across 9 sessions over 12 weeks, producing an independent research paper in their chosen subject area. Research areas span STEM (computer science, data science, medicine, engineering, astrophysics, math), social sciences (economics, psychology, business, sociology, law), and humanities (history, philosophy, etc.). Lumiere was founded by researchers affiliated with Harvard and Oxford. Mentors come from a range of top global universities. The program has Spring, Summer, Fall, and Winter sessions with rolling admissions. Upon successful completion, students are eligible to receive 3 post-baccalaureate credits and a digital transcript from UC San Diego (UCSD) Extended Studies. A non-profit wing (Lumiere Research Inclusion Foundation) offers the Breakthrough Scholar Program - a fully funded equivalent for students demonstrating outstanding academic ability and financial need (households typically earning under $50,000 annually for a typical family of four). The Breakthrough Scholar summer 2026 deadline was June 7, 2026. The paid program charges a fee (check lumiere-education.com for current pricing); the Breakthrough Scholar nonprofit arm is free for selected students. role: FPRI Foreign Policy Research Institute - Research Intern
deadline: Spring term: apply November 2 to November 20 (Summer and Fall application periods are currently closed)
duration: Spring term, February to April (part time)
overview:
The Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI) is a nonpartisan Philadelphia based think tank focused on US foreign policy, national security, and international relations. FPRI offers internships during Spring, Summer, and Fall terms in Research (Asia, Eurasia, or National Security), plus non-research tracks such as Operations, Development, Communications, and Editorial depending on availability. Research interns work under direct supervision of an FPRI staffer and scholar, contributing to literature reviews, data analysis, monitoring current events, and editing.

Outstanding interns can have work published on FPRI's Intern Corner and gain access to all FPRI events; summer interns attend weekly seminars with guest speakers. FPRI welcomes applicants at all stages of study, including high school students who are considered case by case, though the selection process is highly competitive and most interns are college or graduate students. Internships are offered both in person in Philadelphia and remotely. A limited number of paid stipends are available based on financial need; most internships are unpaid, though many interns use university work study funding. The Spring term (February to April) is currently the only term with an open application window, running November 2 to November 20; Summer and Fall periods are closed.
requirements: Strong research and writing skills and genuine interest in international relations or foreign policy. Applicants should specify a research area (Asia, Eurasia, National Security) or a non-research track if available (Operations, Development, Communications, Editorial). Advanced foreign language skills, data analysis experience, or study abroad or field research experience strengthen research applications. No nationality restrictions, but FPRI does not sponsor visa applications. Selection is highly competitive; high school students are considered case by case, as most interns are college or graduate students.
how_to_apply: Prepare one single PDF containing a cover letter stating which internship track you are applying for, a resume, and (for Research and Editorial applicants) a 3 to 5 page writing sample. Submit your application through FPRI's official online application form linked on fpri.org/about/internships. The Spring term application period runs November 2 to November 20 for the February to April term; Summer and Fall periods are currently closed. Applications are not reviewed on a rolling basis. You will only be contacted if selected for an interview.
ApplicationChecklist: Pick your internship track | Write cover letter naming track | Gather resume, writing sample if req. | Combine into one single PDF | Submit via FPRI form by Nov 20

overview: StandOut Connect is a remote internship and professional development program for high school students, run by StandOutSearch (founded in 2020 by University of Chicago and Chicago Booth School of Business students, with backing from UChicago's Polsky Center for Innovation). The program runs in seasonal cohorts (summer, fall, winter, and spring) and combines about five weeks of non-mandatory (but recorded) Sunday workshops on resume building, interviewing, networking, and professional software tools with a two month remote internship at one of over 500 partner companies founded by alumni of top universities, sourced through networks such as Y Combinator, Harvard Ventures, and similar university accelerators. Students can be matched into many fields, including business, finance, computer science, medicine, law, engineering, science, the environment, journalism, and the arts. The program reports admitting roughly 6 percent of applicants since 2023, and says about 80 percent of graduates receive optional return offers from their host company, though these figures are self reported by the company rather than independently audited.

Accepted students pay tuition to confirm their spot, then attend five weekend workshops on Sundays from late January through late February covering internship strategy, interviewing, professionalism, and modern workplace tools. After training, students interview with matched partner companies and complete a two month remote internship, generally running late February through late April.

overview:
The U.S. Department of Education (ED) Student Volunteer Trainee Program is an 8–10 week unpaid internship offered in three sessions per year (Summer, Fall, and Winter/Spring) for students enrolled in accredited educational institutions, including high school. Interns are placed in ED program offices in areas such as policy analysis, data analytics, human resources, communications, project management, and information technology.

The program is offered at ED offices in Washington, D.C., with remote and hybrid options available depending on the office. Interns work 20–40 hours per week during fall and spring sessions, and full-time during summer. Duration and scheduling are flexible and can be negotiated with the assigned office.

Application windows by session:
• Summer (May/June–July/August): Apply January 1 – March 31
• Fall (September–December): Apply May 1 – July 31
• Winter/Spring (January–May): Apply September 1 – November 30

All opportunities are posted on USAJOBS.gov. Questions can be directed to StudentVolunteers@ed.gov.

Eligibility:
• Be at least 16 years of age
• Enrolled at least half-time in an accredited educational institution (including high school)
• Have school permission to participate
• Enrolled in a course of study related to the work to be performed
• International applicants (lawful permanent residents, F-1/J-1 visa holders, DACA recipients) may be eligible with additional requirements

Compensation: Unpaid. Academic credit may be arranged through your school.

overview: The Basic Science Research Internship Program is run by the Institute for Fundamental Biomedical Research (IFBR) at Johns Hopkins All Children's Hospital in St. Petersburg, Florida, not the main Baltimore campus. It provides practical, mentored basic biomedical research experience for actively enrolled high school and undergraduate students working alongside IFBR faculty in areas such as metabolism, endocrinology, oncology, and orthopaedic research. Enrollment runs on a semester cycle of Fall, Spring, or Summer, and students may repeat the program in a different semester with a different mentor. The recommended training length with one supervisor is three to six months, with a minimum in-person commitment of 8 weeks. Depending on their contribution and timing, students may be eligible for co-authorship or acknowledgement in resulting scientific publications. Enrichment activities include in-person instruction from Johns Hopkins faculty on research design, methodology, analysis, and publication, plus IFBR seminars and the Johns Hopkins All Children's Seminar Series in Academia. Acceptance depends on the availability of a suitable faculty mentor, project, and funding. Applicants must submit a completed Basic Science Student Internship Application along with a transcript, resume or CV, essay, letter of recommendation, and verification of current school enrollment. A letter of recommendation from a school official, signed parental consent for students under 18, and Occupational Health clearance are also required. There is no cost for students to participate, and the program does not pay a stipend. The application deadline for the Fall 2026 cycle is Monday, August 10, 2026. Incomplete applications or those received after the deadline are not considered.

deadline: December 1

overview: MIT PRIMES is a free year-long research program run by the MIT Department of Mathematics for high school sophomores and juniors. Students are paired one-on-one or in small groups with MIT mentors, usually graduate students or postdocs, to work on original research in mathematics or computational biology (the program stopped admitting new computer science projects in 2025). There are two tracks: MIT PRIMES for students within driving distance of Greater Boston, who meet mentors in person, and PRIMES-USA for students elsewhere in the US, who meet mentors online. The program year runs in four phases: an advanced reading period from January to mid-March, an active research period from mid-March to mid-June, an independent study period over the summer, and a fall write-up period that ends with a presentation at the PRIMES conference in mid-October. Admission is highly selective and based on demonstrated mathematical ability, with USAMO/USAJMO qualification or advanced coursework viewed favorably though not required.

overview:

High school student interns at NARA work across departments including archival processing, records management, digitization, public outreach, and education programs, gaining insight into how a major federal agency manages the nation's historical and legal records. overview:
The Kimberly Querrey Summer Research Program, hosted by the Division of Pulmonary and Critical Care at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, offers a six to eight week paid research experience for rising high school seniors and undergraduate students interested in the biological sciences. Interns are paired with Northwestern faculty and work on meaningful basic or clinical research projects related to lung disease, gaining hands on research training in state of the art laboratories at the Simpson Querrey Biomedical Research Center in downtown Chicago. The experience is a full time commitment of 40 hours per week, from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday.

Beyond bench work, interns read and discuss current research articles, attend career development workshops, learn about different career paths in science and medicine, shadow a clinician, and take part in data discussions with peers. The program also includes preparation for college and graduate school applications, and it culminates with a presentation at the annual Kimberly Querrey Summer Research Symposium. Interns receive a competitive stipend but are responsible for their own housing and transportation, so many live or stay with family in the Chicago area. Established in 1999 and endowed in 2018 by Northwestern trustees Louis A. Simpson and Kimberly K. Querrey, the program was officially named for Kimberly Querrey in 2022.
requirements: All applicants must be at least 16 years old as of May 31 in the year the program takes place. High school applicants must currently be a junior at the time of application. Undergraduate applicants must be enrolled at an accredited college or university with planned and completed coursework demonstrating a serious interest in the biological sciences or a future career in medicine. overview: The CCNY College Now STEM Research Academy, run by The City College of New York, gives NYC public high school students a two part path into scientific research. Students who successfully complete the spring course may apply for a Summer 2026 research internship, running July 6 through August 6 (dates subject to change), in which 10 of the original 25 students are matched with a CUNY or CCNY faculty mentor and work in a research lab four to five days a week on an independent project. Summer participants present their research on the CCNY campus and at the New York Science Center for Research and Mentoring poster session at the American Museum of Natural History, and those who complete the full program, including the weekly seminar, workshops, and poster presentation, may be eligible for a $1,575 stipend. requirements: Applicants must be a New York City public high school 10th or 11th grader during the Spring 2026 semester. Students need a 75 or higher on the NYS English Language Arts Regents, or a 75 or higher on the NYS Living Environment or Earth Science Regents, or an 85 or higher overall grade in English or U.S. History along with a minimum overall high school GPA of 80. role: Wolfram High School Summer Research Program
deadline: Applications open in November. Early Decision deadline is January 18, with decisions by February 16. Regular Decision deadline is March 22, with decisions by April 17. Exact 2027 dates have not yet been published; based on the recurring annual pattern, similar dates are expected.
duration: About 2.5 weeks in person residential (most recently June 24 to July 11, 2026), plus an optional 2 day virtual pre program workshop before the residential session for less experienced students.
grades: Ages 14-17
overview: The Wolfram High School Summer Research Program is an intensive, project based summer research program run by Wolfram Research for motivated high school students, held in person at Bentley University in Waltham, Massachusetts. It runs for about two and a half weeks, most recently June 24 to July 11, 2026, with an optional two day virtual pre program workshop before the residential session for students with limited coding experience. Students learn the Wolfram Language and computational thinking, then work under expert mentors, including direct interaction with Stephen Wolfram, to complete an original independent research project across fields including computer science, physics, astronomy, medicine, environmental science, social science, and history. Each student produces a computational essay, an interactive research paper published on Wolfram Community, which can be submitted to STEM competitions or presented at the Wolfram Technology Conference. Students also choose a creative minor track such as music, art, writing, or dance. The program is fully residential with no remote or commuter option and costs 5,500 dollars, which covers tuition, room and board, and one year of Wolfram technology access. A 500 dollar deposit is non refundable. Need based financial aid, awarded through a need blind process, can cover up to 90 percent of program costs but does not cover the deposit or travel. Applicants must be between 14 and 17 years old, occasionally exceptional 13 year olds are considered, and international students are welcome provided they secure their own visas. Roughly 80 students are admitted each year from an applicant pool Wolfram describes as hundreds of qualified applicants.
requirements: Applicants must be high school students aged 14 to 17, rarely 13, and cannot turn 18 during the program. Prior coding or Wolfram Language experience is not required, but applicants should be motivated, independent learners with an interest in a STEM subject. International students may apply but must arrange their own visas. Because the program is fully residential and full time, students must be able to commit to living on campus for the entire two and a half weeks and cannot attend other camps or classes concurrently.
how_to_apply: Submit the online application when it opens in early November, including background information, prior STEM experience, and areas of project interest. Complete a short coding challenge assessing problem solving approach and a video interview with the Admissions Director. Submit any financial aid request at the same time as the application. Apply by the Early Decision deadline of January 18, with decisions by February 16, or the Regular Decision deadline of March 22, with decisions by April 17. Late applications are reviewed on a rolling basis, with a waitlist open until May 5. If accepted, pay the 500 dollar non refundable deposit by February 27 for Early Decision or April 26 for Regular Decision, then pay the remaining balance by May 1.
ApplicationChecklist: Submit online application|Complete coding challenge|Attend video interview|Pay deposit by deadline|Pay balance by May 1

overview: UT Southwestern's STARS Summer Research Program for Students is an eight week, non-residential program in Dallas, Texas for high school juniors with a strong interest in science. Students work full time alongside a UT Southwestern faculty investigator in a biomedical research laboratory, receive a paid stipend, and present their research results at the end of the summer. The program does not include clinical or shadowing components and is limited by available funding. Applicants with prior biomedical research experience are not eligible.
requirements: Must be currently classified as a high school junior. Must be at least 16 years old by June 1 of the program year. Must be a U.S. citizen, national, or otherwise eligible to work in the United States. Must not have prior biomedical or research related experience. role: Young Scholars Program (YSP) - Agricultural, Food & Environmental Science Internship
company: University of Georgia College of Agricultural & Environmental Sciences (UGA CAES)
deadline: The 2026 deadline was January 23, 2026 (applications opened November 3, 2025). The 2027 deadline is not posted yet; based on this pattern, expect the application to open around early November 2026 and close in late January 2027.
duration: 5 weeks (June to July)
overview: The University of Georgia Young Scholars Program (YSP) is a paid five-week summer internship for high school students interested in agricultural, food, and environmental sciences, organized by the UGA College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences (CAES). Students work 30 hours per week under the guidance of a faculty research mentor on the UGA Athens, Griffin, or Tifton campus. They attend workshops and visit agricultural operations, gaining exposure to careers in agriculture and environmental science. The program culminates in the three-day Young Scholars Pre-Collegiate Research Conference, where scholars present their research via poster session on the UGA Athens campus. YSP began at UGA Griffin in 1989 and is one of the longest-running high school agricultural science programs in the Southeast. This is a non-residential program; students must commute daily to their assigned campus.
requirements: Must have completed sophomore year of high school and be a first time participant; must be 16 years old by the program start date; must have completed one high school science course with lab and one semester of algebra; must submit two teacher recommendation letters and an official transcript; this is a non residential program, so participants arrange their own housing and transportation; must commute daily to the assigned UGA campus (Athens, Griffin, or Tifton).
how_to_apply: Visit the CAES Young Scholars page and review eligibility. Complete the online application, including a short essay, between November and January. Request two recommendation letters from science or math teachers and have them submitted through the YSP system. Upload your official transcript via the YSP Transcript Upload Form. Submit everything by the January deadline. Selected students are notified in spring and commute daily to their assigned campus for the June to July program.

deadline: January 23
duration: Summer, 6 to 7 weeks (typically early June to early August; contact UCSF Fresno for current year dates)
grades: Rising high school seniors (students in summer between junior and senior year; must reside in Fresno, Kings, Madera, Mariposa, Merced, or Tulare counties in California)
overview: The UCSF Fresno Summer Biomedical Internship Program (SBI) was established in 1988 to give high school students in the Central San Joaquin Valley a genuine biomedical research experience, the first program of its kind in the region. The program matches students, in the summer between their junior and senior year, with a UCSF Fresno faculty mentor who has an active or developing research project. Since 1988 more than 300 students have completed the program, many of whom are now in medical residencies, biomedical or biotech careers, or medical and doctoral programs. Interns work with their mentor for about 6 to 7 weeks starting in June, and also take part in field trips such as hospital tours, clinical skills workshops, Grand Rounds lectures, and informal talks with UCSF medical students and residents. There is no cost to participate, and scholarship funds may be available to help offset transportation costs.
requirements: Applicants must be a current high school junior at the time of application, at least 16 years old by June 1, 2026, and have a GPA of 3.0 or better. Students must live in Fresno, Madera, Merced, Kings, Tulare, or Mariposa County. The application requires a one page typed essay, a one page resume or CV, a current high school transcript including first semester junior year grades, and a teacher email address for a letter of recommendation. Semi-finalist candidates are interviewed, parental permission is required, and interns may not miss more than 3 working days during the program.
how_to_apply: Applications open December 19 and are due by 5 p.m. on January 23 at sjvpremed.ucsf.edu/sbi. Apply online using the Qualtrics application link posted on the program page. Submit the essay, resume, transcript, and letter of recommendation contact by the deadline. Semi-finalist candidates will be contacted for an interview. Contact UCSF Fresno at (559) 499-6423 or sbi@fresno.ucsf.edu with questions.
ApplicationChecklist: ["Apply online by Jan 23, 5 p.m.","Submit essay, resume, transcript","Provide teacher LOR contact","Semi-finalists get interview"]

overview:
The Hutton Junior Fisheries Biology Program is a paid, eight-week summer internship and mentoring program sponsored by the American Fisheries Society (AFS). Since 2001 it has paired high school students, particularly those from groups underrepresented in fisheries science, with a professional fisheries mentor located within a 30-45 minute commute of the student's home for hands-on work such as stream sampling, electrofishing, fish tagging, water quality testing, and aquatic habitat restoration.

Selected Hutton Scholars receive a $3,000 stipend paid in four installments of $750 every two weeks, contingent on submitting biweekly timesheets and mid-summer and final reports. Students work 32 to 40 hours per week over the eight-week period and provide their own transportation to the work site. The program is open to current high school juniors and seniors who are U.S., Puerto Rico, Canada, or Mexico residents; past Hutton participants are not eligible to reapply.
requirements: Open to current high school juniors and seniors (rising seniors and rising college freshmen) who are residents of the United States, Puerto Rico, Canada, or Mexico. Applicants must be at least 16 years old by the application deadline. Past Hutton Program participants are not eligible to reapply. No prerequisite coursework is required, though biology, ecology, or statistics courses are helpful.

1. Apply through the AFS Awards platform at afsawards.awardsplatform.com.
2. Submit a statement of interest and respond to two essay questions, one requiring a 1-2 minute video response.
3. Have a non-family, non-peer reference submit the Hutton Student Reference Form.
4. Upload a current high school transcript.
5. Submit all materials by the application deadline; incomplete applications are not considered.

deadline: Late January annually (2026 cycle: January 26; recommendation letters due one week later)
duration: 8 weeks, full time (40 hrs/week) in-person lab research, June 1 to July 24; 3-day orientation May 27-29; closing symposium July 24
overview:
Since 1991, Washington University's Young Scientist Program has run Summer Focus, a funded eight-week summer research internship for motivated high school juniors from the Greater St. Louis area. Each accepted Scholar is paired with a graduate student, postdoc, or lab staff mentor for hands-on biomedical research such as genetics, cancer biology, neuroscience, microbiology, ecology, or biomedical engineering, plus a separate tutor for academic support. Scholars also take two parallel courses, one on scientific writing and communication and one on college preparation, and the program ends with a closing research symposium where Scholars present their findings.

The program accepts only 15 to 18 students per year and pays a stipend for the summer. Eligibility is restricted to students who have just completed 11th grade and who are permanent residents of the Greater St. Louis metro area in Missouri or Illinois, since the internship requires full-time, in-person lab attendance and the program does not provide housing, though it does provide free monthly transit passes. Applicants submit personal and academic information, short-answer and essay responses, and two letters of recommendation, with interviews held in early March and acceptance notifications sent in April.
requirements: Must have just completed 11th grade, entering senior year. Must be a permanent resident of the Greater St. Louis metro area in Missouri or Illinois. Must be able to work in person, full time (40 hrs/week) in a WashU lab for 8 weeks, missing no more than 3 days. No prior research experience required. Two letters of recommendation required, one from a math or science teacher and one from another adult. Responsible for own transportation; free transit passes provided.
how_to_apply: Apply online via the YSP website during the application window, which opens in fall and closes in late January. Submit personal information, educational history, work experience, an academic transcript, five short-answer questions, and two short essays. Provide contact info for two recommenders. Interviews for shortlisted applicants occur in early March, with acceptance decisions announced in April.
ApplicationChecklist: Apply online, submit transcript and short essays, provide two teacher recommendations, attend interview if shortlisted
Opens: Not publicly stated; typically opens in fall
AcceptanceRate: Not publicly disclosed; accepts approximately 15-18 students per year

role: NIST Summer High School Internship Program (SHIP)
company: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
deadline: Applications generally close in the last week of January; SHIP 2026 closed Jan 26, 2026 at 11:59 PM ET
duration: 7 weeks, mid June to early August (2026 dates were June 22 to August 7).
overview: SHIP is NIST's competitive, unpaid volunteer research internship for high school juniors and seniors, held each summer at NIST's Gaithersburg, Maryland campus and its Boulder, Colorado campus. Selected students spend seven weeks working alongside NIST scientists and engineers on research in materials science, chemistry, physics, engineering, and computer science. NIST has said it may add a stipend in the future pending internal approval, but the program remains unpaid as of the most recent official information.
requirements: Applicants must be U.S. citizens who are high school juniors or seniors, or recent graduates who have not yet started college, with a minimum 3.0 GPA. Students must live within 50 miles of either the Gaithersburg, MD or Boulder, CO campus, or be able to arrange their own housing and transportation for the summer. Applicants must be available in person for the full seven consecutive weeks of the program.
how_to_apply: Apply through the online SHIP application linked from nist.gov/ship. Required materials include a brief resume listing name, email, high school, GPA, and graduation date, a copy of your transcript, a one page personal statement covering your interest in science, preferred NIST laboratory, and post graduation plans, plus contact information for two recommenders, one of whom must be a STEM teacher. A signed availability form confirming your ability to commit to the full program is also required. Recommendation letters are due a few days after the application deadline.

role: MaineHealth Institute for Research (MHIR) Summer Undergraduate Research Program - High School Senior Track
deadline: January 30 each year. The 2026 deadline was January 30, 2026 (applications now closed); selection begins in February and all applicants are notified by April 1. Exact 2027 date not yet posted but expected on the same annual cadence.
duration: 10 weeks, full-time (40 hours/week). 2026 dates were June 1-August 7, 2026.
overview: MaineHealth Institute for Research (MHIR), affiliated with Maine Medical Center and MaineHealth, offers a 10 week full-time summer research program primarily for undergraduates, with a track open to graduating high school seniors who will be at least 18 at the program start. Students work as paid MaineHealth employees in MHIR's Research Centers (Molecular Medicine, Clinical and Translational Science, Interdisciplinary Population and Health Research, and Applied Science and Technology), completing a research project and a final poster presentation. Positions are based at 81 Research Drive in Scarborough, Maine. Students arrange their own transportation and housing, though MHIR provides housing search resources. Pay is $18.00 per hour as of 2026. In 2025 the program received 382 applications and selected 24 participants (about 6%). The 2026 program ran June 1 to August 7, 2026, and its application portal is now closed.
requirements: Graduating high school senior who will be at least 18 years old at the program start (or an undergraduate through graduating senior/postbac/community college student). Minimum 3.0 GPA, though applicants with a lower GPA and an explained special circumstance may still apply. Must be eligible to work in the U.S. (does not require citizenship, but MHIR does not sponsor visas). Cannot have participated in this program in a prior year. Application requires a resume, transcript, grades in the 5 most recent science classes, a 500-word personal statement, and five short-answer responses (250 words each). Formal letters of recommendation are not required.
how_to_apply:
1. Visit mhir.org and review the Summer Undergraduate Research Program page for current details.
2. Complete the MaineHealth Employment Application online.
3. Complete the supplemental MHIR program application, including resume, transcript, personal statement, and short answers.

5. Selected candidates may be contacted for a phone or virtual interview.
6. All applicants are notified of a decision by April 1.

overview: The CCI High School Cybersecurity Internship Program connects rising high school seniors and rising first-year college students who are at least 17 years old with cybersecurity-related companies in Northern Virginia through a paid, 7-week program. It is run by the Children's Science Center in partnership with the Commonwealth Cyber Initiative Northern Virginia Node at Virginia Tech and George Mason University. duration: 6 weeks, full-time (40 hours/week); 2026 dates were June 26-August 7
overview: Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center, the only NCI-designated Comprehensive Cancer Center in Upstate New York, runs the Summer Research Experience in Cancer (SURE-CAN) program for local high school juniors. The 2026 cohort ran June 26 through August 7, 2026 (6 weeks); the 2026 application portal is now closed. Interns experience an immersive curriculum of lectures, group discussions, and hands-on wet-lab or dry-lab research, covering cancer biology, imaging, genomics, AI methods, basic statistics, and research ethics, and culminating in a formal poster symposium. Eligibility is restricted to current high school juniors (graduating class of 2027) who are U.S. citizens or permanent residents, at least 15 years old at program start, and who are both residents of and enrolled in schools within Erie, Niagara, Cattaraugus, or Chautauqua County, NY. This is a commuter-only program with no exceptions, and residency is verified. There is no application fee. Limited subsistence allowances are available for a select number of participants based on outside funding source eligibility; a stipend is not guaranteed to every intern. No official acceptance rate is published. Program contact is Tatiana Shaurova, PhD, Office of Cancer Education and Training.
requirements: Current high school junior, graduating class of 2027. overview:
Cleveland Clinic Research offers research opportunities in its laboratories for high school students who are at least 16 years old, giving them hands on experience with laboratory techniques and a chance to explore careers in biomedical research. The opportunities are coordinated through the Research Education and Training Center at the Lerner Research Institute in Cleveland, Ohio.

There are two pathways to a placement. Students may apply to the formal ten week Summer Research Internship, whose application typically opens in mid December and closes at the end of January, or they may identify a Cleveland Clinic lab and email the principal investigator directly to ask about openings during the summer or school year. The number of labs able to host students varies throughout the year, positions are limited, and acceptance is not guaranteed.
requirements: Students must be 16 years of age or older to work in a Cleveland Clinic Research laboratory. Positions are limited and acceptance is not guaranteed. Placement depends on lab availability and, for direct outreach, on a lab agreeing to host the student.
