overview: Stanford Tech-X: Mental Health + Technology Immersion is a one-week intensive summer program for high school students offered by the Stanford University Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences through its Mental Health Technology and Innovation Hub. The program offers an in-depth look at the intersection of mental health and technology - exploring the current state and future possibilities of digital mental health. Participants engage in interactive seminars led by Stanford staff, faculty, and expert collaborators to explore advanced digital mental health (DMH) tools and the impact of technologies like social media and AI on mental health. Students gain direct exposure to Stanford's leading research and clinical work in psychiatry and behavioral sciences. The program emphasizes collaboration and creativity, encouraging participants to share their lived experiences and diverse perspectives to reimagine how we design safe and effective interventions for youth mental health. Throughout the week, participants work in groups on exploratory projects and present their findings on the final day. Two sessions are offered each summer (2026: Session 1 June 15–19, Session 2 June 22–26). Cost for 2026: $1,450 per session. Scholarships are available for qualified applicants. Compensation: No stipend - program fee of $1,450 applies; scholarships available.

overview: BRAINYAC (Brain Research Apprenticeships in New York at Columbia) is a Columbia University Zuckerman Institute program that immerses high school students in neuroscience research. Students live in MIT dormitories and take five courses spanning math, life sciences, physics, humanities, and a project based STEM elective such as machine learning, genomics, architecture, or electronics, alongside lab tours and college admissions counseling. overview: Teen Conservation Leaders (TCL) is a service learning volunteer program at the Monterey Bay Aquarium for high school students to develop career and life skills, build self confidence, and earn community service hours while supporting the Aquarium's conservation mission. The program begins with a week long training where students build community and learn basic marine biology and ocean conservation topics. Students apply to one of three tracks. The Guest Track focuses on interpretation skills and guest experiences for visitors of all ages. The Animal Care and Engineering Track involves caring for near shore invertebrates and engineering solutions for animal and staff needs, and requires comfort with physical work. overview: Boston University's Research in Science & Engineering (RISE) program is a six-week, residential summer program for rising high school seniors that places students in real university research settings on BU's Boston campus. Students choose between an Internship Track, in which they are matched with a BU faculty mentor and work up to 40 hours per week on an individual research project in a university lab, and a Practicum Track, in which they join a cohort for structured, mentor-led group research such as computational neurobiology or data science, combining daily lectures with hands-on lab work. Both tracks culminate in a poster symposium where students present their research findings. RISE is a competitive, tuition-based program rather than a paid internship; students and families pay tuition and fees to participate.
requirements: Applicants must be entering senior year of high school (grade 12) in fall 2026, hold US citizenship or permanent residency, and submit a full high school transcript starting from grade 9 including fall 2025 grades (screenshots of an academic portal are accepted). Standardized test scores (SAT, ACT, PSAT, or PreACT) are optional for 2026. One letter of recommendation is required from a science or math teacher, counselor, or research supervisor who has known the applicant at least six months. Three short essays are required: choice of subject of interest (max 300 words), academic achievements (250 words), and reasons for wanting to attend RISE (200 words); Internship Track applicants must also name three BU faculty members whose research aligns with their interests (max 250 words). The most competitive applicants have a cumulative unweighted GPA in the A- to A range. A $75 nonrefundable application fee is required; 2026 tuition was approximately $5,930 (roughly $8,500 to $9,500 total with room and board for residential students), with a $1,000 nonrefundable deposit due upon acceptance and limited need-based financial aid available (aid applications due same date as the admissions deadline).
how_to_apply: Visit the BU RISE program page and choose either the Internship or Practicum track, then apply through the BU Summer Term application portal (the 2026 cycle opened around mid-December 2025). Submit the online application with a transcript starting from grade 9, three required essays, one recommendation from a science/math teacher or research supervisor, and, for Internship applicants, a list of three BU faculty members whose research interests align with yours. Pay the $75 nonrefundable application fee, and ensure your recommender submits by the recommendation deadline (about one week after the application deadline). Decisions arrive roughly 6 to 8 weeks after the deadline; admitted students must pay a $1,000 nonrefundable deposit to secure their spot, with full payment due by May 1 or the date on the offer letter. The 2027 application cycle and exact deadlines had not yet been published as of July 2026.

role: U.S. Secret Service High School Internship Program
deadline: Not rolling - announcements posted on USAJOBS twice yearly, in February and July
duration: At least one semester, quarter, or summer session (min 12 hrs/week)
overview:
The U.S. Secret Service Student Volunteer Service Program offers unpaid internship opportunities to high school and college students interested in learning about the federal law enforcement agency responsible for protecting the President, Vice President, and other designated individuals, as well as investigating financial crimes. The program gives students an understanding of the nature and structure of the U.S. Secret Service, with placements in field offices or headquarters depending on location and availability.

Eligibility confirmed from official sources: applicants must be U.S. citizens, at least 16 years old, maintain a 2.5 GPA or better, currently enrolled in high school or an educational institution not above the baccalaureate level, and not be the son or daughter of a current Secret Service employee. A written agreement from the applicant's school is required, along with a limited background investigation and drug screening. Participants volunteer a minimum of 12 hours per week for at least one semester, two quarters, or one summer session. Positions are unpaid, though academic credit may be arranged through the student's school. Announcements for openings are posted on USAJOBS twice per year, in February and July, rather than accepted on a continuous rolling basis. A separate paid Pathways internship track also exists for students 16 and older enrolled at least half time, but that is a distinct program from the Student Volunteer track.

• Currently enrolled in high school (or an educational institution not above the baccalaureate level)

Each scholar explores the impact of health disparities on local communities and presents a health disparities research project at the end of the summer. The program is free for accepted students.

overview: HIP-SAT (Homeschool Internship Program for Science and Technology) is a paid, 8-week summer research internship hosted by the MIT Department of Chemical Engineering and Weill Cornell Medicine, exclusively for homeschooled high school students (age 16 or older by June 1). At the conclusion of the program, students present their work at an August symposium. Projects are tailored to the interests and abilities of each student. overview:
The NIA Summer Internship Program, known as STAR (Summer Trainee in Aging Research), is part of the NIH wide Summer Internship Program and is based at the Biomedical Research Center on the Johns Hopkins Bayview campus in Baltimore, Maryland. Internships run 8 to 10 weeks from late May to mid or late August, with interns working full time in a research lab under a Principal Investigator on aging related biomedical, behavioral, or social science research. Interns receive a stipend based on the level of education completed at the time the fellowship begins, attend weekly scientific seminars presented by NIA scientists, and present their project at the NIA Summer Student Poster Day at the end of the summer. Interns must also show proof of health insurance before starting.

To be eligible, students must be enrolled at least half time in an accredited United States high school, college, or university. Summer interns must be at least 17 years old by June 15 of the internship year. High school applicants must additionally be either juniors or seniors, and any applicant who will not be 18 by June 15 must, at the time of application, live within 40 miles of the NIH campus where they hope to intern. Selection is decentralized, meaning individual Principal Investigators review applications and choose their own interns, so applicants are encouraged to reach out to PIs directly after applying through the NIH Office of Intramural Training and Education application system.
requirements: Must be enrolled at least half time in an accredited United States high school, college, or university. Must be at least 17 years old by June 15 of the internship year. Must provide proof of health insurance. International students are generally not eligible and standard NIH nepotism rules apply.
how_to_apply: Create a profile on the NIH Application Center at training.nih.gov, indicate interest in Summer Internships, complete the eligibility screener for the SIP program, then submit coursework and grades, a CV or resume, a personal statement, and contact information for two references. After submitting, reach out directly to NIH Principal Investigators whose research interests you.

Based on the historical pattern, applications for SASI 2027 are expected to open around September 1, 2026, with Early Decision I closing in late November, Early Decision II in early January, Regular Decision I in late January, and Regular Decision II (the final round) closing around February 20, 2027.
duration: Three tracks: SASI Foundations (2 weeks, on-campus), SASI Clinical Skills (1 week, on-campus), and SASI Virtual (2 weeks, online). Programs typically run late June through early August; exact dates vary by year.
overview:
The Clinical Science, Technology and Medicine Internship is run by Stanford Medicine's Anesthesia Summer Institute (SASI) and comes in three formats: SASI Foundations, a two-week on-campus introduction to clinical medicine, science, and technology; SASI Clinical Skills, a one-week on-campus in-depth look at practical techniques like suturing and airway management; and SASI Virtual, a two-week fully online version of the curriculum. A combined Dual Pathways option lets students complete more than one track in the same summer. Students work on a team capstone project mentored by real patients through the program's ePatient partnership and by Stanford faculty, complete BLS certification training, and attend sessions on obstetric and regional anesthesia, simulation, and crisis management.

SASI describes its admissions as highly selective, and applications are reviewed through phased Early Decision (rounds I and II) and Regular Decision (rounds I and II) cycles rather than on a rolling basis, each with its own close date and decision date. On-campus tracks include the option of Stanford dorm housing, with an added activity fee for residential students, while commuting is also permitted. Tuition for 2026 was $6,490 for Foundations and $4,250 for Virtual, on top of a separate non-refundable application fee, and the program offers limited, need based tuition assistance for applicants who apply during the first Regular Decision round.

Its goals are to promote interest in the biological sciences and medicine, teach how scientific research is done, and increase the diversity of students pursuing careers in these fields.

It is open to rising high school juniors and seniors who live and attend school in the Northern California counties of San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Marin, Alameda, Contra Costa, or Santa Cruz, and it requires a cumulative unweighted GPA of at least 3.0. overview:
The O'Hern Lab at Yale, a jamming and soft matter research group in Mechanical Engineering and Materials Science, studies how disordered materials deform, with a current focus on the structural origin and evolution of shear bands in metallic glasses. Shear bands are plastic instabilities that localize strain and are the primary cause of sudden failure in these materials. The lab is a host lab in the Yale Pathways Research Internships program, hosting a local high school student for a paid summer placement.

The 2026 project investigates how shear bands form and evolve in CuZr metallic glasses under compression. The intern runs molecular dynamics simulations on the Yale computing cluster to generate glassy samples and simulate their deformation, then analyzes the data to track shear band formation and identify defect like weak regions. Experience with C, C++, Python, Matlab, or another language is preferred but not required. The internship runs full time for seven weeks from late June to mid August and pays a 2500 dollar educational stipend. Applicants must reside in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, or Santa Cruz county, be at least 16 by the start date, have an unweighted GPA of at least 3.0, and show some prior knowledge of biology, chemistry, or computer programming. overview: Established in 1990, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory's Partners for the Future (PFF) program connects Long Island high school seniors with CSHL scientists for a full academic year of original research. Students are nominated by their high school science department chairperson, who may nominate up to two juniors per school each year. Semi-finalists are interviewed by CSHL scientists, and selected students work a minimum of 10 hours per week from September through March of their senior year alongside a CSHL scientist mentor in areas such as cancer, plant biology, neuroscience, genomics, or quantitative biology. The program culminates in a symposium where students present their research to mentors, CSHL administrators, parents, and teachers. PFF is a school year program, not a summer program, and many alumni return to CSHL as summer undergraduate researchers. Compensation: unpaid, though CSHL provides a stipend to cover travel expenses for students who need financial assistance.

Must provide your own transportation to and from CSHL.
how_to_apply: Talk to your high school science department chairperson about being nominated; nominations are typically made during the winter of junior year. overview:
The Pre-College Program in Computational Biology at Carnegie Mellon University is an intensive four week residential summer program that immerses high school students in laboratory techniques and the computational methods used to interpret biological data. Taught by faculty including Professor Phillip Compeau and Professor Joshua Kangas, it gives students a rare chance to explore the interdisciplinary frontier where computer science meets modern biology in a university setting.

Each day is split between a teaching lab, where students collect samples and generate DNA sequence data from local microbes, and a hackathon, where small teams write code to answer real research questions about that data, working with tools such as liquid handling robots and machine learning. No prior programming experience is required, and admitted students complete preparatory coding lessons beforehand. Applicants must be current sophomores or juniors, be at least 16 by the start date, and have a B average or better, with most admitted students being juniors. The program is tuition based with residential and commuter options, and scholarship and international applications are due by the early February deadline while the final deadline falls in early March.

company: Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory / Columbia Climate School
deadline: March 2 at 11:59 PM ET annually
duration: 6 weeks, full time, during the summer (June-August)
overview:
The Secondary School Field Research Program (SSFRP) brings high school students, undergraduate mentors, and science teachers to the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory campus in Palisades, New York for six weeks of field and laboratory research each summer. Students work in tiered mentoring teams, each with one or two undergraduate mentors, a teacher liaison, and a Lamont researcher, to conduct environmental and ecological research, primarily at the Piermont Marsh along the Hudson River. Research topics include sediment accumulation, nutrient cycling, groundwater chemistry, bacterial levels, invasive and native plant distributions, and fish species and feeding patterns.

Participants prepare by reading and discussing a scientific journal article about the marsh, then break into research teams to refine sampling protocols and collect and analyze field data over the summer. Each team produces a research poster and presentation for an end of summer symposium at Columbia. Students receive a monetary stipend for participating. The program is not residential; students commute to the Palisades, NY campus and the Piermont Marsh field site daily.
requirements: Must be currently enrolled in grades 10-12 and at least 16 years old at the start of the program. Must be enrolled at one of the program's partner high schools, where an assigned science teacher liaison selects participating students. Not a residential program; students must be able to commute to Palisades, NY and the Piermont Marsh field site. Genuine interest in outdoor fieldwork and science required.
how_to_apply: Students apply through their partner school's assigned science teacher liaison, who selects participants. The process includes a completed online application and an interview to assess interest in outdoor fieldwork and science. Contact Dr. Benjamin Bostick, SSFRP Program Director, at bostick@ldeo.columbia.edu with questions.
ApplicationChecklist: Apply through your school's science teacher liaison, complete online application, attend an interview if selected

overview:

Interns work in BTI research labs on plant science and computational biology projects, including plant molecular biology, plant biotic interactions, bioinformatics, and biological engineering of plant systems. overview:
The CDC Museum Disease Detective Camp (DDC) is a free, five day academic day camp held at CDC headquarters in Atlanta, Georgia, and organized by the David J. Sencer CDC Museum. It is open to motivated students who will be rising high school juniors or seniors, meaning applicants must currently be a sophomore or junior, and applicants must be at least 16 years old by the first day of camp due to a federal laboratory safety requirement with no exceptions. During the week, campers investigate re-created disease outbreaks, hold mock press conferences, work in a laboratory session, and learn about topics such as global health, environmental health, chronic disease surveillance, public health law, and epidemiology from CDC staff and volunteers. The camp does not have a medical treatment focus, though it covers many public health career paths including medicine.

Two identical in person sessions are offered each summer, each with 27 available slots, for a total of 54 spots. The camp is competitive, receiving several hundred applications a year; 702 students applied in 2024, making the acceptance rate roughly 7 to 8 percent. There is no cost to attend, but students are responsible for their own travel and housing in Atlanta, and non-U.S. citizens must provide additional documentation, including a B1 visa if traveling from abroad.
requirements: Must currently be a high school sophomore or junior, since the camp is for rising juniors and seniors. Must be at least 16 years old by the first day of camp with no exceptions. Strong interest in public health is helpful but not required. Must attend the full program from 8:45 am to 4:00 pm each day.

A government issued photo ID is required for security checkpoints.

overview:
Wave Hill's Woodland Ecology Research Mentorship (WERM) is a 14 month paid program for motivated New York City high school students that offers deep exposure to ecological research. WERM interns contribute to New York City's 20,000 acres of natural areas through field research alongside working scientists and restoration practitioners.

Phase 1, the first summer, runs from July to August. Interns take two college credit courses at Wave Hill, accredited through the University of Mount Saint Vincent: Restoration of New York City's Natural Areas, and Mapping New York City's Urban Environment, an introduction to GIS. These courses combine classroom and computer lab instruction with hands on fieldwork in Wave Hill's woodlands.

Phase 2, the academic year, runs from September through June with weekly WERMshops that build scientific knowledge and research skills through projects, lessons, field trips around New York City, presentations, and interaction with local scientists.

Phase 3, the second summer, runs from July to mid August. Interns work full time on a mentored, independent small group research project, culminating in a final poster presentation symposium. Students also take a third college course, Research Methods, accredited through the University of Mount Saint Vincent.

Students earn credit for three college courses, accredited through the University of Mount Saint Vincent and transferable. We particularly encourage students who identify as Black, Latinx, Indigenous and/or come from under-resourced schools and communities to apply. The Ecology Building that houses WERM at Wave Hill is not wheelchair or stroller accessible, with 28 total stairs.

Compensation: Stipend of approximately $3,500, paid across the length of the 14 month program.

New York City resident and legally eligible to work in the United States
Genuine interest in ecology, environmental science, or field research
Ability to work in unpaved natural areas, use heavy tools, and bend at the waist
Ability to travel off site for field trips to parks and cultural institutions around New York City
Available and committed to all three phases of the 14 month program
Ability and motivation to work independently

overview:
Study and Engineering of New Enzymes for Biocatalytic Peptide Synthesis (research opportunity CHE-01) is a summer research project in the Department of Chemistry, offered through the Princeton University Laboratory Learning Program (LLP), a free, in-person research experience for local high school students. The project focuses on the discovery, characterization, and engineering of enzymes that build and modify peptides. Peptides are an important class of biological molecules that act as messengers, hormones, and toxins, and there is strong interest in developing peptides and their mimics as drugs, with insulin and GLP-1 agonists as key examples. Because traditional synthesis can be expensive, the lab is developing enzymes as catalysts for assembling and modifying peptide structures using solution phase chemistry.

The summer student learns to use bioinformatics to identify new enzyme candidates, molecular biology to clone genes, and biochemical and analytical methods to characterize enzyme activity, and also uses mutagenesis to create new variants for protein engineering. The student performs techniques in molecular biology, biochemistry, microbiology, enzyme characterization, and library generation, and is expected to follow instructions carefully, work safely, maintain lab hygiene, and keep a written record of the work. The project runs about six weeks, roughly four to five days per week in person, and offers a stipend of about 150 dollars per week. Eligibility follows LLP rules: applicants must be at least 16 years old by mid June, be US citizens, and live in and attend a local New Jersey high school, with no housing or transportation provided. Applications run February 15 to March 15.

overview:

A central challenge in biomedical science is understanding how the genome, which is shared by all cells in the body, encodes many different cell types whose functions change through development, aging, and disease. This project uses statistical and machine learning approaches to model genome function and the impact of mutations, and to build genome-wide models of how genes work together in biological processes and pathways across different cell contexts.

Working closely with a mentor, the summer student develops and applies methods to understand the molecular basis of cell type diversity and the effect of genetic variants in specific tissue, cell type, and disease settings. No prior research experience is required, though minimal coding knowledge of Python or R is helpful, and applicants with no coding experience are still considered. The project runs about five to six weeks over the summer at roughly 20 to 30 hours per week, and students keep an online lab notebook and prepare a final report. Administered by rising second-year medical students, the program includes lectures on anatomy, physiology, and medical ethics from College of Medicine faculty, problem-based learning sessions, an introduction to research, clinical workshops such as phlebotomy and suturing, and clinical shadowing at OSU Wexner Medical Center and Nationwide Childrens Hospital. The camp is open to Ohio residents only. The 2026 camp ran June 8 to June 26, 2026, 8 AM to 4:30 PM on weekdays, with June 19 off for Juneteenth, and cost 325 dollars in tuition with full and partial scholarships available based on need. As of this verification the 2026 cycle has concluded and 2027 dates have not yet been posted.
requirements: Must be a rising sophomore, junior, or senior at an Ohio high school. Must be an Ohio resident; the program does not currently accept out-of-state applicants. A cumulative GPA of at least 3.0 and a math and science GPA of at least 3.3 are recommended. Two letters of recommendation are required, with at least one from a math or science teacher, signed and preferably on school letterhead. A completed application including extracurricular activities, essays, and a current transcript is required. Students are responsible for their own housing and transportation.

role: SUNY Oneonta Biological Field Station Summer Internship
deadline: Opens each January and closes in mid March each year. The 2026 cycle deadline for high school applicants was March 18, 2026. The 2027 date has not been posted yet; this is an estimate based on last year timing.
duration: 8 weeks (late May through August), full time Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.
overview:
The SUNY Oneonta Biological Field Station runs an eight week summer research internship for New York State residents who are at least 16 years old as of June 20, running from late May through August. Interns join field ecology and limnology work on Otsego Lake and the Susquehanna River watershed, including fisheries surveys, water chemistry, plant surveys, and data analysis, working alongside BFS faculty and staff on a structured daily schedule from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Only one to three high school positions are awarded each year, with at least one reserved for a resident of Otsego County; students from elsewhere in New York are encouraged to apply but must arrange their own housing, since on campus housing is not available to high schoolers. Upon successful completion, high school interns receive a 3,500 dollar stipend and one free semester hour of college credit. Application materials for the next cycle become available in January 2027; an exact deadline had not been posted as of this verification.
requirements:
New York State resident, age 16 or older as of June 20
Strong academic background in environmental or natural sciences
Available full time, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., for 8 weeks at BFS near Cooperstown, NY
Students outside Otsego County must arrange their own housing; a daily shuttle from the SUNY Oneonta main campus is available
At least one of the 1 to 3 available positions is reserved for an Otsego County resident

Check suny.oneonta.edu/biological-field-station/internships for the current application; materials for the next cycle are expected in January 2027

Arrange housing in advance if you live outside Otsego County

overview:
The Atlanta Bar Association's Summer Law Internship Program (SLIP) is a paid, six week internship for Georgia high school juniors and seniors interested in the legal profession. Founded in 1993, SLIP places selected interns with law firms, corporate legal departments, and public interest organizations, mostly located inside Atlanta's perimeter, with a heavy concentration downtown and in Midtown. Interns are paid a total stipend of about 2,000 dollars for the six week program, funded either by their host firm or, for Public Interns, by the Atlanta Bar Foundation. In its first thirty four years the program has provided over 980 paid internships to Atlanta area students.

SLIP is intentionally rigorous and demands full commitment. The 2026 program ran from May 27 to July 17, 2026, and included mandatory orientations, weekly All Intern Meetings, an essay competition on a US Supreme Court decision, and an Oralist Competition. Only current juniors and seniors who are Georgia residents were eligible to apply for SLIP 34, and competition is significant, with over 200 applicants for around 36 spots in 2026.
requirements: Applicant must be a Georgia resident and a current high school junior or senior. Must be able to fully commit to the entire program period with no conflicts from vacations, sports, camps, second jobs, or other commitments. Must attend a mandatory in person interview in professional attire and follow the program's dress and grooming code.
how_to_apply: Applications open online in early February via a form linked from the program blog at abaslip.blogspot.com. Completed applications must be submitted by the March deadline. Applicants who advance are invited to an in person interview, typically held in April, and selected interns are announced in May.

role: American Red Cross VolunTEEN Summer Program
location(Remote/InPerson,Hybrid): Bethesda, MD / Fort Belvoir, VA / Quantico, VA / Arlington, VA

overview:
The American Red Cross VolunTEEN Summer Program is a service learning opportunity for teens ages 14 to 17, run by local Red Cross chapters. The National Capital and Greater Chesapeake region places VolunTEENs with the Service to the Armed Forces team to support military medical clinics and hospitals, including Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Bethesda, Maryland, and Virginia locations such as the Alexander T. Augusta Military Medical Center at Fort Belvoir, the Naval Health Clinic at Marine Corps Base Quantico, and the DiLorenzo Clinic at the Pentagon. Last year Red Cross VolunTEENs logged more than 5,000 volunteer hours combined.

Participants commit to a minimum of two half day shifts each week, either 8 am to noon or noon to 4 pm, plus a weekly training session on Wednesdays, for five to six weeks over the summer depending on location. All participants must be U.S. citizens, and Virginia program participants must also provide proof of flu vaccination. Compensation: unpaid, though participants receive a certificate of completion and can count their time toward community service hours.
requirements: Must be between 14 and 17 years old for the duration of the program and a U.S. citizen. Able to commit to two half day shifts per week plus a weekly Wednesday training session. Must attend mandatory orientation and cannot miss more than one week of the program. Virginia locations require proof of flu vaccination.
how_to_apply: Find your local Red Cross chapter's VolunTEEN program; the National Capital and Greater Chesapeake region serves Maryland and Virginia locations. Review your chapter's program dates and eligibility. Submit the online application before the deadline, which was March 20, 2026 for Maryland and March 27, 2026 for Virginia. Selected participants are notified by mid April. Complete orientation and any required paperwork before your start date.

overview: The Wistar Institute's High School Fellowship in Biomedical Research is a four week paid summer program for Philadelphia area high school students interested in biomedical science. About 15 students work in Wistar's Training Lab learning laboratory techniques, contribute to active research projects, read scientific literature, and present their work at the end of the program. SEPTA passes are provided and a 1,500 dollar stipend is awarded for successful completion. A select number of participants may be invited to continue for an additional three weeks of individually mentored cancer research, funding permitting. No prior research experience is required, though the program prioritizes students in the School District of Philadelphia.

Interns spend the majority of their time engaged in work for the Town Manager, with assignments also distributed to other Hanover town government departments. Assignments evolve over time to match the intern's skills, abilities, and interests with the most pressing needs of the Town. Interns are expected to integrate within the Town Hall team, demonstrate maturity and professionalism, and write a 500-word reflection essay at the conclusion of the internship. The program runs from the end of the school year to the start of the next academic year. Strong preference given to Hanover HS students/alumni, South Shore Voc-Tech students/alumni, and Hanover residents attending private schools.

Over six weeks, students combine a paid workplace internship (about four days a week) with weekly classroom seminars and workshops covering financial markets, financial literacy, and workplace professionalism. Students work roughly 24 hours per week and attend half-day seminars led by business professionals. Past interns have been placed with organizations such as Siebert Brandford Shank and Co., the City of Chicago Department of Finance, and Cabrera Capital Markets. The program has a long track record of encouraging students to pursue higher education in business, economics, and finance.

role: PNNL High School Research Internship (HSRI) / Student Research Apprenticeship Program (SRAP)
deadline: Opens early February, exact close date varies by year so apply as soon as postings open
duration: 10 wks summer (Jun-Aug) or 36 wks school yr (Aug-May)
overview:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) in Richland, Washington offers paid high school internship tracks under two programs: the High School Research Internship (HSRI), an academic year program running August through May in which students attend regular classes for half the day and then work up to 4 hours a day at PNNL with a scientist or engineer mentor, and the Student Research Apprenticeship Program (SRAP), a 10 week full time summer track running June through August. A parallel High School Business Internship (HSBI) track exists for students interested in business functions rather than lab research. Eligible applicants must be a current sophomore, junior, or senior, at least 16 by the start date, hold a cumulative GPA of 3.0 or higher, and be able to commute to PNNL's Richland campus (a small number of SRAP roles exist at other PNNL sites such as College Park, MD). Because interns under 18 cannot enter laboratory spaces per PNNL and federal policy, younger interns are placed in office or computational project work instead.

Compensation: Stipend, hourly wage.
requirements:
- Current sophomore, junior, or senior in a public or private high school
- At least 16 years old by the program start date
- Cumulative GPA of 3.0 or higher (from start of 9th grade)
- Able to commute to PNNL's Richland, WA campus (a few SRAP roles exist at other sites)
- Interns under 18 are restricted from lab spaces and placed in office/computational roles
how_to_apply:
1. Watch for the application window to open in early February on careers.pnnl.gov
2. Search "High School" to find current HSRI, SRAP, or HSBI postings
3. Prepare a resume with two references and a cover letter
4. Get an unofficial transcript from your school counselor
5. Write a short personal statement about your interest in the program
6. Combine all materials into a single PDF, since only one file can be uploaded
7. Submit before the deadline (March for Summer SRAP, June for academic year HSRI)

role: Young Scholars Summer STEMM Research Program (WYSE)
deadline: March 31, 2027 priority deadline for the Summer 2027 cycle (not rolling; applications open each February, reviewed through April)
duration: 6 weeks
overview: The Young Scholars Summer STEMM Research Program is hosted by the Worldwide Youth in Science and Engineering (WYSE) program at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Grainger College of Engineering. It is a primarily in-person, 6 week research experience open only to rising 10th through 12th grade students who reside in Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Missouri, Iowa, or Wisconsin. International applicants are not accepted. For Summer 2026, online orientation ran May 28 and June 10-11, residential move in was June 14, in person orientation was June 15-16, research began June 17, and the program concludes with an in person final symposium on July 31, 2026. Students are placed in one of two research tracks: SpHERES, spanning sociology, physiology, neuroscience, bioengineering, and human development, or GEnYuS, spanning computer science, mechanical, nuclear, aerospace, electrical, civil, and materials engineering. Students commit to 30 to 35 hours per week of research and professional development, present a research poster at a closing symposium, and are matched with a graduate or faculty mentor. There is no cost to participate beyond travel to campus. Housing, meals, and a monetary fellowship payment are provided to accepted students, though no academic course credit is awarded. This is a highly selective, IDEA equity focused program. In 2022 and 2023 it received over 600 applications for only 30 lab spots, though all students who meet the grade and residency requirements are welcome to apply. The application opens in February and requires two personal statement essays plus a separate online recommendation form from a teacher, mentor, or counselor. The Summer 2026 priority deadline was March 31, 2026, with acceptance, waitlist, or rejection decisions sent by the end of April or early May. Admissions are not rolling, so applying early does not improve an applicant chances as long as it is submitted before the deadline.

role: California Academy of Sciences Careers in Science (CiS) Intern Program
deadline: Applications closed for 2026. Check back February 2027 for next cycle
duration: Multi-year, year-round (interns enter in June as rising sophomores or juniors and continue through high school graduation)
grades: Currently enrolled full time as a 9th or 10th grade student in an SFUSD school; maintain a 2.5 GPA and a C or higher in science and math
overview:
Careers in Science (CiS) is a multi-year, year-round, paid internship and youth development program at the California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco. It is designed for local high school students from communities underrepresented in STEM, including girls and students of color. Interns enter the program in June as rising sophomores or juniors and continue through high school graduation, and they are paid above minimum wage to learn, teach, and do science in and around the Academy. On Saturdays during the school year and on weekdays in the summer, interns conduct outdoor fieldwork and facilitate learning experiences for museum visitors on the public floor.

Twice a month interns attend interactive trainings that build science communication skills, introduce careers from practicing STEM professionals, and offer guidance on topics like financial literacy and the college application process. Interns also take college tours, present at STEM conferences and festivals, and help design Academy exhibits and educational materials. As they advance, interns join project groups led by an Academy researcher or partner to work on science research or environmental action projects, serve on the CiS Leadership Council, and may earn individualized mentorships with Academy experts. The program was honored with a 2022 Presidential Award for Excellence in Science, Mathematics, and Engineering Mentorship.
requirements: Applicants must be currently enrolled full time as a 9th or 10th grade student in a San Francisco Unified School District school and must maintain a GPA of 2.5 with a grade of C or higher in science and math. Students need to be able to obtain a valid work permit, which requires US citizenship or other authorization to work in the US. Interns must commit to all attendance requirements for two or three years, through high school graduation, and must be able to commute to the Academy and nearby locations after school and on Saturdays during the school year and on weekdays in the summer, with some remote work possible. No prior science experience is necessary, but applicants should demonstrate interest and enthusiasm for learning, teaching, and doing science.
how_to_apply: Applications are submitted through the California Academy of Sciences Careers in Science page when the cycle is open, which is typically early in the calendar year. The most recent cycle has closed and the Academy advises checking back in February 2027. Selected applicants may be invited to a group interview. Interested students can join the Academy Youth Programs mailing list to be notified when applications open, and questions can be sent to CiS@calacademy.org. Applicants should be prepared to show they can obtain a work permit and to meet the GPA and attendance requirements before the program begins.

Students work alongside a scientist mentor roughly 40 hours a week on projects in areas such as organic chemistry, biochemistry, materials science, environmental chemistry, and pharmaceutical research. First time (Summer I) participants and returning (Summer II) participants each receive a 4,000 dollar fellowship. To be eligible, a student's family annual income must not exceed 300 percent of the Federal Poverty Guidelines for their household size, with documentation required.

Completed or currently taking at least one high school chemistry course.
Available full time, about 40 hours a week, for 8 to 10 weeks at the assigned host site.
Parent or guardian permission required for students under 18.

Applications are accepted on a rolling basis; selecting officials interview students and hire from a pool of qualified candidates.

Past student projects have included DNA sequence classification, microfluidic technology for disease detection, extreme weather event modeling, and computational biology tools. Students work directly with professionals at Seattle-area companies and research institutions. The program has run for more than 10 years, and alumni have gone on to top universities and co-authored IEEE conference papers.

Compensation: Most projects are unpaid, since SPARK is a volunteer-run mentorship program rather than a paid internship. Some individual projects have offered a stipend of up to $500 in past years, entirely at the discretion of the mentor or host organization. Launched in 2018 by the late Dr. William Schnaper and endowed in 2019 by Louis Simpson and Kimberly Querrey, it is based at the Simpson Querrey Biomedical Research Center on the downtown Chicago campus. Since 2018 the program has supported dozens of SciHigh Scholars.

Each scholar is matched with a Northwestern faculty mentor based on shared research interests and develops a research project, largely in kidney and biomedical science, that they work on through the summer and present at the end. Scholars also attend weekly workshops on research development, evaluation, and communication led by experts across STEMM fields. Interns work full time at about 40 hours per week for roughly seven weeks. overview:
The Science Mentorship Institute (sci-MI) is a free, fully virtual research mentorship program for high school students. Its Computer Science Mentorship Program (CSMP) is a seven week summer program in which students pursue an independent computer science research project using open source software, open access papers, and freely available development environments, working with volunteer mentors. Students dedicate about 10 to 20 hours a week and are not required to have any prior coding experience; access to a computer is encouraged but not required. The program runs from late June through early August (June 23 to August 8 for the 2026 cycle). Students present their project and submit a written paper at the end of the program. If spots are limited, priority goes to students underrepresented in computer science or higher education, juniors or seniors with no prior formal research experience, and students unable to participate in other enriching summer activities. Applications for 2026 are now closed. Sci-MI is a registered 501(c)(3) nonprofit.

requirements:

Interest in computer science research; no prior programming experience required.
Commitment of about 10 to 20 hours a week during the program.
Available for most of the program dates, late June through early August.
Priority given to students underrepresented in computer science or higher education if spots are limited.

role: EARTH Program (Environmental Health Sciences Research for Teachers and High School Students)
deadline: May 1 estimate; 2027 date not posted
duration: 10 weeks
overview:
The EARTH Program (Environmental heAlth sciences Research for Teachers and High school students) is a summer environmental health sciences research program run by the Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health in collaboration with Missouri Breaks Industries Research, Inc. and funded by the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences. It serves high school students and teachers from three Native communities in the Northern Plains, centering Indigenous environmental health research priorities, ethics, and practice.

Locally based teams of one high school teacher and up to three students conduct locally relevant research on topics such as drinking water quality, air pollution, uranium and gold mining, and dietary exposures. Over ten weeks the teams meet remotely with Columbia and MBIRI mentors through video conferencing for seminars, workshops, and research meetings, then gather in person for the EARTH research symposium. Students are compensated for up to 32 hours per week and can access professional SAT and ACT preparation, and the program is designed to reduce financial and geographic barriers to research.
requirements: Open to high school students and teachers from three Native communities in the Northern Plains. Students participate as part of a local team led by a high school teacher, with up to three students per team. The program centers Indigenous environmental health research priorities and is designed to reduce financial and geographic barriers to research.
how_to_apply: Students apply as part of a local team with a high school teacher from a participating Northern Plains community. For application details and current openings, contact program director Anne Nigra or deputy director Yoshira Ornelas Van Horne through the Columbia Mailman EARTH program page.
ApplicationChecklist: Be in a Northern Plains Native community|Join a team led by a HS teacher|Team of up to three students|Email director Anne Nigra to apply

overview:
SMUD (Sacramento Municipal Utility District) offers paid 6-week summer internships for local high school juniors and seniors in fields including information technology, engineering, customer service, administrative support, vehicle mechanics, accounting, human resources, and marketing. SMUD is a leader in renewable energy and sustainability.

Eligibility rotates annually among eight school districts in the SMUD service area; not all schools are eligible every year. Candidate selection process: Applications are reviewed; qualifying students are invited to a mandatory orientation. Students who attend orientation enter a computerized random drawing selecting 55 to 60 participants. Those selected complete an unpaid work readiness workshop and video interview. Candidates are then evaluated on resume quality and interview performance, with final in-person interviews with SMUD Department Managers. Up to 25 students ultimately begin onboarding and the 6-week paid internship. Program runs June 22 to July 31, 2026.

Compensation: $16.90 per hour (as of 2026).
requirements:
• Must be at least 16 years of age by June 2 of the program year
• Must be a current junior or senior at an eligible high school (eligibility rotates each year among the eight school districts in the SMUD service area; check sacworks.seta.net for the eligible district in the current year)
• Minimum 2.5 GPA
• Must have no relatives employed at SMUD
• Authorized to work in the U.S. in the Sacramento area
• Note: final selection among qualified applicants is made by computerized random drawing; 55 to 60 interns are selected per year

VTPMD 2990 is a mentored research apprenticeship in applied epidemiology offered through the Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine. Qualified high school students enrolled in Cornell Summer College take part alongside Cornell underclassmen, and are placed in a research laboratory with a designed project under the direct supervision of a research associate such as an upper level graduate student, postdoc, or faculty member.

Over the six week summer session interns complete at least 120 hours of laboratory work, learn epidemiology research methods and techniques, and are graded on preparation, participation, and skill. At the end of the session each student gives a short 15 to 20 minute oral presentation and submits a manuscript in a form suitable for publication. Enrollment requires one year of basic biology, such as a score of 5 on the AP Biology exam or a college level biology course, or permission of the instructor, and students must obtain instructor consent to register.

overview:
ieSoSC (Innovation, Entrepreneurship, and the Science of Smart Cities) is a tuition free summer program at the NYU Tandon School of Engineering in Downtown Brooklyn, designed for New York City high school students interested in the science and technology behind urban infrastructure. Over four to five weeks, students taught by NYU faculty and graduate students build skills in coding, microcontrollers, circuit deployment, and sensor integration while also learning entrepreneurial concepts such as product development, project management, economics, and pitching. Classes run Monday through Friday from 9 AM to 4 PM at the Tandon campus.

In the second half of the program, students form small teams to ideate, prototype, and present a smart city solution using an internet of things approach, supported by a small team budget for materials. Participants receive public presentation training through a partnership with Irondale Theater and culminate the program with a public presentation to engineers, urban planners, STEM professionals, and the general public. Outside class, students can join NYU sponsored activities, college prep workshops, and trips to NYC destinations. The program is fully funded so there is no cost to accepted participants.
requirements: Applicants must currently live in New York City and be enrolled in grades 8, 9, or 10. A strong academic record and demonstrated interest in STEM are expected, along with a basic understanding of physics and coding. Students must be able to commit to the full program schedule, Monday through Friday 9 AM to 4 PM, for the entire session and to get to and from the Brooklyn campus daily.
how_to_apply: Students apply online through NYU Tandon's application portal, submitting information about their academic history along with two short essay responses. There is a single application deadline; admitted students are notified roughly two weeks after the deadline closes.

overview:
The Pathology and Laboratory Medicine Summer Research Internship, also called the Summer Enrichment Program, is run by the Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine at the Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island. It is a paid five week program that gives local high school students from historically marginalized or economically disadvantaged backgrounds an immersive introduction to basic and translational research in pathology. The department selects about six highly motivated students each summer.

Students are placed individually in research labs alongside junior and senior scientists and work on projects in areas such as vaccine development, malaria pathobiology, neural and cardiac development, and neurodegenerative disease. Each week they also shadow pathologists at affiliated hospitals, join career roundtables, and take part in a college essay writing workshop with feedback from Brown Writing Center Fellows, closing the summer with a short research presentation. The program is for Rhode Island students only, rising juniors and seniors are encouraged to apply, and students in other grades are considered. For the 2026 cycle the deadline was May 22 with program dates of July 6 to August 7, and students apply through an online form linked on the department Community page.
requirements: The department seeks about six highly motivated high school students from historically marginalized communities or economically disadvantaged backgrounds. Rising juniors and seniors are encouraged to apply, and students in other grades are considered. This opportunity is for Rhode Island students only. Interns take part in the full five week program, which combines lab research, weekly clinical shadowing, and career and college preparation activities.
how_to_apply: Apply through the online Summer Research Internship application form linked on the department's Community page. The application deadline for the 2026 cycle was May 22, 2026, with program dates of July 6 to August 7. Questions about the form can be directed to Elizabeth Boynton at elizabeth_boynton@brown.edu.

grades: High school student; NYC resident (all five boroughs); must be at least 13 years old; no prior science courses or lab experience required
overview:
The Urban Barcode Research Program (UBRP), operated by the Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory DNA Learning Center (DNALC NYC) in Downtown Brooklyn, is a competitive year long science research program in which NYC high school students conduct original biodiversity research using DNA barcoding technology. The program is supported by the Pinkerton Foundation. Students develop their own research questions, collect environmental samples from NYC parks and urban ecosystems, isolate DNA, amplify DNA barcoding regions, sequence genetic barcodes, and analyze bioinformatics data to identify species and study urban biodiversity. Approximately 36 students are accepted per year.

Students apply in the spring and may be invited for an in person group interview at DNALC NYC in Brooklyn, followed by a second round individual Zoom interview if selected to move forward. Accepted students must attend mandatory two week lab training at DNALC NYC in Brooklyn in late August, plus additional training and workshop sessions scheduled during the academic year. Students then complete a minimum of 55 hours of independent research with a scientist mentor, culminating in a poster presentation at a research symposium held at the end of spring. Students who complete the research and present at the symposium receive a $500 stipend, and mentors receive a $2,000 stipend plus coverage of specimen sequencing costs.
requirements:
• High school student from New York City (all five boroughs); must be at least 13 years old
• Available for the full-day in-person group interview at DNALC NYC in Brooklyn during the week of July 6–10
• Available for the mandatory 2-week lab training August 24–28 AND August 31–September 4 at DNALC NYC in Brooklyn
• Able to complete a minimum of 55 hours of independent research with a scientist mentor during the academic year
• Must attend the spring symposium
• No prior science courses, lab experience, or molecular biology background required

2. Submit an online application - due May 26, 2026 (confirm current year deadline); write a paragraph explaining your interest in the program
3. If selected, attend a full-day in-person group interview at DNALC NYC in Brooklyn (week of July 6–10)
4. If advancing, attend an individual Zoom interview the week of July 27–31
5. If accepted, attend mandatory 2-week lab training August 24–28 and August 31–September 4
6. Contact DNALC via dnabarcoding101.org for questions
Paid/Unpaid/Stipend: Stipend ($500 upon completing research and presenting at spring symposium)

overview: The University of Toronto Summer Psychology Research Initiative (SPRINT) is a free ten-day outreach and access program for Ontario high school students to learn about a broad range of psychology topics, gain hands on research experience, and connect with peers and researchers at U of T. overview:
The Ocean, Climate, and Ecosystems (OCE) Data Science Research Internship at Brown University sits at the intersection of earth science, data science, and environmental studies. It is run jointly by the Department of Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences, the Data Science Institute, and the Institute at Brown for Environment and Society, with a mission to advance students in STEM. The program lasts one year and combines two in person sessions at Brown of about two weeks each with remote participation and regular mentor meetings.

Through a series of modules, interns build skills in scientific programming with Python and MATLAB, learn foundational concepts in oceanography and climate science, and practice searching scientific literature before designing and carrying out their own research project. Strong students can publish in peer reviewed journals and present at conferences. Coding experience is helpful but not required because the program teaches programming from the start. Applications run in an annual cycle, and the 2026 to 2027 round is closed with the next round opening in spring 2027. For details, interested students contact Professor Emanuele Di Lorenzo at e.dilorenzo@brown.edu.
requirements: Open to high school students interested in ocean, climate, and data science. It requires a one year commitment, attendance at two in-person sessions at Brown, and remote participation with weekly mentor meetings between sessions. Coding experience is helpful but the program teaches Python and MATLAB from the start.
how_to_apply: Applications are submitted through the program during its open cycle. The 2026-2027 cycle is closed and the next round opens in Spring 2027. For details, see the program page and contact Professor Emanuele Di Lorenzo at e.dilorenzo@brown.edu.
ApplicationChecklist: Email e.dilorenzo@brown.edu|Submit the application form|Write a statement of interest|Apply when 2027 round opens

overview: The Carnegie Youth Fellowship at iCivics is a stipended, year long civic leadership program for United States high school students in grades 9 through 12. Selected fellows take part in virtual meetings and group projects, build and lead student voice campaigns, and serve as youth ambassadors for civic education. Fellows also attend a required multi day symposium in Washington, DC at the start of the program, with travel, lodging, and program costs covered by iCivics. Each year iCivics selects about 34 fellows from a pool of more than 500 applicants representing roughly 46 states.

Finalists are invited to complete a Zoom interview before final selection. Fellows must be able to attend the required Washington, DC symposium at the start of the program.

overview:
The World Politics Summer Institute is a three week virtual program offered by the UCLA Department of Political Science, which runs one of the nation's most prestigious programs in the social sciences. It is designed specifically for high school students and introduces them to the study of world politics and the present day international system. Morning lectures cover topics such as the causes of war, international institutions, violence by nonstate actors, international trade, international law, human rights, and the global environment, drawing on theoretical perspectives, applied statistical analysis, and case studies.

Afternoon sessions let students apply what they learn to contemporary foreign policy issues and build professional discussion and research skills, and students complete a group project that they write and present to a public audience at a capstone event. Participants earn five units of UCLA college credit through Political Science 20. The program is open to students in grades 9 through 12 in the spring before the program who are at least 15 years old by the first day of Summer Sessions and who submit an unofficial transcript showing a cumulative GPA of 3.2 or higher. All sessions run online in Pacific time, and admission is granted on a rolling basis starting February 15.
requirements: Open to students in grades 9 through 12 in the spring before the program. Applicants must be at least 15 years old by the first day of Summer Sessions and submit an unofficial transcript reflecting a cumulative GPA of 3.2 or higher. No prior knowledge of political science is required.
how_to_apply: Apply through the online UCLA Summer Precollege Focus Series registration. Submit an unofficial transcript from grade 9 to present and a short value statement during registration. Admission is granted on a rolling basis and applicants are notified by email within about three weeks.

overview:
The NYAS Junior Academy is a completely free, global online STEM program run by The New York Academy of Sciences. Students ages 13–17 form international teams on the Launchpad virtual platform to solve practical challenges in science, technology, engineering, and math. Each year, two 10-week Innovation Challenges are offered: one in the Fall (mid-September to mid-November) and one in the Spring (mid-February to mid-April). Challenges are sponsored by industry-leading companies.

Students self-select into teams after a kick-off week covering research methods, design thinking, and data analysis. STEM professionals serve as mentors and judges. One winning team and two finalist teams are selected per challenge; prizes are educational. Students who fully complete a challenge (all milestones submitted on time) receive a certificate of completion and a free Young Membership to NYAS. Challenges take place entirely virtually with no travel required.

Fall 2026 recruitment: Applications open April 1, 2026 and close July 2, 2026. Admission decisions sent by August 31, 2026.

Time commitment: 3–4 hours per week during challenge periods.

Compensation: Completely free - no cost, no membership fee required, no stipend.

overview: TKS (The Knowledge Society) is a global virtual innovation accelerator for students ages 13 to 17 (you may apply at 12). The program runs 10 months, from September 2027 to June 2028, with weekly live 2 to 3 hour sessions held on weekends or weekday evenings in a cohort of about 40 students that can be scheduled across multiple time zones. Students explore 40 plus emerging technology and science learning modules, covering topics such as artificial intelligence, blockchain, space exploration, genetic engineering, quantum computing, brain-computer interfaces, and cellular agriculture, then choose a Focus area to build real projects with mentor support. Students also work on practical challenges submitted by organizations such as the United Nations, Google, Microsoft, and Airbnb, and complete a Harvard Business School case study. Tuition is 489 USD per month plus a 1,000 USD deposit, with need-based financial aid and full scholarships available for eligible high-potential applicants that do not need to be repaid. TKS reports thousands of alumni, more than 1,000 internships landed by alumni, and dozens of alumni-founded startups.
requirements: Applicants must be between the ages of 13 and 17, though you can be 12 years old at the time of applying. You must be proficient in English and have access to a reliable internet connection. No prior technical or coding knowledge is required, though it can be helpful. TKS states it does not evaluate grades or academic performance as part of its admissions decision.
how_to_apply: Start your application at application.tks.world by selecting the virtual program and submitting basic information, which takes about 2 minutes. Next, answer three short written questions about your experiences and motivations, which takes about 15 to 30 minutes. If you advance, you will be invited to a live interview with a TKS program director, lasting about 30 minutes, to assess your fit for the program. If accepted, you can apply for need-based financial aid, select your preferred cohort time zone from several weekly session options, and pay the 1,000 USD deposit to enroll. The application portal for the next cohort closes July 31, though it may close earlier if all seats fill first.

Teens learn about food justice, job readiness, culinary skills, and sustainable food systems through hands on experience in the school garden, in the kitchen, and at the farmers market. The program runs three sessions each year. The Seed and Grow sessions run after school for about 10 weeks in fall or spring, and the summer Cultivate session runs 6 weeks with job placements in the local food community. Current SFUSD partner schools are Thurgood Marshall Academic High School on Tuesdays and John O'Connell High School on Thursdays, both from 4 to 6pm. The program is free to join and pays participating teens a stipend, and it prioritizes BIPOC students and students who qualify for free or reduced price lunch.
requirements: Must be a current high school student in grades 9 to 12 enrolled at Thurgood Marshall Academic High School or John O'Connell High School, the current SFUSD partner schools. Priority is given to BIPOC students and students who qualify for free or reduced price lunch. Must be able to attend after school sessions on the assigned weekday, Tuesdays or Thursdays from 4 to 6pm, for the full 10 week fall or spring session or the 6 week summer session.
how_to_apply: Check foodwise.org/programs/foodwise-teens for current partner schools, since only students at partner SFUSD schools may apply. Applications open about six weeks before each session start date. Complete the online application when your session opens, then attend all required after school sessions if accepted.

role: Strong Future Las Vegas Youth Employment Program

overview: The Strong Future Las Vegas Youth Employment Program is a City of Las Vegas workforce initiative run with the Mayor's Fund for Las Vegas LIFE, connecting youth and young adults ages 16 to 24 with paid summer jobs and after-school employment. Participants complete a seven session workforce readiness course taught by the University of Nevada Cooperative Extension covering resume writing, time management, interview techniques, ethics, and professionalism. Youth are matched with local employers and supported by an adult advisor throughout the placement. Summer placements typically run about seven weeks from early June to early August at 25 to 30 hours per week; after-school jobs continue during the school year with case management and support services. Applicants must be at least 16 years old, authorized to work in the United States, and have a valid ID and Social Security number. The program is based in and centered on the Historic Westside of Las Vegas.
requirements: Must be age 16 to 24, authorized to work in the United States, and have a valid government ID and Social Security number. Applicants must submit a high school transcript, a letter of recommendation, and proof of school enrollment, and must complete the Strong Future Las Vegas employability readiness training to be eligible for job placement.
how_to_apply: Interested youth sign up through the City of Las Vegas Strong Future program or the Mayor's Fund for Las Vegas LIFE. Contact the city team or the Mayor's Fund for current openings. Staff screen candidates and coordinate interviews with participating employers before placement.

overview:
Audubon Vermont's Junior Conservation Technician (JCT) Program, part of the Youth Conservation Leadership Program (YCLP), is a paid opportunity for Vermont teens ages 14 to 18 to gain practical skills in outdoor and environmental education, wildlife and habitat conservation, and naturalist work. JCTs earn an hourly wage of about 15 dollars while working alongside Audubon staff and Vermont conservation professionals on projects such as bird banding, bird friendly forest management, trail maintenance, and native plant gardening at the Green Mountain Audubon Center in Huntington, Vermont. The program builds leadership, teamwork, and resume skills for teens interested in conservation careers.

The program runs from January through June and meets during school breaks, occasional weekends, and the start of summer, totaling about 150 hours across the 6 month term. It is one of five youth programs offered under the Youth Conservation Leadership Program, alongside Counselors in Training, Youth Conservation Interns, Seasonal Educators, and AmeriCorps positions. overview:
The Mao Research Lab at Kent State University, led by Professor Hanbin Mao, studies mechanoanalytical chemistry, single molecule biophysics, and the structures of nucleic acids such as DNA and RNA. The group brings together graduate students and high school researchers and currently includes three high school students working alongside its doctoral researchers.

company: U.S. Army / Army Educational Outreach Program (AEOP)
deadline: Varies by host site. Each lab sets and publishes its own deadline independently on the AEOP portal. There is no single AEOP-wide deadline.

overview: The Army Educational Outreach Program (AEOP) High School Internship Program places students in paid summer research positions at Army research laboratories and partner university labs across the United States. Rather than one centralized internship, it is a network of dozens of independently run host sites, including Johns Hopkins HEMI, Penn Engineering's GRASP Lab, Northwestern's Center for Synthetic Biology, and NJIT, that each recruit and select their own interns through the shared application portal at aeopinternships-fellowships.org. Students work one on one with a scientist or engineer mentor on Army relevant research spanning materials science, cybersecurity, biology, physics, chemistry, and engineering.
requirements: Applicants must be U.S. citizens or permanent legal residents currently enrolled in grades 10 through 12, with most host sites preferring rising juniors or seniors. Minimum age requirements vary by host site, generally ranging from 14 to 16 years old by the program start date. A genuine interest in STEM research plus a resume, transcript, and short essay are typically required, and some sites also request a teacher recommendation, though exact criteria are set independently by each host lab.
how_to_apply: Create an account on the AEOP Internships and Fellowships portal at aeopinternships-fellowships.org, then use the Search Openings tool to browse current host lab positions by location, research field, or education level. Each posting lists its own eligibility details and deadline, set independently by the host site and commonly falling between late February and mid April. Submit the requested materials, typically a resume, transcript, and short essay, directly through the portal for the specific position. Selection decisions are made by the individual host laboratory rather than a central AEOP office.

overview: The Summer Health Care Internship Program (SHCIP) is a paid internship for high school and postsecondary students, authorized under Minnesota Statute 144.1464 and administered by the Minnesota Hospital Association under contract with the Minnesota Department of Health's Office of Rural Health and Primary Care. Participating hospitals, clinics, nursing facilities, assisted living facilities, and home care providers employ students between Memorial Day and Labor Day for six to 12 weeks. Interns are paid at least Minnesota minimum wage, and the program reimburses employers for up to half of each intern's hourly wages. In 2025, SHCIP placed 117 students in more than 30,000 hours of internship experience across 60 hospitals, clinics, and long term care organizations. Students do not apply through a central portal, they contact and apply directly to a participating site, and each site sets its own process and requirements. The list of participating employers is posted on the Minnesota Hospital Foundation's SHCIP page and updated weekly through the employer sign up deadline each spring.
requirements:
Currently a high school junior or senior, or a postsecondary student.
Genuine interest in a health care career.
No statewide GPA or test score requirement.
Specific requirements vary by participating employer.
Must apply directly to a participating Minnesota hospital, clinic, nursing facility, assisted living facility, or home care provider.
how_to_apply:
1. Visit the Minnesota Hospital Foundation's SHCIP page at mnhospitals.org for program background and the current employer list.
2. Identify a participating hospital, clinic, nursing facility, or home care provider near you.
3. Contact that site directly and apply following its own process; there is no central application portal.
4. Confirm each site's specific deadline and requirements before applying.
5. Apply early in the spring, since positions fill before the summer season begins.

duration: About 10 weeks per cycle, 1-2 hrs/week
overview:
Earth Day Initiative is a New York based environmental nonprofit founded in 1990 that runs year round sustainability programs alongside its annual Earth Day events. Its High School Sustainable Food and Clean Energy Education Fellowship is a remote, seasonal opportunity for high school students who want hands on experience in environmental education. Fellows support the organization sustainable food and clean energy work, which centers on negotiation simulations that place students into stakeholder roles to solve hypothetical challenges around food systems and clean energy in communities such as New York City. The commitment is light, roughly 1 to 2 hours per week over a cycle of about ten weeks, and fellows receive a $200 stipend upon completion. Because it is fully virtual, students from anywhere can take part while building communication and problem solving skills.

Specific fellowship and internship postings rotate throughout the year and are listed on idealist.org, so the exact dates, hours, and stipend can vary by posting. Recent cycles have run in the spring, for example a spring cohort that ran from late March through the end of May. Interested students should watch for the current listing on Idealist and apply through the instructions in that posting, since old listings are removed once a cycle is filled. General questions can be directed to Earth Day Initiative through its website.
requirements: Currently enrolled in high school. No prior experience required, only interest in sustainability, sustainable food, or clean energy topics. Reliable availability for the light weekly commitment of about 1 to 2 hours per week. Because the fellowship is remote, students from any location may apply, though some other Earth Day Initiative roles prefer applicants based in or near New York City.
how_to_apply: Search idealist.org for the current Earth Day Initiative High School Sustainable Food and Clean Energy Education Fellowship posting, since listings rotate seasonally and are removed once filled. Follow the application instructions in the active posting, which typically ask for a short statement of interest and basic contact information. For general inquiries, contact Earth Day Initiative through earthdayinitiative.org or events@earthdayinitiative.org.

overview: The U.S. Department of State's Pathways Internship Program includes two components: the Internship Experience Program (IEP) and the Internship Temporary Program (ITEP). Both are open to U.S. citizens enrolled in accredited educational institutions from high school through graduate school. Interns are paid for the work they perform and explore federal careers. IEP: Interns are appointed to non-temporary, excepted service positions expected to last the length of the academic program; eligible for noncompetitive promotions; eligible for federal employee benefits (life, health, retirement if appointment exceeds 1 year); eligible for noncompetitive conversion to competitive service within 180 days of program completion. ITEP: Temporary appointments (not to exceed 1 year or projected graduation, with extensions possible); allows work during seasonal and holiday breaks as well as year-round; interns working 130+ hours/month for 90+ days may enroll in a health benefits plan; no promotion potential (must reapply through USAJobs for higher-graded positions); not eligible for most other benefits until conversion to competitive service. Vacancy announcements are posted on USAJobs.gov year-round on an as-needed basis. High school students are best suited for ITEP.
requirements:
U.S. citizen
At least 16 years of age by the closing date of the specific vacancy announcement
Currently enrolled in an accredited high school (or higher educational institution)
Minimum 2.0 cumulative GPA at the time of application and throughout internship
Must be able to obtain and maintain a Secret or Top Secret security clearance
Resume and unofficial transcripts required
Proof of enrollment required
Subject to random drug testing
how_to_apply:
1. Visit https://careers.state.gov/interns-fellows/pathways-programs/pathways-internship-programs/ for program overview
2. Search USAJobs.gov for "Department of State Pathways Intern" vacancy announcements
3. Apply to specific vacancy announcements before their listed closing date
4. Follow instructions in each individual vacancy announcement for required documents (resume, transcript, etc.)
