role: Chesapeake Bay Foundation Student Leadership Program
deadline: Rolling (year-round program; check cbf.org/join-us/education-program/student-leadership for enrollment)
duration: Year-round (monthly virtual meetings; optional in-person advocacy and action events; multi-day summer expeditions available separately)
overview:
The Chesapeake Bay Foundation (CBF) Student Leadership Program connects, educates, and inspires the next generation of environmental stewards. CBF was founded in 1967 and is the largest independent conservation organization dedicated solely to saving the Chesapeake Bay.

The Student Leadership program is open year-round to high school students in grades 9–12 living within the Chesapeake Bay watershed (Maryland, Virginia, Pennsylvania, and Washington, D.C.). The program is primarily virtual (monthly Zoom meetings) with optional in-person advocacy, action, and restoration events throughout the watershed.

Program activities include:
• Monthly meetings via Zoom
• Advocacy events (Rally Your Reps in state capitals, meetings with representatives and policymakers)
• Action events (tree plantings to restore riparian buffers, tabling at outreach events)
• Student Action Plan (SAP or SAPling): students select a watershed issue and develop and implement evidence-based community solutions
• Optional multi-day overnight Student Leadership Summer Expeditions (open to rising 9th–12th graders; separate registration required; spots are limited)

NOTE: CBF’s formal internship program (Sally Dudley internships) is for undergraduate and graduate-level degree-seeking students only per CBF’s official FAQ. This Student Leadership program is NOT a paid internship.

Competitiveness: CBF’s own application confirmation page states “This is a competitive process, and space is limited.” Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis.

Compensation: Unpaid - the Student Leadership program is free with no stipend or wage.
requirements:
• Must be a high school student in grades 9–12
• Must live within the Chesapeake Bay watershed (Maryland, Virginia, Pennsylvania, or Washington, D.C.)
• Year-round commitment required: attend monthly virtual meetings, participate in advocacy and action events, and develop a Student Action Plan
• Must follow CBF’s Student Leadership Code of Conduct
• No prior environmental experience required
how_to_apply:
1. Visit https://www.cbf.org/join-us/education-program/student-leadership/ for program information
2. Click "Join the Student Leadership Program" and review the expectations and Code of Conduct
3. Complete the online application: provide required information and answer four short-answer prompts
4. Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis; CBF will notify you shortly of your acceptance status
5. Contact SLcoordinator@cbf.org with any questions

overview:
The ACLU offers internship opportunities through its national office and its state affiliates across the country. High school students are most likely to find placements through a local ACLU affiliate, such as ACLU of Georgia, which explicitly welcomes interns at the high school, undergraduate, graduate, and post graduate level for legal, policy, communications, community engagement, and voter access work. National office internships are 10 to 12 weeks long, remote or hybrid, and include a stipend, though these positions are generally geared toward college students and recent graduates.

Because eligibility, pay, and application windows differ by affiliate, students interested in an ACLU internship should identify the state affiliate nearest them and review that office's specific internship page before applying. Most affiliate internships ask for a resume and a short application form, and some request a writing sample or references. Given the ACLU's mission, this experience suits students interested in civil rights law, policy research, and advocacy work.
requirements: Open to high school, undergraduate, graduate, and post graduate students depending on affiliate (for example ACLU of Georgia). Strong research, writing, and communication skills are expected. Applicants must apply directly through the specific state affiliate's internship page rather than the national ACLU site. how_to_apply: Identify your state's ACLU affiliate online, review that office's current internship openings, and submit the requested resume, application form, and any writing sample directly to the affiliate.

role: Personality Across Development Lab (PADLab) High School Internship
deadline: Rolling
duration: Summer session

overview:
The Personality Across Development Lab (PADLab) at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois is directed by Dr. Jennifer Tackett and studies child and adolescent personality and how it connects to behavior, friendships, and relationships with parents. Researchers examine how early personality traits inform later outcomes, including leadership emergence and entrepreneurial success, how personality can best be measured across development, and how personality, temperament, and psychopathology relate in youth. The lab draws on methods such as clinical interviews, surveys, and behavioral tasks.

Each summer the lab accepts a small class of high school interns who help with tasks such as coding interview data and supporting data collection for ongoing studies. The internship is in person at the lab on Maple Avenue in Evanston and is unpaid, and there is no fixed deadline because interns are taken on a rolling basis for the summer. To be considered, an interested student emails a resume and a short paragraph explaining why they would be a good fit to tackettlab2@gmail.com. Because the class is small, reaching out early improves the chance of a spot.
requirements: The lab accepts a small class of high school interns each summer. Interested students submit a resume and a short paragraph explaining why they would be a good fit for the lab. Work is in person at the lab in Evanston, Illinois. No specific coursework is listed, but a genuine interest in personality psychology and developmental research is expected.
how_to_apply: Email a copy of your resume and a short paragraph about why you think you would be a good fit for the lab to tackettlab2@gmail.com. There is no formal deadline, and interns are taken for the summer, so reach out early to be considered.

Its Teen Internship Program gives high school writers ages 15 to 18 real experience in journalism, education, or publishing. After a short virtual training, interns work in one of three tracks. The Editorial Assistant track is fully virtual and open nationwide, limited to 10 participants, and involves creating original content for PWN marketing and the Bridge Ink young adult literary magazine.

The Interview Project track is in person only, limited to Monmouth County, New Jersey residents, limited to 8 participants, and has interns write narrative journalism pieces published in Bridge Ink. The Teaching Assistant track is also in person only for Monmouth County, New Jersey residents, limited to 8 participants, and has interns assist instructors teaching writing to children in PWN's summer programs. All positions are unpaid, first come first served, and earn community service hours. As of this update, all 2026 positions have been filled, and applications for 2027 are expected to open in February 2027.

overview:
The Miami-Dade State Attorney's Office runs a High School Volunteer Internship Program that gives students a firsthand look at how one of the largest prosecutor's offices in the nation operates within Florida's Eleventh Judicial Circuit. After completing an initial training period, volunteers take on hands-on responsibilities that can include assisting members of the public with criminal and civil questions in person and by phone, taking sworn testimony from victims and witnesses, sitting in on bond hearings, contacting victims for pre-file conferences, running criminal history checks, helping victims with Injunctions for Protection, interviewing subjects, and researching case law. Placements are typically made within units such as Criminal Intake, the Domestic Violence Unit, and the Victim/Witness Unit, so the day-to-day work depends on where a student is assigned.

Interns receive orientation and ongoing training in professional responsibility and ethics, courtroom practice and procedure, and how to work respectfully with victims, witnesses, judges, court staff, and police officers. Most participants are aspiring attorneys, paralegals, or legal assistants, though students interested in social work or criminal justice also take part, and many earn school credit for the experience. The position is unpaid and asks for a commitment of 16 to 20 hours per week for at least one semester, or a minimum of three months, and every applicant must pass a criminal background check before placement. While high schoolers are welcome to apply, the office gives placement preference to undergraduates studying criminal justice or a law enforcement field, and it gives real weight to this experience when later hiring for paid positions.

role: NOAA Fisheries Volunteer and Citizen Science Opportunities
company: NOAA Fisheries (NOAA National Marine Fisheries Service)
deadline: Rolling, no fixed deadline; opportunities depend on each regional office's current needs.
duration: Varies widely by office and project, from single one time citizen science events to multi week or summer long volunteer placements
grades: Grades 9-12 can generally join lighter citizen science activities such as species reporting, but formal in office or in lab volunteer placements often set stricter minimum ages that are not standardized nationwide; the NOAA Fisheries West Coast Region specifically accepts volunteers only 18 or older on a case by case basis, which excludes most high schoolers there
overview: NOAA Fisheries does not run one single, centrally administered high school volunteer program. Instead it offers decentralized, informal volunteer and citizen science opportunities through its regional offices, including Alaska, West Coast, Pacific Islands, Southeast, and Greater Atlantic, and through individual science center labs nationwide. Activities can include tagging fish, monitoring sea turtles and marine mammals, assisting with at sea biological sampling surveys, and supporting lab based research such as at the Milford Laboratory in Connecticut. Because there is no single national portal, opportunities, eligibility, and openings vary by office and season, so students should expect to contact local staff directly rather than submit one common application. Students seeking a structured, paid, high school fisheries research internship should also look at the Hutton Junior Fisheries Biology Program, which is run by the American Fisheries Society with many NOAA Fisheries scientists serving as mentors.
requirements: Requirements vary by office since there is no unified program. General citizen science participation, such as species reporting or shellfish and turtle monitoring, has few restrictions and is open to students of many ages, often with parental involvement expected for minors. Formal volunteer placements inside NOAA Fisheries labs and vessels tend to require a minimum age; for example the NOAA Fisheries West Coast Region generally only accepts volunteers 18 years or older on a case by case basis, which excludes most high school students in that region specifically. Prospective volunteers should confirm the exact age minimum, any school credit or liability waiver paperwork, and citizenship or background check requirements with their chosen regional office before applying, since these details are not standardized nationwide.
how_to_apply: There is no single national application. Interested students should identify the nearest NOAA Fisheries regional office or science center, then check whether that office uses a Volunteer Interest Form, as several regions including the West Coast do, or otherwise email a resume and short letter of interest directly to that office's volunteer or education coordinator. Students can also browse NOAA's broader student opportunities database and CitizenScience.gov for open, less age restricted citizen science projects that support NOAA Fisheries research.
ApplicationChecklist: Find nearest NOAA Fisheries office|Check for a Volunteer Interest Form|Email office's volunteer coordinator|Submit resume and letter of interest|Confirm age rules for that office

role: Law: Analyze, Argue, and Advocate Like a Lawyer
deadline: Rolling (multiple start dates offered year-round)

overview: Georgetown University offers an online pre-college course titled Law: Analyze, Argue, and Advocate Like a Lawyer, open to students ages 13 and up. It has two formats: an Enrichment Course costing 1,895 dollars that runs 1, 2, or 4 weeks with 20 to 30 hours of instruction and a Pass/Fail grade, and a College Credit Course costing 3,995 dollars that runs 6, 8, or 12 weeks with 128 hours of instruction, a letter grade, and transferable Georgetown college credit. Both formats are self paced online, include mentor or TA support, and end with a Final Capstone Project analyzing a legal scenario. The curriculum covers the foundations and sources of law, fact investigation and discovery tools, legal argument construction, courtroom advocacy and witness examination, and constitutional rights such as the Fourth Amendment. The course is taught by Alexandra Clark, J.D., a practicing attorney and Georgetown faculty member. Admissions run on a rolling basis with multiple start dates throughout the year, and the site describes the application process as simple with a prompt decision. Need based scholarships are available for students who cannot pay the full tuition, requested after submitting the application. Students receive a Certificate of Completion, and College Credit students also receive an official Georgetown transcript. This specific course is delivered entirely online with no in-person Washington D.C. component.
requirements: Ages 13 and up. No prerequisite coursework listed. Tuition payment required; need-based scholarships available for qualifying students who submit a scholarship request after applying.
how_to_apply: Apply online at georgetown.precollegeprograms.org/law. Rolling admissions with multiple course start dates year-round. Application process is described as simple with a prompt admissions decision. Scholarship requests are made after submitting the application.

Students choose a self paced curriculum track in Game Design, Data Science, Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity, or Web Development and take roughly six to seven weeks to complete course projects at their own pace. deadline: Rolling
duration: Summer plus school year
overview:
The Burke Lab at the University of Missouri, led by Dr. Donald Burke, is an interdisciplinary research group based in the Bond Life Sciences Center in Columbia, Missouri. The lab studies the biochemistry and biology of RNA and related nucleic acids, using aptamers and ribozymes generated through SELEX to investigate questions ranging from the origin of life and the RNA World to anti-HIV gene therapy and targeted molecular delivery.

For several years the research team has included exceptional high school students, drawn from local Columbia high schools such as Rock Bridge and Hickman, who work half to full time during the summer before their senior year and up to about 10 hours per week during the school year. Students are fully integrated into designing, running, and analyzing original research, so reliability, attention to detail, and communication matter. The position is unpaid with no fixed deadline, and interested students apply by emailing Dr. Burke directly and looping in their guidance counselor and science teachers.
requirements: The lab looks for reliable, detail oriented students with a strong interest in RNA biochemistry and molecular biology who can commit to in person lab work at the Bond Life Sciences Center in Columbia. Past high school members have come from local Columbia high schools, reflecting the ongoing time commitment during the school year.
how_to_apply: Contact Dr. Donald Burke through the lab at burkelab@missouri.edu. Also contact your guidance counselor and science teachers so they can help you plan how the research experience fits into your school and college plans. The page lists no fixed deadline.

role: Summer Research Program with Columbia University
deadline: Rolling

overview:

The first two weeks cover foundational skills including the R programming language, data visualization, data cleaning and wrangling, web scraping, and research protocol. In the remaining three weeks, students join a research team led by Columbia PhD researchers and apply what they learned to a real, faculty guided data science project spanning fields such as medicine, finance, and sports analytics.

overview: The Northrop Grumman High School Involvement Partnership (HIP) is a highly selective two year mentoring program for high school juniors and seniors at Northrop Grumman partner schools across the United States, with about 100 students selected nationwide each year. deadline: Rolling

overview:

HEPL occasionally offers summer internships and research positions in its labs for undergraduate students and, at times, for high school students. Placements depend on current lab needs and availability, so interested students inquire directly rather than applying to a fixed program.

overview: The Los Angeles City Attorney's Office - one of the nation's largest municipal law offices - accepts high school students as volunteer interns through its Law Clerk and Volunteer (Internship) Program. The Office has over 1,000 legal professionals including 500 attorneys and provides the City of Los Angeles with legal services ranging from prosecuting criminal misdemeanors and advising on homelessness initiatives to defending civil lawsuits. High school student volunteers assist City Attorney staff with legal research, document preparation, and administrative support. The standard internship is unpaid (volunteer). overview:
The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of New York (USAO-EDNY) offers unpaid student volunteer internships throughout the year in both the Brooklyn and Central Islip offices. The EDNY covers Brooklyn, Queens, Staten Island, Nassau, and Suffolk counties.

CONFIRMED FROM OFFICIAL EDNY PAGE (justice.gov/usao-edny/employment/internship-programs):
• High school eligibility is specifically for ENTERING SENIORS (rising 12th graders) - not open to all grades 9-12
• ALL students must be U.S. citizens - this is a firm requirement
• Internship areas include: pre-law, criminal justice, accounting, information technology, library management, human resources, and community crime prevention
• All offers are contingent on receiving a federal security clearance

Application materials required: cover letter (including area of placement interest, educational course of study, and degree goals), updated resume, most recent unofficial school transcript, and a list of three references (academic or professional).

Send application package to: USANYE-SummerInterns@usdoj.gov

Applications are reviewed on an ongoing basis. Students are called for an interview by a supervisor in the office.

Compensation: Unpaid - student volunteer positions. Academic credit can be arranged through your school.
requirements:
• Must be an entering senior (rising 12th grade student) in an accredited high school
• Must be a U.S. citizen - this is confirmed as a firm requirement
• Strong interest in law, criminal justice, public service, accounting, IT, library management, HR, or community crime prevention
• Must successfully complete a Department of Justice background/security clearance process before starting
• Available on a consistent schedule for the duration of the internship session
how_to_apply:
1. Prepare your application package: cover letter (indicating area of interest, educational course of study, degree goals), updated resume, most recent unofficial transcript, a list of three academic or professional references, AND name and contact information of a representative from your school
2. Email the complete package to: USANYE-HRRequest@usdoj.gov for general or fall/spring positions; USANYE-SummerInterns@usdoj.gov for summer positions
3. If applying to multiple areas, specify each area of interest in your cover letter
4. Applications are reviewed on an ongoing basis
5. If selected, you will be contacted by a supervisor to schedule an interview; schedules are flexible
6. If offered a position, complete all required security clearance documents before starting (background investigation required; can take several weeks)
7. Visit https://www.justice.gov/usao-edny/student-internship-opportunities for full details

overview:
The Ecology & Aquaria Academy is a practical apprenticeship and training program offered by the Environmental Learning Center (ELC), a nonprofit nature center on a 64-acre campus on an island in the Indian River Lagoon in Vero Beach, Florida. It is open to teens, college students, and adults ages 16 and up, and is a separate, ongoing program from ELC's seasonal summer internship, which is limited to Indian River County residents and runs on its own yearly application cycle.

This fee-based program gives participants 30 hours of practical training that can flex around the participant's schedule. Topics covered include water quality and chemistry, filtration systems, animal nutrition, life support systems, animal identification and collection techniques, quarantine procedures, and disease identification and treatment. The program is led by Brent Rupnik, ELC's Senior Aquarist, and is designed to build resume experience and give participants insight into careers in environmental education and aquarium management.

Compensation: Paid program, students pay a $750 program fee. Need based scholarships are available through ELC's Maggy Bowman Scholarship for those who qualify.
requirements: Applicants must be at least 16 years old; the program is open to teens, college students, and adults. A $750 program fee is required, though need based scholarships are available through ELC's Maggy Bowman Scholarship for those who qualify. The program involves practical work with aquarium water quality and chemistry, filtration systems, animal nutrition, life support systems, and live animal handling. Applicants apply through the online form linked from the ELC internships page, and spaces are limited.
how_to_apply: Go to discoverelc.org/internships and find the Ecology and Aquaria Academy section. If you need fee assistance, review the Maggy Bowman Scholarship page and application. Click Apply Today and complete the online Google Form to apply. Coordinate with ELC to schedule your 30 training hours around your availability. Pay the $750 program fee, or confirm your approved scholarship, to secure your spot. Attend practical training sessions led by ELC's Senior Aquarist, Brent Rupnik.
ApplicationChecklist: Visit discoverelc.org/internships|Check Maggy Bowman Scholarship page|Click Apply Today, fill out form|Schedule 30 hours of training with ELC|Pay $750 fee or confirm scholarship|Train under Senior Aquarist Brent Rupnik

duration: Internships run year-round; length and weekly hours vary by the county department and assignment
overview:
The Student Internship Program with the County of Santa Clara is designed to nurture the educational and professional development of promising job candidates while they are still in school. Student Intern, Level I is the entry tier of the program, reserved for high school students who are enrolled in regular high school classes, enrolled in an alternative vocational high school, or working toward a high school equivalency credential. Interns assist professional and technical county employees in the performance of their duties under close supervision, with specific tasks varying widely depending on which county agency or department the student is placed with. Placements run year round based on departmental need rather than a fixed academic calendar.

Because assignments are distributed across dozens of county departments including the Office of the District Attorney, Behavioral Health Services, Public Health, and Parks and Recreation, the day to day work and subject matter can span many fields such as administration, law and advocacy, social services, environment, and public health. There is currently no open Level I posting, so interested students are encouraged to sign up for email alerts on the Student Intern, Level I job specification page or to contact specific county departments directly to express interest, since departments can reach out to the program coordinator when they want to hire a candidate. Compensation is a genuine hourly wage set on the county's five step student intern salary schedule, and students may be required to pass a Live Scan background check or physical examination depending on the assignment.
requirements: To qualify for the Student Intern, Level I classification, applicants must have a legal right to work in the United States and be enrolled in an accredited high school, an alternative vocational high school, or working toward high school equivalency (or have graduated within the last six months). Applicants must have an overall grade point average of at least 2.5 on a four point scale. High school students under eighteen years old will need a work permit, obtainable through a high school counselor or the California Employment Development Department. Depending on the assignment, applicants may also be required to pass a Live Scan background check or a physical examination. A completed county job application, official or unofficial transcript, and proof of current enrollment or a course schedule are required as part of the application.
how_to_apply: Because there is no active Level I posting at this time, students should sign up for email job alerts by visiting the Student Intern, Level I classification specification on the county's GovernmentJobs site and clicking the subscribe button, so they are notified the moment a posting opens. In the meantime, students can also reach out directly to individual county departments they are interested in (such as the District Attorney's Office, Behavioral Health Services, Public Health, or Parks) to express interest, since departments may contact the Student Intern Coordinator to request a specific candidate be brought into the program. When a posting does open, applicants submit an online application along with their most recent transcript and proof of enrollment through the county's GovernmentJobs careers portal. Applications are reviewed as departments submit staffing requests, and inactive applications are purged after six months, after which a student may reapply.
ApplicationChecklist: Sign up for job alerts|Gather official transcript|Provide enrollment proof|Get work permit if under 18

role: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Student Volunteer Internship
deadline: Rolling; varies by EPA office and posting
duration: Varies (typically 8 to 12 weeks, flexible)
grades: Grades 9-12 (varies by office)
overview:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency offers several types of internship opportunities for students, including high schoolers, through individual EPA offices across the country. Paid Pathways internships, open to students enrolled at least half time in college, are posted on USAJobs.gov and are competitive, with salaries based on the GS-02 to GS-07 pay scale. Unpaid Student Volunteer placements are also listed by individual offices, including the ten regional offices and the Washington DC headquarters, though availability specifically for high school volunteers is not guaranteed and varies by office and year.

Because there is no single national application portal for high school volunteers, students should identify the EPA office nearest them and reach out directly to ask about current openings. The EPA careers site also lists internship FAQs and hiring FAQs to help students understand federal internship pathways, along with externally funded placement options through partner organizations such as the Hispanic Association of Colleges and Universities, the National Congress of American Indians, and the Washington Center. Compensation: unpaid for student volunteer placements; Pathways internships are paid but require at least half time college enrollment.
requirements: Currently enrolled in high school with permission from your school to participate. Strong interest in environmental science, policy, public health, or a related field is helpful. Most EPA offices require U.S. citizenship or work authorization. Specific eligibility varies by office.
how_to_apply: Visit epa.gov/careers/students to review internship types and FAQs. Identify the EPA regional office or headquarters office closest to you. Contact that office's HR or volunteer coordinator directly to ask about high school volunteer openings. Prepare a resume and short cover letter describing your interest in EPA's mission. If accepted, complete any required volunteer agreement and background paperwork.
ApplicationChecklist: Visit epa.gov careers/students page|Find your nearest EPA office|Email office about volunteer openings|Send a resume and cover letter|Complete volunteer paperwork

The Tumber-Dávila Lab at Dartmouth College studies forests, roots, and global change, working to understand interactions between ecosystems and a changing climate.

The Solar Energy Activity Lab, known as SEAL, is a Caltech outreach program in which graduate students and postdocs mentor high school clubs conducting research on sustainable energy.

Participants develop research questions, perform literature searches, and build problem solving skills.

overview: The Teen Writers Collective (TWC) at 826NYC is a free, year long creative writing and leadership program for New York City teen writers in grades 8 through 12. The group meets weekly on Friday afternoons from 4:30 to 6:00 PM at 826NYC Park Slope center in Brooklyn to write, workshop, and build a community of young authors, poets, and playwrights. Throughout the year, members create original work in a variety of genres, publish a professionally designed book, take field trips, and learn from guest authors, culminating in a public celebration of their writing. TWC is limited to students whose families fall at or below 80 percent of the Area Median Income, about 137,000 dollars a year for a family of four. Students who are 14 or older and who have participated in TWC for at least three months become eligible to apply for 826NYC separate paid summer internship, which supports younger workshop students and includes a creative capstone project. overview: Gaylor Electric High School Summer Internship is a paid 8 week program, early June to late July, that places students as entry level electricians either on a traditional construction job site or in one of Gaylor's Production and Innovation Centers. The program begins with a week of orientation at the students local Gaylor Electric office, after which the student is assigned to a site generally within about 30 miles of home. Interns work standard field hours for 40 hours a week and are paid hourly, and they receive resume development, interview prep, professionalism training, and a craft skills assessment. deadline: Rolling, no fixed deadline (student summer research opportunities are arranged informally through a QuarkNet affiliated physics teacher or the local QuarkNet center; contact your teacher or the Fermilab/University of Chicago/College of DuPage QuarkNet Center to inquire)
duration: Summer (schedule varies by year and host center; contact the local QuarkNet center for current dates)
grades: Not specified (high school students)
overview:
QuarkNet is a nationwide National Science Foundation funded partnership between the University of Notre Dame and Fermilab that connects high school physics teachers and their students with particle physics research. Fermilab operates a local QuarkNet Center together with the University of Chicago and the College of DuPage, one of about 50 QuarkNet centers nationally. This local center periodically hosts high school students for informal summer research placements with Fermilab scientists, in addition to teacher workshops, classroom support, and single day Masterclass events where students analyze real particle physics data. There is no online application, deadline, or stated pay for these placements, since participation is arranged through a student's own QuarkNet affiliated physics teacher rather than a published national process.

Students who want a formally structured, paid Fermilab high school summer program should instead look at Fermilab PRISM (Program for Research Innovation and STEM Mentorship) at internships.fnal.gov, a four week paid program for Illinois high school seniors and recent graduates that pays $500 per week and runs a defined January through March application window ahead of a mid July start. QuarkNet remains the right listing for students whose physics teacher already has a QuarkNet affiliation and who are exploring an informal, teacher arranged summer research connection at Fermilab, Batavia, IL.
requirements:
Enrolled in high school with a strong interest in physics, mathematics, or particle physics
A connection to a QuarkNet affiliated teacher or center is typically required
Must be able to arrange own housing and transportation to Fermilab in Batavia, IL for any in person research period
Specific eligibility (grade level, citizenship, availability) is set by the local QuarkNet center each year
No stated pay for QuarkNet placements; see Fermilab PRISM (internships.fnal.gov) for a paid, formally structured alternative
how_to_apply: Ask your physics teacher whether your school participates in QuarkNet, or find a nearby center at quarknet.org. Contact the Fermilab/University of Chicago/College of DuPage QuarkNet Center directly at quarknet.fnal.gov/fnal-uc for current summer research availability, or email the Fermilab Education Office at spasero@fnal.gov with questions. Students interested in a formally structured, paid Fermilab high school summer program with a published deadline should also consider Fermilab PRISM at internships.fnal.gov.

overview:
Genesys Works is a national workforce development nonprofit that prepares high school juniors from underserved communities for career success through professional skills training and a paid corporate internship. Students apply during the fall or winter of their junior year at a partner high school, then complete eight weeks of summer skills training covering technical and professional competencies before beginning a year long, 20 hour per week paid internship at a corporate partner such as Accenture, JPMorgan Chase, 3M, or Target during their senior year.

The program operates in nine metro regions: the Bay Area, Chicago, Houston, Jacksonville, Nashville, the National Capital Region, New York City, Tulsa, and the Twin Cities, and only accepts students from partner high schools in those areas. Interns earn between ten thousand and thirteen thousand dollars over the internship year and receive ongoing college and career coaching, along with alumni support after graduation to help them navigate postsecondary education.

how_to_apply: Confirm whether Genesys Works partners with your high school in one of its 9 markets (check genesysworks.org/for-students-and-families). Participants also attend weekly Scientific Seminars from Coriell faculty and outside speakers, take part in small-group career development sessions on resumes, interviewing, and career planning, and finish the program with a formal presentation to Coriell staff and peers. overview: Immerse Education's actual online computer science offering is the Computer Science Online Research Programme; a program named SPARK does not appear anywhere on Immerse Education's website. Immerse Education is a UK based provider, founded in 2012, best known for in-person Oxbridge style summer schools, that also runs online research programmes across subjects including computer science, artificial intelligence, and coding. The programme pairs each participant one to one with a dedicated subject tutor, typically a current or former student at Oxford, Cambridge, or an Ivy League institution, to complete a university style academic research project in computer science. The Classic Online Research Programme option totals 10 hours of tutoring for participants ages 13 to 18 and costs 2,995 British pounds. The program is supported by NSF award 2109688 and focuses on providing opportunities for students underrepresented in STEM. Each cohort includes about 3 to 4 high school students who meet lab members, learn about ongoing research, and are introduced to computing and data analysis techniques including Python and R programming, genomics, and longitudinal data analysis. Lunch and a one week prepaid Metro card are provided; there is no wage or stipend.

overview: Launched in 2007, the Diversity Pipeline Internship Program gives rising seniors from underserved public high schools a paid opportunity to learn about the legal profession, prepare for higher education, and build practical life skills. Interns assist various administrative departments at the firm while taking part in a curriculum of weekly seminars covering the practice of law, the college application process, and resume and interview skills. Highlights include a mock trial program, a negotiation clinic, a college panel with attorneys and law and undergraduate students, a field trip to the local courthouse with a judge, and a field trip to a corporate client. Attorneys and staff mentor interns throughout the program and continue supporting them into the college application season. The firm has had 69 interns since 2007, and in 2024 four interns came from Balboa High School in San Francisco through the Bar Association of San Francisco Law Academy.

Kalei Akiona at 415-954-3530 or Emily Nord at 415-954-3516, for current application details.

overview: The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) Student Volunteer Employment Program (SVEP) provides students with an opportunity to gain valuable work experience in a federal immigration services agency while in school. USCIS processes applications for visas, green cards, citizenship, and asylum. Student volunteers are placed at USCIS offices across the country based on geographic preference and area of interest. Managers nationwide are looking for students with a range of interests and skill sets to help fulfill the USCIS mission. Available areas of interest include immigration, policy development, criminal investigation, IT, public affairs, human resources, and many more. The internship is unpaid, but students can arrange to earn school credit. USCIS has offices in dozens of cities, making this accessible to students across the country. Compensation: Unpaid. Academic credit available.

Southwest Airlines periodically offers a paid summer High School Internship through its Campus Reach program at its Corporate Campus in Dallas, Texas. As of this check, Southwest is not actively listing an open high school internship posting on its K-12 resources page; the page instead directs interested students to a general interest form and highlights partner programs such as the Organization of Black Aerospace Professionals ACE Academy and Women in Aviation International's Girls in Aviation Day.

Students who want to be considered for a future internship should submit the high school interest form linked on the K-12 resources page. overview: The Maureen and Mike Mansfield Center at the University of Montana, founded by an Act of Congress in 1983, is a nonpartisan academic center focused on public diplomacy, ethics in public affairs, and East Asian studies. The Center offers short term internships, generally five to eight weeks long, for outstanding Montana high school students interested in public diplomacy and international exchange. Internship hours can be scheduled after school, during the summer, and in some cases on weekends or evenings, depending on the student and the specific Mansfield program involved. There is no fixed application deadline; interested students work with Mansfield Center staff to create an internship by submitting an online interest form. The Center also runs several other high school programs, including the Mansfield Civics Institute, the Civics Forum, the Taiwan Spring Study Tour, and Project Bridge, though these are separate programs from the general internship track. Contact the Center directly to confirm current details.

Contact the Mansfield Center directly with questions about current openings.

overview:
Seaside Sustainability is a Gloucester, Massachusetts based 501(c)(3) environmental nonprofit running a year round, primarily virtual internship program for high school students. Interns commit to a minimum of 15 hours per week (up to 40) for at least a 5 month term, renewable in 2.5 or 5 month increments. Interns choose a team such as Climate Action and Advocacy, Green Scholars, Marine Science and Technology, Sustainability Consulting, Business Operations, Grant Writing, Human Resources, Marketing and Public Relations, or Website and Technology. A seasonal in-person option also exists for the Marine Science and Technology team in the Cape Ann and Gloucester, MA area, running roughly May through October, involving fieldwork such as eelgrass and seabin monitoring and water quality testing.

Compensation: Unpaid. Interns can receive academic credit through their own school and may qualify for the President's Volunteer Service Award. Interns who complete a term in good standing are also offered a free membership in the National STEM Honor Society.

company: New York University (Jonesy Lab, Department of Chemistry)
deadline: Rolling (contact lab)
duration: 5 weeks
overview:
The LiNC Program is a summer research outreach program run by the Jonesy Lab in the NYU Department of Chemistry. Its name reflects its mission of linking STEM-focused high school students with undergraduate and graduate mentors who are just steps ahead of them to study the largely uncharacterized world of long noncoding RNA. Each year the lab organizes a team of graduate students, Jonesy Lab undergraduates, and high school students to probe RNA structure and RNA protein interactions both bioinformatically and experimentally.

Over five weeks students learn to plan and carry out experiments, work through the math related to chemistry, present their research in talks and writing, and can be acknowledged in publications, with students returning each summer to continue the work. The program takes four to six students per year who work in groups of two or three and must be present for all five weeks. It is free and provides a stipend, with housing offered for out of state participants, and it is supported by NSF RAHSS, VWR, and the NYU Office of the Dean for Science.
requirements: Open to high school students who live in the United States and have completed at least their freshman year of high school. Students must have at least a B average in their science, math, and physics courses and be genuinely interested in scientific research. Participants must be present for all five weeks. The program takes four to six students per year who work in groups of two or three.
how_to_apply: Applications are handled directly by the Jonesy Lab. Interested high school students should reach out through the lab outreach page to express interest and learn the current cycle process. Participants receive a stipend, and housing is provided for out of state students. The program is supported by NSF RAHSS, VWR, and the NYU Office of the Dean for Science.
ApplicationChecklist: Live in US, freshman year done|Keep a B average in science/math|Available all five weeks|Contact Jonesy Lab to apply

Each training earns a certificate of participation equal to one hour of community or volunteer service, which students can use toward school service hour requirements. Ambassadors who share how the program helped them create impact in their community may be featured in the program newsletter, Impact! Note: this is not a paid internship placement program. Participants are volunteers who receive service hour certificates rather than compensation.

Interns work in remote teams with mission-driven young people nationwide to amplify youth civic engagement and work on issues they care about. Responsibilities include grassroots team functions, local voter registration and turnout projects, writing summaries and reflections shared across teams, and research into the history of activism, civics, and social justice. Interns develop communication, leadership, critical thinking, writing, collaboration, public speaking, and grassroots organizing skills, and are encouraged to engage with a network of guest speakers. deadline: Rolling
duration: At least 2 months
overview:
The Torres-Vazquez Lab at NYU Langone Health, led by Associate Professor Jesus Torres-Vazquez in the Department of Cell Biology, studies the cellular and molecular mechanisms that shape the development and function of blood and lymphatic vessels. The lab uses the transparent zebrafish embryo as its primary model and welcomes students and individuals to volunteer and support its research mission.

Volunteers gain hands on exposure to techniques such as confocal imaging, gene expression analysis, transgenesis, genome editing, cell transplantation, cell culture, and biochemistry. Applicants must be at least 16 years old when they apply, which opens the role to high school students, and are asked to commit for at least two months and to share their weekly availability. Work happens primarily on weekdays and can range from a few hours to 40 hours per week, and volunteers are onboarded through NYU Langone Human Resources as Non-Employee Volunteers about 30 days after the principal investigator agrees to the placement. The position is unpaid and is open to anyone the lab can accommodate.
requirements: Volunteers must be at least 16 years old at the time they apply, which makes the opportunity open to high school students. The lab asks volunteers to commit for at least two months and to share their weekly availability. Volunteers are onboarded through NYU Langone Human Resources as Non-Employee Volunteers, which takes about 30 days after the principal investigator agrees to the placement.
how_to_apply: Email Dr. Jesus Torres-Vazquez at Jtorresv@NYULangone.org to inquire about volunteering. Specify your availability by days and times so the lab can assess feasibility. After the principal investigator agrees, expect about 30 days for Human Resources authorization and onboarding as a Non-Employee Volunteer.
ApplicationChecklist: Be at least 16 when you apply|Email Jtorresv@NYULangone.org|Share days and times you are free|Commit at least two months

role: National Park Service Youth Conservation Corps (YCC) Internship
deadline: Varies by park; 2027 dates not yet posted
duration: 8-10 weeks (up to 18 in some parks), Summer, full-time (40 hrs/week)
overview:
The Youth Conservation Corps (YCC) is a federal youth employment program administered by the National Park Service, U.S. Forest Service, and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Participants aged 15-18 work at national parks, forests, wildlife refuges, and fish hatcheries on projects such as trail building, fence maintenance, campground cleanup, wildlife habitat improvement, historic preservation, and STEM-based field science, while earning at least state or federal minimum wage for roughly 40 hours a week.

Most YCC placements are day programs: participants commute to the site daily and must arrange their own transportation and housing, since the NPS generally does not provide either. Yellowstone National Park is the sole exception, offering an overnight program with onsite housing for non-local applicants. Each participating park sets its own session dates (mostly early June through early to mid August), deadlines, and point of contact, so applicants must check the annually updated opportunities list and contact the specific park directly.
requirements: Applicants must be 15 through 18 years old and permanent residents of the United States. Because YCC is a local, commuter-based program, applicants generally need to be able to travel to and from the host park site daily (Yellowstone is the exception, providing onsite housing).
how_to_apply:
1. Review the YCC Participating Parks list on nps.gov to find a park near you (or Yellowstone, which offers housing).
2. Download and complete the DI-4014 YCC Application form (PDF).
3. Email the completed form directly to that park's listed point of contact using the firstname_lastname@nps.gov format.
4. Confirm the park's specific session dates and deadline, as these vary by location.
ApplicationChecklist: Visit nps.gov YCC opportunities page|Pick a participating park near you|Download DI-4014 application form|Email completed form to park POC|Confirm session dates and deadline
Opens: Varies by park; 2026 apps opened ~Jan, closed Feb-Jun

overview:
The Delaware Museum of Nature and Science in Wilmington, Delaware offers several teen involvement opportunities. The S.T.E.A.M. Separately, through the New Castle County Youth Workforce Development Program, the museum hosts up to five youth ages 14-21 in paid summer (and possibly year-round) positions at a rate of $12.50 per hour. deadline: Rolling
duration: One year
grades: Grade 11 (juniors)
overview:
The PCTA Robotics Internship is a year long program created through a partnership between Brown University's Department of Computer Science and the Providence Career and Technical Academy (PCTA), a technical high school in the Providence Public School District. Running since 2016, it serves roughly 50 PCTA pre-engineering students and is built around a curriculum modeled after Brown's Introduction to Robotics course, designed by Associate Professor of Computer Science Stefanie Tellex. Students learn the fundamentals of robotics by building and programming drones on the Brown campus, mentored by Brown computer science faculty and staff.

Pre-engineering students first tour the Brown robotics labs as sophomores, then complete the hands on internship as juniors, working alongside lab coordinators and researchers. The experience helps fulfill the PCTA requirement that students complete 80 hours of work based learning before graduation. The internship is embedded in the PCTA pre-engineering pathway rather than offered through a separate public application, so it is open only to enrolled PCTA students in Providence, Rhode Island, and there is no cost to participate and no stipend.
requirements: Open to pre-engineering students at the Providence Career and Technical Academy in the Providence Public School District. Students tour the robotics labs as sophomores and complete the internship as juniors. The internship helps fulfill the PCTA requirement of 80 hours of work-based learning before graduation.
how_to_apply: The internship is offered through the pre-engineering program at the Providence Career and Technical Academy in partnership with the Brown Department of Computer Science. Interested students should speak with their PCTA pre-engineering instructors. There is no separate public application.
ApplicationChecklist: Enroll at Providence Career Tech Academy|Join the pre-engineering program|Tour Brown robotics labs as sophomore|Start year-long internship as junior

deadline: Rolling

overview: UpCode by theCoderSchool is a virtual summer internship designed to give high school students (ages 15 to 18) a real software engineering experience. Students work in small teams of 3 to 6 to build a software product based on a client's requirements, collaborating using industry standard tools like GitHub and Slack, managing deadlines and sprint milestones, and receiving guidance from a Project Manager and Client Partner. Each team's project culminates in a formal group presentation and private performance evaluations. All interns also receive a free group session from Collegewise on how to highlight the UpCode experience on college applications. For Summer 2026 the program is remote, with the possibility of in-person teams depending on team member locations. A program fee of $3,000 applies, and students or their families pay to participate. Financial aid may be available.
requirements: Must be a high school student ages 15 to 18. company: NYC Department of Citywide Administrative Services (DCAS) Fleet Division
deadline: Not publicly posted (coordinated through school)
duration: Six weeks and/or 150 hours, starting the beginning of July
grades: Open only to students attending one of nine NYC Department of Education Career and Technical Education automotive high schools: Alfred E. Smith CTE High School, A-Tech, Aviation CTE High School, Co-Op Tech, Ralph McKee CTE High School, Thomas Edison CTE High School, Tottenville High School, Transit Tech CTE High School, and William E. Grady CTE High School. Not open to general NYC high school students.
overview:
DCAS partners with the NYC Department of Education's Career and Technical Education (CTE) automotive high schools to offer a paid summer internship giving students hands-on experience maintaining high-profile City vehicles. Interns are placed with partner agencies such as the NYPD, FDNY, DOT, DSNY, and DCAS itself, and work alongside City fleet professionals who service one of the largest municipal fleets in the country. Interns gain experience diagnosing equipment, performing basic maintenance, using automotive shop equipment, and learning fleet and claims management.

The program begins in early July and runs for six weeks and/or a total of 150 hours. It is open only to students at nine designated CTE automotive high schools: Alfred E. Smith CTE High School, A-Tech, Aviation Career and Technical Education High School, Co-Op Tech, Ralph McKee CTE High School, Thomas Edison CTE High School, Tottenville High School, Transit Tech CTE High School, and William E. Grady CTE High School. There is no public application process for students, as participation is coordinated through each school's CTE program. Agencies interested in hosting interns apply directly by contacting DCAS Fleet at NYCfleet@dcas.nyc.gov; no fixed public deadline is posted for student applicants.
requirements:
Must attend one of the nine participating CTE automotive high schools: Alfred E. Smith CTE HS, A-Tech, Aviation CTE HS, Co-Op Tech, Ralph McKee CTE HS, Thomas Edison CTE HS, Tottenville HS, Transit Tech CTE HS, William E. Grady CTE HS
Legally authorized to work in New York City, with a work permit if under 18
Able to commute to an assigned fleet repair garage in the five boroughs
how_to_apply:
This internship is coordinated through the participating CTE automotive high schools rather than a direct public application
Speak with your automotive CTE teacher or school coordinator about applying
Agencies interested in hosting interns can email DCAS Fleet at NYCfleet@dcas.nyc.gov
ApplicationChecklist: Confirm enrollment at a participating CTE automotive high school|Speak with CTE teacher or coordinator|Obtain work permit if under 18|Await placement with a City fleet garage

role: U.S. Department of Energy Student Experience Program
deadline: Rolling; apply each semester
duration: 8-16 weeks
overview:
The U.S. Department of Energy's Student Experience Program is an unpaid volunteer internship open to students from high school through graduate school, offered year round across DOE headquarters and field offices nationwide. Participants can be placed in roles spanning communication, cybersecurity, human resources, information technology, law, policy, STEM, public affairs, personnel security, and safety, with DOE tailoring each placement to the student's interests and skills.

To qualify, applicants must be enrolled at least half time, be at least 18 years old, maintain a 2.0 GPA or higher, be a U.S. citizen or national, and commit to an assignment of 8 to 16 weeks tied to a fall, spring, or summer semester. DOE does not pay interns or provide housing, though a transportation stipend may be available. Students apply on a rolling basis through DOE's Handshake page by submitting a resume, unofficial transcripts, and a letter of enrollment verification.
requirements: Enrolled at least half-time in high school (typically senior year), trade school, or college. Minimum 2.0 GPA on a 4.0 scale. Must be a U.S. citizen or U.S. national. Commit to an 8-16 week assignment. Must complete a background investigation and fingerprinting if selected.
how_to_apply: Create a Handshake account, browse DOE opportunities at app.joinhandshake.com/emp/employers/44165, and submit a resume, unofficial transcripts, and an enrollment verification letter.
ApplicationChecklist: Resume, transcripts, enrollment letter

company: Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History

overview: Elite yearlong advisory council founded in 2014 for high-achieving middle and high school students (grades 8–12) strongly interested in American history. Members meet virtually on the second Saturday of each month at 1 p.m. ET. Each meeting includes: providing feedback on Gilder Lehrman Institute programs and materials; a presentation about a historical document from the Gilder Lehrman Collection by a curator; and guest speaker presentations or presentations by fellow SAC members. Over 200 members nationwide and internationally. Members may also speak at the Institute's book prize ceremonies and annual gala.

role: Meaningful Teens - Virtual ESL Tutor / Volunteer Intern
deadline: Rolling
duration: Flexible, ongoing during the school year, a few hours per week
overview:
Meaningful Teens is a nonprofit, founded in April 2020, that connects teen volunteers age 14 and older with free virtual tutoring and literacy programs for underserved communities, with all sessions held over Zoom. As of this update, open ongoing projects include Project Speak Together, one on one English conversation with 7 to 13 year old students in Ukraine on Saturdays at 9 to 9:45 AM PST; Project Dialogo, English fluency practice with students in Mexico on Sundays at 5 to 5:45 PM PST; Project Soile, an English speaking club for students age 14 and older in Kazakhstan on Sundays at 7 to 8 AM PST; Project Hope, one on one English tutoring with students in China on Saturdays at 4 to 5 PM and 8 to 9 PM PST; Project Udaan, English tutoring for underserved girls in India on Saturdays at 7:30 to 8:30 PM PST and 8 to 9 AM PST; Project 1234 Home Reading Helper, offline reading assistance for families in Oakland, California with no fixed hours; and Meaningful Debates, a student discussion forum currently on hold.

Project Omega Math, Project Omega Literacy, Project Kuunganisha, Project Diversidad, and the Finance First financial literacy program are currently full or closed and not accepting new volunteers. A new initiative, Project Warriors, supporting literacy and 529 college savings education for low income California families, is expected to launch in September and will run fully virtually with flexible hours. Volunteers earn certified community service hours for all projects.
requirements: Age 14 or older. Strong English communication skills. Consistent availability of a few hours per week for the chosen project. Open to volunteers internationally.
how_to_apply: Visit meaningfulteens.org/programs to review currently open projects. Complete the sign up Google Form linked on the Programs page, indicating your preferred project and availability. Contact the team at meaningfulteens.org/contact with questions.
ApplicationChecklist: ["Review open projects at meaningfulteens.org/programs","Confirm your preferred project is not full","Submit the sign up Google Form","Indicate preferred project and availability","Contact team with any questions"]

role: Building-U High School Virtual Business Internship
deadline: Rolling; internships run year-round, apply anytime via internships@building-U.com
duration: 3 months or more (flexible, year-round)
overview:
Building-U is a nonprofit organization that empowers high school students by placing them in real leadership and business operations roles within the organization. The fully virtual internship runs year-round with rolling admissions and is free to join.

Students join one of several specialized teams, each focused on solving real business problems for Building-U:
- Resource R and D: Research and write up the programs featured in Building-U's database
- Marketing: Develop and analyze Google Ad campaigns and Google Analytics data
- Blog Squad: Write articles and host discussions on land-based education and sustainability
- Coding Team: Learn web and database development (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, Node.js)
- Business and Development: Cultivate partnerships and develop funding strategies
- Social Media: Create and analyze digital content for Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, and TikTok
- Animation: Work on branding animations and storyboarding
- Data Privacy: Learn about data rights and responsibilities in partnership with Knowledgeflow

Students from the US, Canada, and around the world participate. The program is free, fully online, and builds teamwork, communication, and real-world business skills.

Compensation: Unpaid (free to participate; no stipend).
requirements:
• Currently enrolled in high school (grades 9–12)
• Reliable internet access and ability to participate in virtual team meetings
• Interest in business, marketing, technology, writing, or nonprofit operations
• No prior experience required - all skill levels welcome
• Time commitment: flexible, part-time (specific hours vary by team)

role: Teen Research and Education in Environmental Science (TREES)
deadline: No 2027 cycle announced; not offered in 2026
duration: 6 weeks
overview:
The Teen Research and Education in Environmental Science program, known as TREES, is a tuition free summer research and mentorship program run by the Center of Excellence in Environmental Toxicology at the University of Pennsylvania. Its goal is to introduce and inspire motivated high school students toward careers in environmental science and health through a mentored research experience, and students work one on one with a mentor on a project that they choose and design.

During the first two weeks students receive hands on instruction in basic laboratory skills, then spend the rest of the roughly six week program on an independent research project involving in depth library research, training in scientific methodology, hands on bench science, and where possible fieldwork. Toward the end of the summer students write a research report and present their projects at a public presentation. The program is open to students who have completed grade 9, 10, or 11 by the summer and have a GPA of at least 3.0 out of 4.0, requires parental consent, and expects students to commute to and from the Philadelphia campus, so it is aimed at Philadelphia area students. TREES will not be offered in Summer 2026 and no 2027 cycle has yet been announced.
requirements: Students must have completed grade 9, 10, or 11 by the summer and have a GPA of at least 3.0 out of 4.0. A strong interest in the environment and scientific research is expected. Parental consent is required and students must be able to commute to and from the Philadelphia campus, so the program is aimed at Philadelphia area students.
how_to_apply: When the cycle is open, applicants complete an online application form and email supplemental documents to ceet@pennmedicine.upenn.edu. Required documents are a current official transcript, two letters of recommendation with at least one from a math or science teacher, a resume of activities and honors, and PSAT or SAT score reports if available.
ApplicationChecklist: Complete online application form|Email official transcript to CEET|Two rec letters, 1 math/science|Resume, PSAT/SAT scores if any

deadline: 2026 course full; waitlist only
duration: 3 weeks
overview:
Pathways in World Politics is a three week pre-college immersion course offered by the University of Chicago Summer Session and taught by research faculty in the Department of Political Science. It introduces high school students to the scientific study of world politics and international relations, focusing on issues such as the creation of international organizations like the United Nations, the regulation of the global economy, and applied diplomacy. The course combines standard classroom material of lectures, readings, and discussion with hands on diplomacy simulations.

The course is writing, reading, and discussion intensive, with students writing at least three essays or papers, reading around 30 pages per night, and spending most class time in seminar style learning. It is open to students in grades 9 through 11 and runs as a residential Session 2 immersion with course dates of July 7 to July 23 and class meeting weekdays from 9am to 3pm. The cost is 9300 dollars with need based financial aid available, and applicants who apply after the course fills may still be considered from the waitlist as spots open.
requirements: Open to high school students in grades 9 through 11. No specific prerequisite beyond a strong interest in world politics and readiness for a reading and writing intensive seminar.
how_to_apply: Apply through the University of Chicago Summer Session pre-college application. A complete application includes a transcript, two short essays, one letter of recommendation, a writing sample, an application fee, and a submitted parent confirmation.
ApplicationChecklist: Apply via UChicago Summer Session|Transcript, 2 essays, writing sample|1 recommendation letter, app fee|Submit parent confirmation

overview: Alamo Academies is a nonprofit STEM career pathway program operated by the San Antonio Manufacturers Association (SAMA) in partnership with Alamo Colleges and more than 25 public, private, and charter school districts across the greater San Antonio, Texas area. Students apply as high school sophomores and, if selected, spend their junior and senior years taking college level courses at Alamo Colleges campuses, earning 30 or more college credits and industry certifications alongside their high school diploma. Career tracks include Aerospace, Advanced Technology and Manufacturing, Information Technology and Security, Health Professions, Diesel Technology, and Welding Technology. An essential component is a paid summer internship between the junior and senior years, 8 weeks full time at a SAMA partner company, where students earn an average of $3,000 for the summer. Partner employers include Boeing, Toyota, CPS Energy, H.E.B., StandardAero, Cox Manufacturing, and HOLT CAT. 94 percent of graduates pursue higher education, the armed forces, or high wage employment after graduation.
requirements: Must be a current high school sophomore at the time of application, attending a participating school in the greater San Antonio, Texas area. Interest in manufacturing, aerospace, IT and security, healthcare, diesel technology, or welding. Available for both the two year academic program and the required summer internship between junior and senior year. Authorized to work in the United States.
how_to_apply: Visit alamoacademies.com/apply-now to complete the online application. You must be a current high school sophomore to apply. Select an academy track and rank your choices. Provide your school, grade, address, and citizenship information. Contact Alamo Academies at (210) 485-0811 or your school's CTE counselor with questions.

role: Expanded Horizons College Access and Success Program
deadline: Rolling admissions accepted year round. Preference given to students who live or attend school on the Lower East Side. Limited slots available for seniors.
duration: Eight years, ninth grade through college graduation; after-school programming at least once a week during high school
overview: Expanded Horizons is Henry Street Settlement's free, eight-year college access and success program for high school students, designed to help students become college-ready, get admitted to a college that fits their interests and abilities, and graduate on time. Students who complete the program receive a four-year renewable scholarship from Henry Street. The program provides after-school programming with an emphasis on college and internship readiness along with identity and social justice education, a year-long SAT preparation course for 11th graders, individualized guidance through the college and financial aid process, academic coaching through high school and college, college tours, career exploration workshops, and help identifying internship and summer opportunities. The program is open to current 9th, 10th, and 11th graders, with a limited number of slots available for seniors. Preference is given to students who live or attend school on the Lower East Side of Manhattan, and these applications are reviewed first, with remaining slots filled by other NYC students. Students accepted into the program are expected to participate in all of its programming, since components like SAT prep are not offered as a standalone service.

deadline: Rolling through TST BOCES enrollment
duration: Two weeks
overview:
Launched in 2022, the CNF ATLAS Program (Accelerated Training for Labor Advancement in Semiconductors) is run by the Cornell NanoScale Science and Technology Facility (CNF) at Cornell University. It brings high school seniors into the CNF cleanroom for an in depth look at micro and nano fabrication and the semiconductor workforce.

Over about two weeks students complete a virtual Technology and Characterization at the Nanoscale short course, tour the cleanroom and the Duffield Hall support infrastructure, take part in a hands-on deconstruction of a plasma system with CNF staff, and fabricate a device on a silicon wafer using photolithography, deposition, and plasma etch. The program is unpaid and open only to seniors enrolled in the Tompkins Seneca Tioga (TST) BOCES New Visions Engineering program, so participation is arranged through that program rather than an individual application.
requirements: Open to high school seniors enrolled in the Tompkins Seneca Tioga (TST) BOCES New Visions Engineering program. Participation is arranged through that program rather than an individual application.
how_to_apply: Students take part through the TST BOCES New Visions Engineering program. Contact the Cornell NanoScale Facility or the New Visions Engineering instructor to learn more.
ApplicationChecklist: Enroll in TST BOCES New Visions Eng|High school senior|Arranged through your program|Interest in nanofabrication

deadline: 2026 course full; waitlist only
duration: 3 weeks
overview:
Pathways in Economics is a pre-college immersion program offered by the University of Chicago Summer Session and taught by full-time lecturers in the Department of Economics. The course introduces high school students to the approaches to economic research and experimentation that have made UChicago a world leader in the field, with classes covering macroeconomics, microeconomics, game theory, and field experiments that apply the tools and insights of economics in new ways.

Students apply what they hear in lectures during small group discussion sections led by current UChicago students, along with labs, problem sets, and group projects. The program is open to students in grades 9 through 11 who have completed pre-calculus and have a strong interest in using math to determine economic patterns. It runs as a residential Session 1 immersion with course dates of June 15 to July 2 and arrival and departure between June 13 and July 3, and the cost is 9300 dollars with need based financial aid available. Admission is selective, and applicants who apply after the course fills may still be considered from the waitlist as spots open.
requirements: Open to high school students in grades 9 through 11. Prerequisite of pre-calculus and a strong interest in using math to determine economic patterns.
how_to_apply: Apply through the University of Chicago Summer Session pre-college application. A complete application includes a transcript, two short essays, one letter of recommendation, a writing sample, an application fee, and a submitted parent confirmation.
ApplicationChecklist: Apply via UChicago Summer Session|Transcript, 2 essays, writing sample|1 recommendation letter, app fee|Submit parent confirmation
