company: Forage (formerly InsideSherpa; now part of EAB)
deadline: Rolling
duration: Self-paced (1-6 hours per module)
overview: Forage, formerly known as InsideSherpa and now part of EAB, is a free platform hosting virtual job simulations built by real employers including Pfizer, Johnson and Johnson, Citi, Goldman Sachs, and JPMorgan Chase. Students create a free account and complete self paced simulations, typically 1 to 6 hours each, then compare their work against model answers to earn a certificate from the sponsoring company. There is no application, interview, or fee, and the platform is generally used by high school students (about age 16 and up), undergraduates, and graduate students. Forage hosts over 250 job simulations from more than 90 employers across many industries, and more than 9 million students have signed up. Healthcare focused simulations include options such as Johnson and Johnson MedTech and Pfizer programs. Available simulations change over time, so students should search by career interest on theforage.com to see current healthcare offerings.
requirements: There are no formal eligibility requirements, cost, or application; the platform is generally used by high school students (about age 16 and up), undergraduates, and graduate students. A computer with reliable internet access is needed to complete simulation tasks and video content.
how_to_apply: Go to theforage.com and create a free account. Search or filter simulations by career interest, such as health care, and enroll in one. Complete the guided tasks using the provided videos and example answers, then receive a digital certificate from the sponsoring company.
ApplicationChecklist: Create free account at theforage.com|Search healthcare simulations|Complete tasks (1-6 hrs)|Earn certificate from employer

deadline: Rolling
duration: School year, about 6 hours per week
overview:
The Cornell Hydroponics Learning Labs are run by Cornell University Cooperative Extension NYC (CUCE-NYC) as part of its Hydroponics and STEM Education program. Founded by Professor Philson A. A. Warner in collaboration with CUCE-NYC and Food and Finance High School, the labs use industry standard hydroponic and aquaponic systems to teach soilless growing to high school students, teachers, and community members in New York City.

Working in the labs about six hours a week during the school year, interns learn to plant, transplant, harvest, and maintain water quality while growing leafy greens, herbs, and fruiting crops. The produce is used in classroom instruction, school events, and community food distributions. The program is hands on and open to New York City high school students, primarily those at the partner school where the labs are based, with participants recruited on a rolling basis.
requirements: Open to students at the high schools housed on the Park West Educational Campus in Manhattan. Up to two dozen students each year work about six hours per week in the labs and are paid through their schools.
how_to_apply: Ask your school at the Park West Educational Campus about its Cornell Hydroponics Learning Labs internship process. The public Cornell page does not list a separate application or deadline.
ApplicationChecklist: Attend a Park West campus school|Ask your school about openings|Commit about 6 hours per week|Follow your school application process

role: Social Science Summer Pre-College Research Experience
deadline: Registration opens spring 2027 (dates TBD)
duration: 3 weeks
overview:
The Social Science Summer Pre College Research Experience is a summer program run by the Henley Research Lab in Wilkinson College at Chapman University in Orange, California. It is designed to give high school students an edge when applying to college by immersing them in real social science research. Fellows work with faculty advisors and current Chapman students on a research project in political science and sociology, using the nationally known Chapman Survey of American Fears to explore their own research questions.

Throughout the program students build skills in data analysis, critical thinking, academic writing, research poster design, and public speaking, and they practice presenting their findings in a professional setting before receiving a certificate of completion. Sessions are held in person on weekdays from 9am to 12pm, and participants are expected to take part in all activities. The inaugural program ran in 2026, and registration for the summer 2027 session opens in spring 2027.
requirements: Participants must be entering grades 10 to 12 in the fall after the program, or be in the summer after high school graduation before starting college. A GPA of 3.5 or higher is suggested along with a genuine interest in social science research. Students bring a laptop running Windows 10 or 11 or macOS 10.15 or higher and purchase the SPSS grad pack for about 35 dollars.
how_to_apply: Registration is completed through the online Henley Social Science Research form on the program page. Registration for the summer 2027 program opens in spring 2027. For questions, contact program director Dr. Ann Gordon at agordon@chapman.edu.
ApplicationChecklist: Register via chapman.formstack.com|Bring Win 10/11 or macOS 10.15+ laptop|Buy SPSS grad pack, about $35|3.5+ GPA suggested to apply

company: Stanford Center for Artificial Intelligence in Medicine & Imaging (AIMI)
deadline: By invitation
duration: About 30 weeks
overview:
The Stanford AIMI Academic Year Research Internship is a mentored research program for high school students who have already completed a Stanford AIMI summer program. Over approximately thirty weeks from September to May, students work in small teams on projects at the intersection of artificial intelligence, health, and medicine, guided by Stanford mentors, students, and researchers. Work can span medical imaging, clinical decision support, responsible AI, bias and fairness, and healthcare operations, and students may analyze data, develop and evaluate AI models, conduct literature reviews, and contribute to scientific writing and presentations.

The program is virtual, with an optional in person capstone at Stanford during Stanford Health AI Week where students present a research poster and take part in AIMI programming. Eligible returning interns may continue through a Research Continuation Track that lets them build on prior work with greater independence toward an expanded study, abstract, poster, or manuscript.
requirements: Open by invitation to alumni of the Stanford AIMI Summer Research Internship and Summer Health AI Bootcamp who are enrolled in high school during the academic year. Admission is limited and based on available project and mentorship capacity.
how_to_apply: Eligible alumni of Stanford AIMI high school summer programs may be invited to participate. The official page does not publish a separate open application. Questions can be sent to aimi-hs-programs@stanford.edu.
ApplicationChecklist: Complete an AIMI summer program|Enroll in high school this year|Wait for invitation from AIMI|Email aimi-hs-programs@stanford.edu

deadline: Rolling. Join through your local Club; no fixed application deadline.
duration: Year round; local internship and job-shadow placements vary by Club.
grades: Ages 13-18 (Boys & Girls Club members)
overview: CareerLaunch is Boys & Girls Clubs of Americas career exploration and workforce readiness program for Club members ages 13 to 18. Through CareerLaunch, teens assess their interests and skills, explore career paths, and make educational decisions with support from Club staff and mentors. The program includes guest speakers, job shadowing, and hands-on activities and job training for teens. Local Clubs also connect teens to real-world work experiences, including internships, job shadows, and apprenticeships with community employer partners; availability of these placements varies by Club. The CareerLaunch curriculum itself is free to Club members. There are more than 5,400 Boys & Girls Club locations across the country, and CareerLaunch is part of BGCAs broader Life and Work Readiness programming for youth ages 6 through 18. Compensation varies: the CareerLaunch curriculum is free to participate in, while any local internship or job placement a teen is connected to may or may not be paid depending on the employer.
requirements: Current member of a Boys & Girls Club, ages 13 to 18. Participation in CareerLaunch curriculum activities at the local Club. Availability for part-time work or job shadowing if connected to a local placement. Parental or guardian permission required for participants under 18, per local Club policy.

overview: The Robotics and Autonomous Systems Laboratory at Vanderbilt University develops robots and intelligent computer systems that interact naturally with people, including virtual reality systems that sense human emotion and robots that assist individuals with autism, schizophrenia, dementia, and stroke recovery. Although primarily a graduate research lab, RASL welcomes members from many backgrounds including mechanical, electrical, and biomedical engineering, computer science, and psychology, and provides research experience to undergraduate and high school students.
requirements: The lab provides research experience to high school students and welcomes students from many technical backgrounds. The official page does not publish separate high school prerequisites, a schedule, or a guaranteed placement process.

deadline: Multiple cohorts run year-round (Fall, Winter, Spring, Summer); each cohort has its own application deadline set a few weeks before that cohort starts, so this is not a single-cycle deadline. Check veritasai.com/ai-fellowship for current cohort dates.
duration: 12-15 weeks
overview: Fully remote AI Fellowship for high school students (advanced middle schoolers may also apply), founded and run by Harvard graduates. Students work one on one with a mentor who is an AI practitioner or researcher, drawn from universities including Harvard, Stanford, Oxford, Columbia, Cornell, and Carnegie Mellon, to independently develop a novel AI project, an app, software, or research paper, in a field of their choice. The 12-15 week program includes 12 one on one mentor sessions across three phases: exploration and learning (weeks 1-4), ideation and data exploration (weeks 5-8), and execution (weeks 9-15), ending with a project presentation to peers. The Fellowship also includes publication and showcase support, helping students submit finished work to a research journal, competition, or presentation. Requires basic Python experience or completion of the Veritas AI Scholars program. The program costs $5,900, with need based financial aid able to cover up to 100 percent of the cost. Students who complete the program are eligible for 3 post-baccalaureate credit units from UC San Diego Extended Studies.
requirements: High school students, grades 9-12 (advanced middle school students with a coding background may also apply); basic Python programming experience or completion of the Veritas AI Scholars program is required.

Indicate financial aid need directly within the application if needed. 4. Optionally attend a live info session, bookable via the Calendly link on the site. 5. If admitted, pay the program fee, or your approved reduced fee, to confirm your seat and receive mentor onboarding details.
ApplicationChecklist: Review program at veritasai.com|Apply at bit.ly/VeritasAIApplication|Note financial aid need in application|Book info session via Calendly link|Pay program fee upon acceptance

overview:
The Diehl Lab in the Department of Psychological Sciences at Kansas State University studies why some individuals develop resilience after trauma while others develop conditions such as post traumatic stress disorder. The lab uses rodent models of fear and avoidance learning combined with circuit mapping to probe the neural basis of these behaviors.

Students learn behavioral paradigms and neuroscience methods such as single unit recordings and in vivo optogenetics, along with data interpretation and scientific literacy. The lab welcomes high school students as well as those between stages of enrollment, and interested students are encouraged to email the principal investigator to discuss available options. Research takes place on campus in Manhattan, Kansas.
requirements: High school students are welcome to ask about available research options. The lab does not publish additional high school prerequisites.
how_to_apply: Email Dr. Maria Diehl at mmdiehl@ksu.edu for more information about current opportunities.

deadline: Rolling
duration: Varies
overview:
The Needleman Lab at the Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences studies biological self organization, combining physics and cell biology to understand living systems through their mechanics, energetics, and organization. The group works on questions such as how cells build and control internal structures, using approaches that span quantitative microscopy, custom instrumentation, and computational analysis. The lab is based in the Northwest Lab building on the Cambridge campus.

High school students have contributed to past and current lab projects, working under the mentorship of a graduate student or postdoc on an independent research question tied to one of the lab's major themes. Recent student projects have involved microscopy, developing hardware for biophysical measurements, and image analysis. The position is in person in Cambridge, Massachusetts and is unpaid, and there is no formal online application. Prospective students should have a strong interest in biophysics and quantitative biology and are expected to reach out directly to discuss possible projects and time commitment.
requirements: Open to motivated high school students with a strong interest in biophysics and quantitative biology. Students work under the mentorship of a graduate student or postdoc on an independent project. Prospective students should reach out directly to discuss possible projects and time commitment.
how_to_apply: There is no formal online application. Email current lab members or Professor Dan Needleman to introduce yourself and discuss possible projects, as described on the lab Join Us page.
ApplicationChecklist: No formal online application|Email dan.needleman@gmail.com|Or contact a current lab member|Share research interests + resume

Two application essays under 400 words each, one letter of recommendation, an official transcript, and a 100 dollar nonrefundable application fee are required, waived for School District of Philadelphia students. overview:
The Computational Biomedicine Lab at the University of Houston runs a summer internship for motivated secondary and high school students, alongside undergraduates, in artificial intelligence and machine learning applied to real world biomedical and societal challenges. Interns join one or more ongoing research projects, help form research questions and testable hypotheses, design and implement experiments, and write and run code to test them while working directly with graduate students and researchers.

The internship runs six to twelve weeks between June and September on the University of Houston campus. Interns are expected to bring essential coding ability in Python or another language, strong problem solving and analytical skills, and a willingness to study background material and commit to full time, results oriented research.
requirements: Essential coding ability in Python or another programming language, strong problem solving and analytical skills, self motivation, and willingness to study background material and commit to full time results oriented research.

deadline: 2026 course full; waitlist only
duration: 3 weeks
overview:
A three week residential pre-college immersion course at the University of Chicago that introduces the science of human behavior. Students explore a breadth of topics including sensation and perception, emotion, memory, development, and psychological disorders through lectures, textbook and academic journal readings, discussions, field trips, and hands-on research lab demonstrations.

Working in small groups, students design and carry out their own experimental research project as the final assignment. The course meets Monday through Friday from 9 am to 3 pm during Session 2 in July, and students live on campus for the duration. It is offered only to high school students in the ninth through eleventh grades.
requirements: Open only to high school students in 9th, 10th, or 11th grade. A complete application includes a transcript, two short essays, a letter of recommendation, a writing sample, an application fee, and a submitted parent confirmation. Students seeking need-based financial aid must indicate this before submitting the application.
how_to_apply: Apply online through the University of Chicago Summer Session pre-college application. Submit the transcript, two short essays, letter of recommendation, writing sample, application fee, and parent confirmation. Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis and the course fills early, so applying soon is encouraged. Financial aid must be requested within the application.
ApplicationChecklist: Submit transcript and essays|Add rec letter and writing sample|Pay application fee online|Submit parent confirmation

overview:
Project SEED is an American Chemical Society program that places economically disadvantaged high school students into research laboratories for a paid summer experience. The Cincinnati Section of the ACS runs a local version that hosts students in University of Cincinnati chemistry research laboratories for eight weeks during the summer. The section typically invites about four students each year, each working under the direct supervision of a faculty or research mentor.

Selected students receive a generous educational stipend and gain hands on experience with real chemistry research in a university lab. The program is intended for students from families that meet the Project SEED economic eligibility guidelines who have completed at least one high school science course and one high school math course, generally current sophomores, juniors, or seniors. Students must be able to attend in person in Cincinnati, Ohio for the full eight week program. Interested students, teachers, and host chemists connect with the program coordinator to begin the application process.
requirements: For students from families that meet the Project SEED economic eligibility guidelines. Applicants should have completed at least one high school science course and one high school math course and be a current sophomore, junior, or senior. Students must be able to attend in person in Cincinnati, Ohio for the eight week summer program.
how_to_apply: To express interest or learn more, contact Anna Gudmundsdottir at Anna.Gudmundsdottir@uc.edu. Students apply through the Cincinnati Section Project SEED process.
ApplicationChecklist: Meet Project SEED income guidelines|Finish 1 HS science + 1 math course|Email Anna.Gudmundsdottir@uc.edu|Apply via Cincinnati Project SEED

role: University of Arizona Astronomy Camp: Advanced Teen Camp
company: University of Arizona Alumni Association (Steward Observatory)

overview:
The University of Arizona Astronomy Camp Advanced Teen Camp is a residential program held at the Mount Lemmon Observatory near Tucson, Arizona for students ages 14 to 19 who have completed Algebra II or Geometry. Over seven nights, campers use research grade telescopes, including the 61 inch Kuiper telescope, working alongside professional astronomers and university faculty. Each camper devises and completes an original research project that is presented to the whole group on the final night.

Tuition for the Advanced Camp is about 995 dollars and covers lodging, meals, local transportation in Tucson, and all materials, with partial need based scholarships available. Admission is competitive and spots fill quickly after applications open in late November, so early application is encouraged.
requirements: Ages 14 to 19; completed Algebra II or Geometry; able to attend the full residential session and complete an original research project. A competitive essay is required with the application.
how_to_apply: Apply through the Astronomy Camp website by submitting the application form, a personal essay, and one letter of recommendation. Applications open in late November and are reviewed on a rolling basis until the camp fills, so apply early. Submit a financial aid form if you are requesting a scholarship.

Using human behavioral experiments, eye tracking, electroencephalography, and functional MRI, the lab studies how people flexibly implement strategies and avoid processing distracting information. The lab recruits new members including high school students, and interested applicants are encouraged to contact lab members.
requirements: The lab recruits high school students who are interested in its research. High school applicants should contact a current lab member for information about possible openings. The detailed academic and technical qualifications on the page apply to the undergraduate research assistant position.

overview:
The Oono Lab in the Ecology, Evolution, and Marine Biology department at UC Santa Barbara studies how symbiotic associations evolve and shape plant and fungal communities. Projects include fungal endophyte community genetics, insect plant fungus relationships, pine associated endophytes, and legume rhizobia symbiosis.

Students gain experience in field collection, culturing, molecular methods, and bioinformatics while contributing to research on plant microbe interactions. The lab fosters a community of curious, life long learners and invites interested students to reach out about joining. Research takes place on campus in Santa Barbara, California.
requirements: High school students outside UCSB may inquire about volunteer projects, especially during summer. Openings are very rare because UCSB undergraduates are prioritized. Strong experience, unique skills, motivation, and the ability to work independently improve an applicant's chances.
how_to_apply: Email Professor Ryoko Oono at ryoko.oono@lifesci.ucsb.edu to ask about a possible volunteer project. Briefly explain your relevant experience, skills, research interests, and summer availability.

deadline: Rolling
duration: Flexible
overview:
The Chiel Lab at Case Western Reserve University studies the neural and biomechanical basis of adaptive behavior using the marine mollusk Aplysia californica. Research combines neurophysiology, mathematical modeling, computer simulation, and new techniques for measuring the biomechanics and neural control of feeding.

The lab sits at the intersection of biology, neuroscience, and biomedical engineering and mentors students interested in how nervous systems and bodies interact to produce behavior. Undergraduate and high school students are welcomed as volunteers, working directly with lab members after an initial email expressing their interest. Positions are based on campus in Cleveland, Ohio.
requirements: Interest in neuroscience, biology, or biomedical engineering and willingness to learn laboratory or computational methods. Availability depends on current lab openings.
how_to_apply: Email Professor Hillel Chiel at hjc@case.edu with an initial note about your interests and a one-page resume.
ApplicationChecklist: Email Dr. Chiel (hjc@case.edu)|State your interest in research|Attach a one-page resume|Ask about volunteer openings

deadline: Rolling
duration: Semester-long for the Normal Community High School partnership; other opportunities vary
overview:
The Vidal-Gadea Lab at Illinois State University investigates the genetic and neuronal basis of behavior using the nematode C. elegans alongside human muscle cell cultures. Research spans Duchenne muscular dystrophy, detection of the Earth's magnetic field, crustacean neurogenetics, and how organisms respond to extreme environments such as simulated Martian gravity.

Students join an active research group and learn techniques including behavioral assays, microscopy, molecular biology, optogenetics, and calcium imaging. The lab has a strong mentoring record, having trained more than 210 students over ten years with most going on to STEM careers. High school students who are interested can reach out to arrange a placement on campus in Normal, Illinois.
requirements: The lab welcomes driven high school students. Its Normal Community High School partnership offers semester-long graded internships with independent research projects. Other opportunities may be available by contacting the lab directly.
how_to_apply: Email Professor Andres Vidal-Gadea at avidal@ilstu.edu with a short note describing your interest in the lab and your availability. Placements are arranged directly with the lab.
ApplicationChecklist: Email Andres Vidal-Gadea|Note your interest in the lab|Attach a resume or CV|Share your availability

overview:
The Blekhman Lab at the University of Chicago, led by Professor Ran Blekhman, is a computational genomics group that studies the human microbiome. Researchers combine large scale sequencing data, machine learning, and multi omic integration to understand how microbial communities differ between people, interact with host genetics and biology, and shape human health and disease.

The lab is part of the Section of Genetic Medicine in the Biological Sciences Division and works closely with campus resources such as the Duchossois Family Institute and the Microbiome Center. It welcomes high school students who are curious about the computational analysis of genomic data. A quantitative background or programming experience is helpful, but motivated students who are eager to learn are also encouraged to reach out and take part in ongoing research.
requirements: Open to high school students interested in computational genomics and analysis of genomic data. A quantitative background or computer programming experience is helpful, but the lab also welcomes students who are eager to learn. Placement is by inquiry and depends on fit and availability.

overview: Empowerly's Startup Internship Program (SIP) connects high school students with real internship placements at startup companies. Empowerly is a private, fee-based college counseling company, and SIP is one of its paid specialized programs, listed as Inquire for Pricing separately from its core counseling packages. Students who enroll receive one-on-one resume and cover letter help plus interview preparation, then apply to open startup roles during a specific cohort period. Internships run in fall, spring, and summer cohorts and are not offered on a rolling basis, exact dates are set with an enrollment specialist. Program length ranges from two-week intensive sessions to multi-month engagements. Students have worked in a wide variety of technical (software engineering and coding) and business roles depending on what each partner startup needs. Internships can be remote or in-person depending on the hiring company, and pay varies by company, some offer stipends or hourly pay while others are unpaid but provide mentorship and networking. Placement with a startup is not guaranteed and depends on the student passing that company's interview.
requirements: Currently enrolled high school student (the official program page is also marketed to college students). No published GPA or test score requirement. Students must enroll in the paid Startup Internship Program before they can apply to startup listings, the exact program fee is available only by inquiry and is billed separately from Empowerly's core counseling packages. Students must complete Empowerly's resume and interview preparation process, then pass an interview with the hiring startup to be placed. Must be available during one of the fall, spring, or summer cohort windows, since internships are not offered on a rolling basis.

Enroll in the Startup Internship Program, a paid specialized program billed separately from Empowerly's core packages (fee available upon inquiry). 3. Work with your Empowerly counselor on your resume, cover letter, and interview preparation. 4. Apply to open startup internship listings during the current cohort's application window (fall, spring, or summer). 5. Interview directly with the hiring startup, placement is not guaranteed. 6. If selected, complete your remote or in-person internship for that cohort's term.

role: American Psychological Association (APA) Internal Internship Program (IIP) - Remote
deadline: Rolling, reviewed year round for spring, summer, fall, and winter terms
duration: Flexible, part-time or full-time hours negotiated with the hiring manager, across spring, summer, fall, and winter terms
overview: The APA Internal Internship Program (IIP) is a fully remote internship at the American Psychological Association, a nonprofit membership association of more than 157,000 members, housed within APA's Education Directorate as part of its Strategic Plan. Interns work in departments such as policy, research, communications, operations, publishing, and education, reporting to a supervisor for daily tasks. Two internship types are offered: a paid position and an unpaid academic-credit position, both requiring a cover letter, resume, and sometimes a writing sample. All APA internships are currently remote. Applicants must be eligible to work in the United States (verified via the Department of Homeland Security e-verify service) and must reside in a state where APA is registered as an employer. Remote interns may not work from Alaska, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Guam, Hawaii, Iowa, Louisiana, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, New York, North Dakota, Ohio, Puerto Rico, Rhode Island, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Washington, or Wyoming, and APA does not register as an employer in any foreign country, so international applicants are not considered. Students under 18 must submit an official District of Columbia work permit with their application. Applications are accepted on a rolling basis year-round through the APA Online Internship Application Portal.
requirements: Eligible to work in the United States, verified through the Department of Homeland Security e-verify service. Must reside in a U.S. state where APA is registered as an employer, excluding the states listed in the overview. Students under 18 must submit a D.C. work permit. Resume and cover letter required, plus a writing sample for some positions. Academic-credit interns must submit a letter from their academic institution on letterhead if selected. Applicants may apply to up to 3 internships, each requiring a separate application.
how_to_apply:
1. Visit apa.org/about/apa-jobs/internships and review current openings in the APA Online Internship Application Portal.
2. Applications are not accepted by email; combine your resume, cover letter, and writing sample into one document before uploading.
3. If under 18, arrange a D.C. work permit through your school.
4. You may apply to up to 3 positions, each with a separate application.
5. Only applicants selected for an interview will be contacted.
ApplicationChecklist: Confirm your state is eligible|Prepare resume, cover letter, writing sample|Get D.C. work permit if under 18|Submit via APA portal only|Apply to up to 3 positions

overview: Turning Green Internship Program is a year round, competitive remote internship for high school seniors, college, gap year, and graduate students interested in environmental and social justice work. role: Biomaterials and Regenerative Medicine Lab (Su Lab)
deadline: Rolling
duration: Flexible
overview:
The Biomaterials and Regenerative Medicine Lab (Su Lab) is a faculty research group led by Dr. Ni Su, an assistant professor of biomedical engineering in the Stanley and Karen Pigman College of Engineering at the University of Kentucky in Lexington. The lab harnesses the immune system and engineered biomaterials to advance regenerative medicine, building biomaterial platforms that modulate immune responses to promote healing and tissue regeneration and constructing humanized in vitro disease models for discovery and drug screening.

The lab recruits motivated trainees at every level, from postdocs and PhD candidates to undergraduates and high school students drawn from the local Math, Science and Technology Center (MSTC) program. High school members work on hands-on projects at the Healthy Kentucky Research Building over an extended commitment, often across two years, gaining experience in chemistry, biomedical engineering, biology, and immunology. There is no fixed application cycle and no cost to participate, and interested students reach out directly by email on a rolling basis.
requirements: The lab recruits motivated trainees at multiple levels and takes high school students from the local Math, Science and Technology Center program. Relevant interests include chemistry, biomedical engineering, biology, and immunology.
how_to_apply: Send an inquiry email to Dr. Ni Su at Ni.Su@uky.edu with your CV and a statement of research interest. There is no fixed application cycle and inquiries are considered on a rolling basis.

Students hear from practicing attorneys, federal agents, forensic scientists, and law school representatives, stay in university dorms two to a room, and can earn a Certificate of Achievement plus optional college credit through George Mason University. deadline: First come, first served until full
duration: 2 weeks
overview:
The Waksman Institute Summer Experience (WISE) is a two week, non-residential summer program held at the Waksman Institute on the Busch campus of Rutgers University in Piscataway, New Jersey. Run through the Waksman Student Scholars Program, it engages high school students in an authentic molecular biology and bioinformatics research project centered on the DNA sequence analysis of genes from the duckweed Landoltia punctata, a freshwater aquatic plant of interest to the scientific community.

Sessions meet Monday through Friday and combine daily seminars led by Rutgers faculty with hands-on laboratory work purifying and analyzing DNA fragments. Students use the same bioinformatics tools as practicing scientists and can submit vetted sequences for publication on GenBank, where each accepted sequence credits the student by name. The program is open to students who have completed a high school level biology course, carries a required non-refundable fee of 2200 dollars due about two weeks after the application is approved, and fills on a first come first served basis because laboratory space is limited.
requirements: Open to high school students who have completed a high school level biology course. Students must attend all seminar and laboratory sessions, which run Monday through Friday, and complete independent homework assignments.
how_to_apply: Apply online through the WISE application on the program website. Applications are accepted on a first come first serve basis until each session fills. A non-refundable program fee of 2200 dollars is due about two weeks after the application is approved.
ApplicationChecklist: Finish a high school biology course|Apply online at wssp.rutgers.edu|First come first served until full|Pay $2,200 fee after approval

overview:
The Waksman Student Scholars Program (WSSP), run by the Waksman Institute of Microbiology at Rutgers University, gives high school students and their teachers the chance to conduct an authentic molecular biology and bioinformatics research project and publish their findings. Students, teachers, and research scientists work together on a genuine research problem, sequencing and analyzing DNA from organisms such as duckweed and contributing real data to public databases like NCBI.

The program runs for a full academic year and begins each summer with an institute for teachers and one or two of their students, then expands back at each high school during the school year, where more students join in either a class or club setting. By actually doing science, students learn how research operates and are encouraged to continue their education and careers in a science discipline. Participation is through a student's own high school and teacher rather than an individual public application, so interested students should ask a science teacher whether their school takes part in WSSP or contact the program at wssp@waksman.rutgers.edu.
requirements: Open to high school students whose teacher and school participate in WSSP. The program begins with a summer institute for teachers and one or two students, then expands through a class or club at the participating high school.
how_to_apply: Students participate through their high school and teacher rather than through an individual public application. Ask a science teacher whether the school participates in WSSP or contact the program for information.
ApplicationChecklist: Attend a participating high school|Ask if your teacher joins WSSP|Join the class or club project|Email wssp@waksman.rutgers.edu

role: Summer High School Internship in Computational Biology
deadline: 2026 positions closed; 2027 dates not announced
duration: 8 weeks
overview:
The Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) offers an eight week in person summer high school internship in computational biology at its Richland, Washington campus. Interns work with mentors in the Earth and biological sciences directorate on projects supporting the computational biology group and PNNL's internal Predictive Phenomics Initiative, with computational biology and data science as the common theme across projects.

Every intern first completes a required two week morning bootcamp, meeting about 2.5 hours each day, where computational biologists teach Python, R, and biology to bring the whole cohort to a shared baseline. Interns then work on their research project and present their progress to mentors and lab leaders. No previous experience is required, though demonstrated interest in STEM is preferred, and interns who are 18 or older may be able to work directly in a laboratory. The internship pays a stipend, runs on an early or late summer start date, and PNNL posts separate high school application links, including an 18 and over track, on its careers portal.
requirements: Open to high school students. No previous experience is required, but demonstrated interest in STEM is preferred. All interns attend the required two-week morning computational biology bootcamp, and the full internship is in person at the PNNL Richland campus. Interns age 18 or older may be able to work directly in a laboratory depending on the project.
how_to_apply: PNNL posts high school internship openings on the official Predictive Phenomics program page and the PNNL careers portal, typically opening for the summer cohort in spring. There are separate application links for the general high school position and an 18 and over track that can work directly in a lab. Watch those pages for the next posting since summer 2026 positions have closed.

overview: Free, self-directed digital media literacy course for students developed by Poynter's MediaWise initiative and MediaWise Campus Correspondents. MediaWise launched in 2018 with a goal of reaching 1 million Gen Zers with fact-checking skills; it has since reached over 151 million people across 30 countries. The Digital Media Literacy 101 course teaches students how to identify misinformation, verify sources using lateral reading, and evaluate online information critically. The course uses video-based lessons and is available free on the MediaWise website at any time. Students can also explore the Teen Creator Network (formerly the Teen Fact-Checking Network), a separate competitive program in which selected middle and high school students produce fact-check and media literacy videos for MediaWise's social media channels. company: SUNY College of Environmental Science and Forestry
deadline: Rolling admission each semester
duration: Flexible, 45 hours of lab work per credit (1 to 3 credits)
overview:
The SUNY College of Environmental Science and Forestry Forest Ecology Lab, led by Dr. Ruth Yanai, offers curious and motivated high school students a free research opportunity through the ESF 296 course as part of the Multiple Element Limitation in Northern Hardwood Ecosystems (MELNHE) project. The lab studies how nitrogen, phosphorus, and calcium limit growth in northern hardwood forests, running nutrient manipulation experiments at the Bartlett and Hubbard Brook Experimental Forests and Jeffers Brook in New Hampshire alongside collaborators at Miami University and Cornell.

Working in Baker Laboratory on the Syracuse campus, students process soil samples, sort live roots into size classes, sort leaf litter by species, enter and check data, and build skills such as leaf identification and soil texture analysis. Each credit requires 45 hours of lab work, students register for 1 to 3 credits on a rolling basis through the ESF in the High School program, and they receive a letter grade. The experience is free and open to high school students, and students who are 18 or older can also learn to acid wash, grind, digest, and analyze samples using ICP. Motivated students may also pursue an independent project with Dr. Yanai.
requirements: Open to motivated high school students. Students register through the ESF in the High School program on a rolling basis and receive a letter grade. Each credit requires 45 hours of lab work, completed in person at Baker Laboratory on the SUNY ESF campus in Syracuse. Students 18 or older can also learn to acid wash, grind, digest, and analyze samples using ICP.
how_to_apply: Register through the ESF in the High School program to enroll in ESF 296 for 1 to 3 credits. Current or past ESF in the High School students can contact the lab and the team will handle registration. Reach the lab at 315-470-4917 or visit the program page for the syllabus and details.
ApplicationChecklist: Enroll via ESF in the High School|Register for ESF 296, 1 to 3 credits|Complete 45 lab hours per credit|Call the lab at 315-470-4917

overview:
The Manufacturing Innovation Network (MIN) Lab at the University of Wisconsin Madison offers high school students a self-paced data science experience using artificial intelligence and machine learning applied to real world manufacturing problems. The project runs in steps, beginning with statistical and AI or ML analysis of ultra precision machining data on sapphire, then progressing to hands-on work with real industrial problems and IoT devices, and finally to research engagement. Students may stop after completing the first step or continue further, and a certificate is issued upon completion.

Reading materials and project data are provided with a password after a student is enrolled, and the first step walks students through organizing data, performing analysis, and writing a brief report on their findings. The experience is remote and open to motivated high school students interested in data science, statistics, machine learning, and coding.

overview:
The Emma Bowen Foundation (EBF) has operated since 1989 as a diversity pipeline into the media, entertainment, and technology industries. Graduating high school seniors and current undergraduates are placed in multi-year paid internships at partner companies, gaining experience across three tracks: Content, covering journalism, production, and digital media; Business, covering finance, marketing, PR, and sales; and Innovation, covering computer science, data science, and software development. The fellowship begins the summer after high school and continues each summer through college graduation. Fellows also receive need-based academic scholarships, mentorship through the Link Mentoring Initiative, and access to the annual EBF Summer Conference. Each year EBF receives thousands of applications and selects about 150 fellows.

Compensation: Stipend. Pay varies by partner company and is set at or above local minimum wage; only students who are hired by a partner company are considered EBF Fellows for that summer.
requirements:
- Be a graduating high school senior or a current undergraduate
- Plan to attend or currently attend a 4-year accredited U.S. college or university
- Have a cumulative GPA of at least 3.0
- Be a U.S. citizen or permanent resident authorized to work without sponsorship
- Be interested in pursuing a career in media, entertainment, or technology
- Speak and write English fluently
- Be able to commit to a summer internship of at least 8 consecutive weeks, full-time
how_to_apply:
1. Visit emmabowenfoundation.org/apply and review the eligibility requirements
2. Create an account and complete the online application, including a resume and LinkedIn profile link
3. Apply as early as possible since placements fill on a rolling basis; the yearly cycle typically runs from fall through spring
4. Watch your email for EBF staff updates about potential placements and next steps
5. Note that only candidates hired by a partner company are considered EBF Fellows for that summer
6. Contact recruitment@emmabowenfoundation.org with questions
ApplicationChecklist: Review eligibility on EBF website|Create account and start application|Add resume and LinkedIn profile link|Check email for EBF placement updates|Confirm hire with a partner company

deadline: Discontinued (cancelled since 2024)
duration: Summer (approximately 1 week; residential at UW)
overview: The Black 14 Social Justice Summer Institute remains discontinued as of 2026. It was cancelled in May 2024 after Black 14 alumni withdrew participation when Wyoming state lawmakers eliminated funding for the University of Wyoming's Office of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion. That office was formally closed in July 2024 and replaced by a Vice Provost for Access and Engagement. In 2025, Wyoming House Bill 147 prohibited public universities from running programs that are exclusionary or preferential based on race or sex, which would further block a race restricted institute like this one from resuming in its original form even if funding were restored. No 2025 or 2026 revival has been announced. When it was active, the institute was a one week residential program specifically for Black high school students, rising juniors and seniors, at the University of Wyoming in Laramie. Students researched contemporary issues related to the Black community, explored diversity, equity, and inclusion principles, participated in leadership workshops, and connected with members of the original Black 14, the 14 Black UW football players dismissed from the team on October 17, 1969, for seeking permission to wear black armbands protesting racial injustice. The university issued an official apology in 2019. The program launched in 2022 with 6 participants and grew to 24 participants in 2023 before being cancelled in 2024.
requirements: Black high school student, rising junior or senior, grades 10 to 12; the program was specifically designed for Black students. Genuine interest in social justice, civil rights, equity, and community advocacy. Able to travel to and live on the University of Wyoming campus in Laramie, WY for the program duration. The program has been cancelled since 2024 and is further blocked by 2025 Wyoming state law restricting race based programming; contact the University of Wyoming Office of Access and Engagement to verify if it has resumed before applying.
how_to_apply: Visit uwyo.edu/acadaffairs/access-engagement for the University of Wyoming's Office of Access and Engagement, the successor to the former Office of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion. Email principles@uwyo.edu or call the Academic Affairs main line at (307) 766-4286 to ask about current status. The Black 14 Social Justice Summer Institute has not resumed since its 2024 cancellation and no phone line for the former DEI office remains active. Verify the program's status before assuming it will run again.
ApplicationChecklist: Program cancelled since 2024|No 2025 or 2026 revival found|Blocked by WY HB147 race law (2025)|Contact UW Access & Engagement office|Verify status before assuming it runs

overview: The Senate Page Program is a one week in-person experience during the NC Senate legislative session that lets students in grades 10 through 12 observe and assist with the legislative process. Pages work on the Senate floor and in committee meetings, deliver messages and documents, and help with clerical tasks. Each applicant must be sponsored by a sitting member of the NC Senate, and selection is described by the Senate as competitive, with final appointments made by the Senate President Pro Tempore based on Senator recommendations on a first come first served basis once the application window opens. Housing is not provided, so pages and their families must arrange their own lodging and transportation, and business attire is required. As of this check the 2026 session weeks are full, with 2027 availability to be posted in early 2027.
requirements: Applicants must be in grade 10, 11, or 12, be in good academic standing at their school, and secure sponsorship from a sitting member of the NC Senate, which in practice means contacting the Senator who represents their home district. role: Kaiser Permanente Summer Youth Employment Program (SYEP) High School Internship
deadline: No single fixed deadline is published. High school interns are recruited through schools and community partners on a rolling, site by site basis, with recruitment generally happening in spring for the summer cohort. Confirm current dates and site contacts at community.kp.org.
duration: 6 to 8 weeks in summer (June to August), part time at 20 hours per week
overview: The Kaiser Permanente Summer Youth Employment Program (SYEP), also known as KP LAUNCH (Learn About Unlimited New Careers in Healthcare), is a paid part time summer internship that introduces high school students to careers in health care. Interns work about 20 hours per week over 6 to 8 weeks between June and August in administrative, clerical, and health care support roles at Kaiser Permanente medical centers across Southern California and Hawaii. The program pairs work experience with weekly educational sessions that build career readiness and exposure to health care career paths. Interns are paid an hourly wage at the local minimum wage, so this is treated as a stipend. High school interns may participate only once, but are encouraged to apply for the college internship when eligible. Dependents of Kaiser Permanente employees and PMG physicians are not eligible.
requirements:
At least 16 years old (KP program materials cite ages 16 to 20). Priority is given to grades 11 and 12, and some sites accept grade 10.
Must reside in the community close to the medical center you apply to, in Southern California or Hawaii.
Must provide proof of eligibility to work in the United States.
Must be available part time, 20 hours per week, for the full summer program. Hours are typically Monday to Friday, 8am to 12pm, and vary by site.
Students under 18 must submit a valid work permit before the program starts.
All students must pass a drug screening. Students under 18 need a parent or guardian present.
Students 18 or older by June 1 must pass a standard background check.
Must complete Kaiser Permanente health screenings, which may include a TB test.
Cannot be a dependent of a Kaiser Permanente employee or PMG physician.
how_to_apply:
1. Visit community.kp.org and review the Summer Youth Employment Program page for current information and site contacts.
2. High school interns are recruited through schools and community partners, so connect with your school or a partner organization about the current cycle.
3. Prepare your application materials, which may include a resume, a personal statement or essay about overcoming an obstacle, and references. Requirements vary by site.
4. If you are under 18, obtain a valid work permit that covers the full program before it starts.
5. After selection, complete the health screenings and, if you are 18 or older, a background check arranged by the Kaiser Permanente facility.
ApplicationChecklist: Check you live near a KP medical center|Ask your school about SYEP recruiting|Submit the application and essay|Get a work permit if under 18|Pass the drug test and health screening

The organization was co-founded by Dave Eggers and Nínive Clements Calegari in 2002. The 826 Network serves close to 350,000 students ages 6 to 18 each year via 826 Digital and through the nine chapters.

IMPORTANT ACCURACY NOTE: Formal internship programs at 826 chapters are for college students (typically 18+), not high school students. Per 826 Boston internship descriptions, "Applicants must be over the age of 18." Per 826 National's own listing on Youth Engaged 4 Change, internships "require at least 15 hours per week for at least 12–16 weeks" and are unpaid. High school students at 826 chapters generally participate as volunteers or in writing programs, not as paid interns.

Exception: 826LA is participating in the Los Angeles County Bloomberg Arts Internship for Summer 2026, offering paid internship placements for 3 public high school students entering their junior or senior year near the Echo Park location (June 15–August 7, 2026; this is a third-party city program, not a standard 826 offering).

826 chapters are known for their whimsical storefronts (a pirate supply store at 826 Valencia, a superhero supply store at 826NYC, a spy store at 826CHI) and vibrant creative communities. Students interested in writing, publishing, and community literacy should contact their nearest chapter directly.

Compensation: Unpaid (volunteer) for high school participants at most chapters. 826LA offers a paid internship for 3 HS students via the Bloomberg Arts Internship (third-party LA County program, Summer 2026).

• Passion for writing, storytelling, or creative/expository writing education
• Interest in community literacy and youth writing programs

role: Bloomberg Arts Internship (BAI) - LA County Summer
company: Los Angeles County Department of Arts and Culture
deadline: Rolling (apply directly to worksites; positions close once filled)
duration: 8 weeks
overview: The Bloomberg Arts Internship (BAI) is a paid summer arts program for rising public high school seniors in Los Angeles County, run by the LA County Department of Arts and Culture in partnership with Bloomberg Philanthropies as part of the Creative Career Pathways for Youth initiative. Interns work three days a week at a local arts or cultural organization in roles such as marketing, production, social media, communications, and arts education, while attending two Program Days per week of workshops hosted at their designated Regional Hub. Interns complete 120 hours of paid work over the 8 week period plus a stipend for 90 percent participation in Program Days, alongside college readiness workshops, resume building, mentorship, and cultural field trips. Compensation includes hourly wages for the 120 hours of internship work, approximately 15 hours per week, plus a participation stipend for Program Days, with transportation and lunch provided on Program Days. Students who complete the summer program may continue into BAI School Year, an 8 month paid extension for high school seniors. Since 2012, the broader Bloomberg Arts Internship initiative has supported 2,250 plus internships at 250 plus cultural organizations across multiple cities.
requirements: Applicants must be rising public high school seniors, meaning current juniors entering 12th grade in fall 2026. For 2026, eligible applicants must live and attend a public high school in the San Fernando Valley, Metro Los Angeles, or South Los Angeles. Applicants must be legally authorized to work in the United States. Applicants cannot be a current or former employee, board member, trustee, officer, or director, or a relative of one, at the host organization they apply to. Applicants must be able to commit to 3 internship days per week plus 2 Program Days per week for the full 8 week summer program, and must provide a high school ID to verify school district and grade level.
how_to_apply: Visit lacountyarts.org/BAI-students to review the program overview, schedule, and eligibility. Click Explore Positions to browse the BAI Summer internship listings by city and organization. Pick one or more open positions matching your interests from the listings table. Apply directly to each participating worksite, following that organization's own instructions. If selected, provide your high school ID and proof of US work authorization. Once placed, attend your assigned Regional Hub Program Days alongside your worksite placement. Applications for 2026 BAI Summer are now closed; interested students should check the site in spring 2027 for the next cycle.

overview: The Zhou Lab at Vanderbilt University, led by Dr. Qiangjun Zhou, studies fundamental questions in cell biology and neuroscience by combining mechanistic and functional studies with advanced structural approaches. overview: Polygence is an online research mentorship program that matches high school students with PhD-level researchers and domain experts for one-on-one research projects. Students propose a research question and, with 1-on-1 mentor guidance, conduct structured independent research over their chosen timeline. The Core Program includes 10 one-hour sessions with a mentor, structured around 3 milestones and regular assignments; projects typically take 3–6 months. Students can produce a research paper, technical prototype, podcast, web application, blog post, or other format. Polygence mentors are PhD researchers and domain experts from top universities across 40+ fields including STEM, social sciences, and humanities.
